blocks.html: Dedication
To Michael, my friend, my brother, my father in this craft.

You carried Charlie across fifty years and placed him in my hands,
one story at a time. Without you he would have stayed a name on a book
cover. Because of you, I can hear his laugh.
This book is yours. I only kept what you gave me.
Your friend, brother and son,
Mohamed Ahmed

Foreword: Six years of
letters

In September 2020 I wrote to Michael Archer to thank him for The
Goodman CODEX. I had searched for it everywhere, and I told him it had
saved my world. He answered. Six years and thousands of messages later,
I know it was the best reply I ever received.

I never met Charles B. Goodman. Michael did, for eleven years, from a
July morning in 1973 at the Peavey office in Denver. Everything I know
of the man, his laugh, his silences, the way he called Michael "Dad", I
know because Michael wrote it down for me and kept writing, one email at
a time.

This book gathers those emails. It also gathers my side of the
conversation: my questions, my doubts, the books I read, the arguments
we had and the research I sent back. A teacher gives, and a student
answers. Both belong here.

How to read it. Every chapter is short and has one idea. Each opens with a line that names the idea, tells the story in Michael's words, says what Charlie meant, and ends with something you can try on your next chart. Read one chapter a day or read the whole book on a flight. The order is built so that each chapter prepares the next.

Michael once wrote to me, "If it wasn't for you all the stories of
Charlie would surely be lost." It is the kindest thing anyone has said
to me. It is also not true: it was Michael's memory that kept them alive
for fifty years. I only held the page.
The Ladder
This book climbs a ladder that Charlie himself described:

"Information is so plentiful as to be nearly worthless. Knowledge is when you combine information for something useful, practical. Wisdom is rarest. It is when knowledge is combined to achieve truth."

Each rung asks one question. Each opens with Charlie's stories as
Michael told them, then gives my side: my letters, my research and my
mistakes, with their dates, because my answers changed over six years
and the change is part of the lesson.

Rung Question What you will find 1 · Being Who was Charlie? The man behind the method 2 · Knowing How is truth learned? Examples over explanations; induction, deduction, abduction 3 · Seeing What is a market? People before prices; my market studies 4 · Deciding Is it a Setup? Goodman's tools: boxes, overlays, volume, propagation, 3-C 5 · Acting How do I manage the trade? Dagger, Nest, breakeven, Under, Over and the Line 6 · Measuring How much do I risk? Thirty souls, the Golden Ratio, risk of ruin 7 · Doing Right How do we treat each other? The oboe, the gift, the $50 investment 8 · Feeling Where do we trade from? Relaxed and excited at once 9 · Learning Who carries it on? Students, studies, the feedback loop 10 · The System How does it all move together? The trader as a dynamic system

The last rung shows the ladder was a circle all along. Every ending
starts a new move. Everything is a 1-2-3.
My Trading Explained (2023)

I wrote this walk-through for Michael in 2023: two real trades, on GBPCHF and NZDJPY, chart by chart, as I saw them. For this book every chart has been redrawn from real market data with the same structure; each caption names the data used.

In these few pages I explain how I trade every day, long or short.
First of all, I trade with defined risk, suited to my equity. My
psychology must be ready: a quiet place and a mind clear of everything
else, so I can be proactive with the market. I listen to music until the
wanted moment jumps in front of me. It usually takes ten to thirty
minutes to sync with the market; matcha or chamomile tea helps.

These are the pairs I use for short-term trading. Every week I plan
on the daily chart, then zoom in to find a low-risk trade. A trade that
does not fit the daily chart, I filter out: most of the time it is
unable to propagate.

• USD majors: GBPUSD, EURUSD, AUDUSD, NZDUSD, USDCHF, USDJPY, USDCAD

  • CHF crosses: NZDCHF, GBPCHF, CADCHF, AUDCHF, EURCHF

  • JPY crosses: CADJPY, AUDJPY, GBPJPY, NZDJPY, EURJPY, CHFJPY

  • EUR, GBP and AUD crosses: EURGBP, EURAUD, GBPAUD, EURNZD, GBPNZD, AUDNZD

  • CAD crosses: EURCAD, GBPCAD, AUDCAD, NZDCAD
Example 1

Figure: The 5-minute: a Jumbo sell-off, a rebound 1-2-3 and the
Return; selling should not repeat after a Jumbo at a critical point
(here the Return dips only 12 pips under the Jumbo low). Real data:
GBPCHF, 5-minute, 1–2 March 2022. (The original chart was GBPCHF,
5-minute, 3–6 March 2023; this one shows the same structure on the same
symbol, in the window the data covers.)

This is the 5-minute chart (GBPCHF in my original trade), as I watch
for significant changes.

Figure: The 1-hour: a large Outward up leg (A to B), then sellers in
control from B with no cancel count. Real data: GBPCHF, 1-hour, 21
February – 2 March 2022. (The original chart was GBPCHF, 1-hour, 3–6
March 2023; this one shows the same structure on the same symbol, in the
window the data covers.)

On the 1-hour chart, Outward, there is no cancel count. I link the
significant change to the big picture: is there any demand from 1-hour
traders? Is it promising demand? Let's look at the daily chart (redrawn
here on the 4-hour). It doesn't fit: day traders are selling.

Figure: The longer frame does not fit: the latest bars are bear bars.
Real data: GBPCHF, 4-hour (in place of the daily), 14 February – 2 March
2022. (The original chart was GBPCHF, daily, 3–6 March 2023; this one
shows the same structure on the same symbol, in the window the data
covers.)

On the 2-minute chart I look for the Dagger, the spark where buyers
must start their propagation.

This is how a bad trade looks: buyers and sellers are not in
consensus. The 1-hour is still selling; the 5-minute shows temporary
buying from profit-taking; the 2-minute is unable to break the upper
line of the Dagger, the line where sellers renew their selling to
protect the downtrend. Trades like this can break an inexperienced
trader's account. Goodman theory is based on PROPAGATION!

Figure: The 2-minute Dagger fails: a poke above the upper line, then
sellers renew and break the lower line, so the bad trade is avoided.
Real data: GBPCHF, 2-minute, 1–2 March 2022. (The original chart was
GBPCHF, 2-minute, 3–6 March 2023; this one shows the same structure on
the same symbol, in the window the data covers.)
Example 2

A flat Jumbo? Can it propagate? And the 6&6 is very small, with
volume too; it suggests something is cooking. The 1-hour chart is a
message for combination.

Figure: Example 2 on the 5-minute: a steady decline, the Jumbo, and a
small 6&6 box at the bottom with volume. Real data: GBPJPY,
5-minute, 28 February – 1 March 2022. (The original chart was NZDJPY,
5-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows the same structure.)

The 1-hour chart is near the Return Zone. Here we must think whether
buying will come in to propagate, but we should not expect it to follow
through to the Line, because the daily does not fit properly. Still,
demand coming from the Return Zone on the 1-hour is worth a try. The
daily chart (redrawn here on the 4-hour):

Figure: The 1-hour: a 1-2-3 up, then a decline back into the Return
Zone where the count began. Real data: GBPJPY, 1-hour, 21 February – 1
March 2022. (The original chart was NZDJPY, 1-hour, 3–7 March 2023; this
one shows the same structure.)

Figure: The longer frame shows bear bars, so it does not fit
properly. Real data: GBPJPY, 4-hour (in place of the daily), 14 February
– 1 March 2022. (The original chart was NZDJPY, daily, 3–7 March 2023;
this one shows the same structure.)
The 2-minute chart: a nested 6&6.

Figure: The 2-minute after the Jumbo: a first low, a bounce and a
lower low. Real data: GBPJPY, 2-minute, 1 March 2022. (The original
chart was NZDJPY, 2-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows the same
structure.)

Stop loss on the 2-minute chart. Buy, and watch how buyers propagate
on the 2-minute. There are different ways to buy; some buy at the break
of the trendline, but with the spread on a 2-minute chart there is not
much difference. Just buy anywhere near the bottom, and watch how the
buying comes in.

Figure: The nested 6&6: the upper and lower lines close in after
the Jumbo. Real data: GBPJPY, 2-minute, 1 March 2022. (The original
chart was NZDJPY, 2-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows the same
structure.)

Watch my entry, where buyers appear and start to propagate; their
first step is to break the line, as they did correctly. We need to set a
target where we judge whether buyers will continue or end their
momentum: 3-C. We need an idea of when to sell what we just bought. Then
follow the buyers' steps. If something goes wrong before they reach the
target, be ready to move to breakeven, or just run! They don't want to
propagate, and I must protect myself if they don't propagate
properly.

Figure: Buy near the bottom at the break of the upper line, with the
stop below the low on the 2-minute. Real data: GBPJPY, 2-minute, 1 March
One vote is a hint. Two v2022. (The original chart was NZDJPY, 2-minute,
3–7 March 2023; this one shows the same structure.)

Figure: The entry: the Jumbo bar (dotted), the box, and the target
set by the 3-C count. Real data: GBPJPY, 2-minute, 1 March 2022. (The
original chart was NZDJPY, 2-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows the
same structure.)

A small-time hash, and the reaction. A second-chance (SS) propagation
of the 1 is possible.

Figure: After the break buyers hold above the TP of the fall. Real
data: GBPJPY, 2-minute, 1 March 2022. (The original chart was NZDJPY,
2-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows the same structure.)

This behavior happens many, many times: after a 6&6 it propagates
into a second chance, as a PTS setup.

Figure: Propagation 1 completes and the reaction (SS) gives a second
chance. Real data: GBPJPY, 2-minute, 1–2 March 2022. (The original chart
was NZDJPY, 2-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows the same
structure.)
A knot: who is dominant? The buying matrix!

Figure: The count is projected again from point 2: a multiple 3-C
count. Real data: GBPJPY, 2-minute, 1–2 March 2022. (The original chart
was NZDJPY, 2-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows the same
structure.)

Buyers buy aggressively and re-enter the market with fresh orders as
volume develops.

Figure: A knot above the TP: who is dominant? The buying matrix. Real
data: GBPJPY, 2-minute, 1–2 March 2022. (The original chart was NZDJPY,
2-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows the same structure.)

Now buyers are aggressive enough to take all the offers that come in
at the TP. That is evidence of a healthy propagation. One way to predict
the near future is Complex–Flat: where the FPS is complex, expect
flat.

Figure: Buyers re-enter with fresh orders as volume develops. Real
data: GBPJPY, 2-minute, 1–2 March 2022. (The original chart was NZDJPY,
2-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows the same structure.)

It is amazing to watch the market through a propagation lens: 1-2-3 →
LARGER 1-2-3.

Figure: Complex, then flat: where the first count is complex, expect
the next part to be flat. Real data: GBPJPY, 2-minute, 1–2 March 2022.
(The original chart was NZDJPY, 2-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows
the same structure.)

Here one can book some profit from the propagation. It is an
intersection with the TP: sellers who believe the market will fall
further sell into this rally, which produces an abnormal reaction (SS).
The selling erases most of the buying gains, and the sellers'
intersection with the return point shows why it is important to take
some profit at the Under, as we did. Sellers who entered at the last
price now feel wrong, because the market no longer acts as before.
Sellers are slow now, and that adds to the buyers' propagation
power.

Figure: The larger picture: the TP of the leg from the Jumbo top to
the low is reached, as the 1-2-3 grows into a larger 1-2-3. Real data:
GBPJPY, 2-minute, 1–2 March 2022. (The original chart was NZDJPY,
2-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows the same structure.)

This is the sellers' last chance to add to their orders; otherwise
the bulls are in control, with a small double 6&6 nested in the box.
A buying sign, and buyers re-enter. It is a difficult trade to manage: I
take some profit, but I play for a larger one. Our stop has still not
been hit. Remember, this is a 2-minute development; traders usually go
Inward only for timing, but it is a chance to watch how Goodman theory
works at two minutes. Let's look at the 5-minute.

Figure: The larger 1-2-3 completes; price returns toward the zone
above the box line while the stop holds. Real data: GBPJPY, 2-minute,
1–2 March 2022. (The original chart was NZDJPY, 2-minute, 3–7 March
2023; this one shows the same structure.)
Back to the 2-minute.

Figure: The 5-minute view of the Jumbo, the base and the first rally.
Real data: GBPJPY, 5-minute, 1–2 March 2022. (The original chart was
NZDJPY, 5-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows the same
structure.)

Buyers enter with much more volume and much faster; the sellers are
tested and fail to push lower.

Figure: Back to the 2-minute: sellers test and fail to push lower.
Real data: GBPJPY, 2-minute, 1–2 March 2022. (The original chart was
NZDJPY, 2-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows the same
structure.)

The buying runs fast. That suggests sellers are few; otherwise buying
would be much slower than before!

Figure: Slow down, fast up: the latest buying runs much faster than
the fall. Real data: GBPJPY, 2-minute, 1–2 March 2022. (The original
chart was NZDJPY, 2-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows the same
structure.)

What is going on: buyers are trying to break the Dagger line to
complete the 1-2-3, on the 5-minute chart.

Figure: On the 5-minute, buyers press against the Dagger line to
complete the 1-2-3. Real data: GBPJPY, 5-minute, 1–2 March 2022. (The
original chart was NZDJPY, 5-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows the
same structure.)
A new count develops toward the Under of the green.

Figure: A new count develops from the new low, toward the Under of
the green. Real data: GBPJPY, 2-minute, 1–2 March 2022. (The original
chart was NZDJPY, 2-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows the same
structure.)
The fastest gain bar: a significant sign of bullishness.

Figure: The fastest gain bar: a significant sign of bullishness. Real
data: GBPJPY, 2-minute, 1–2 March 2022. (The original chart was NZDJPY,
2-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows the same structure.)

While the larger Outward overlay (1-hour) is still active, I re-enter
at the reversal bar. Someone may ask why I did not move my stop; it
looks very dangerous. Anyone who enters a trade must specify the maximum
risk. Some use a tight stop, others a wider one, but as a day trader I
use a very tight stop, simply because trades come every day, and if I
increase the risk, the R/R changes. Buyers re-enter at the reversal bar,
as I do, and propagate, showing clear power in a trading range.

Figure: Sellers sell above the rally and push below the box line; the
re-entry comes at the reversal bar. Real data: GBPJPY, 2-minute, 1–2
March 2022. (The original chart was NZDJPY, 2-minute, 3–7 March 2023;
this one shows the same structure.)

After my entry the market propagates and carries the trade overnight,
with a breakeven stop. It shows the ability to propagate and reaches the
target. The gap looks bearish, but sellers cannot develop it: there is
no follow-through.

Figure: After the re-entry buyers propagate and the stop moves to
breakeven; sellers get no follow-through. Real data: GBPJPY, 2-minute,
1–2 March 2022. (The original chart was NZDJPY, 2-minute, 3–7 March
2023; this one shows the same structure.)

The trade was amazing and reached the target exactly. Then sellers
entered and changed the trend for a while, until buyers stepped in.

Figure: Buyers carry the trade to the target, the high of the move;
then sellers enter. Real data: GBPJPY, 2-minute, 2–3 March 2022. (The
original chart was NZDJPY, 2-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows the
same structure.)
Here is where buyers set in again, as cancel evidence.
To summarize it all in two words: propagation lens.

Figure: Cancel: after the selling, buyers appear again as
re-propagation. Real data: GBPJPY, 5-minute, 1–3 March 2022. (The
original chart was NZDJPY, 5-minute, 3–7 March 2023; this one shows the
same structure.)

Rung 1 · Being: Who Was
Charlie?
Before the method, the man. Four short chapters on who Charlie was.
1. Twelve hours in the field
A mind trained by long, quiet work.

Charles B. Goodman was born on 23 October 1916 and grew up in Eads,
Colorado, where his family farmed corn and, Michael believes, rye
through the dust-bowl years. He told Michael he once planted three times
in a single season before a crop took hold. As a teenager he spent
twelve to fourteen hours a day in the field. "He had a lot of time to
think about life," Michael wrote.

To trade, he drove to the nearest brokerage house, in Garden City,
Kansas, beside the railroad tracks. In the 1930s that meant a long trip
on unkept dirt roads. "On the drive he had a lot of time to think about
the markets!"

He once told Michael that when the sun was hot and he felt he was
dying after ten hours of work, he did not think of pleasant things. He
thought of the world and of mankind, and asked why this and why that.
"It keeps the pain away and I keep working."
What it means. Charlie's method came from hours of slow attention, not from a screen. Depth comes from time spent with one question.
Try this. Pick one chart and sit with it for twenty minutes without trading. Write one question about what you see.
2. "Listen to every damn word"
How a 23-year-old was chosen.

Michael met Charlie in July 1973 at the Peavey & Company office
in Denver. Charlie had quit trading professionally. "I've made mine," he
said. But he loved the act of trading: studying charts and comparing the
markets with life.

The office was crowded with traders, and Charlie rarely spoke to new
ones. Whenever he talked over one of the extra-large charts he kept at
the office, people gathered around to catch a small morsel of his
wisdom. When the manager, Pete Rednor, saw Charlie sharing his secrets
with the new kid, he advised Michael: "Listen to every damn word he
says!"

Why Charlie chose Michael, Michael says he will never really
know.
What it means. The best lessons are often offered to the person who shows up and keeps showing up.
Try this. Find one person whose work you respect and ask one good question this week. Then listen.
3. The cat on the doorstep
The only time Michael saw him so sad.

Charlie was not fond of pets. When Michael once brought his dog to
the house, Charlie grew nervous, and the dog had to wait in the
bedroom.

Then one day he came home and found an injured stray cat on his
doorstep, bleeding after a fight. He wrapped it in a towel and took it
to the vet. The vet stitched it up and gave medicine, but would not keep
the cat. Charlie tried to give it away. No one wanted it. Reluctantly,
he kept it.

Soon they were good friends. The cat rode in Charlie's car between
Eads and Denver. After about a year the old cat fell sick and had to be
put down. The next day, when Charlie told Michael what had happened,
Michael saw him wipe tears from his eyes. "I think it was the only time
I saw him so sad."
What it means. The man who could read a market in silence was gentle with a hurt animal. Calm in the markets and kindness at home came from the same character.
Try this. After your next hard trade, do one small kind thing before you open another chart.

4. The house on Colfax and
Fillmore
A roll-top desk, a window, and a library of mimeographed secrets.

Charlie's Denver house stood on the corner of Colfax and Fillmore.
His huge roll-top desk faced a large window onto Fillmore Street, where
he usually kept two or three of his Corvairs parked. The other house, in
Eads, had three stories and about six thousand square feet. Michael
remembers it as beautifully furnished.

Charlie collected privately published system books and monographs
from the 1930s to the 1960s. Some were proper books and some were ten or
fifteen mimeographed pages, printed in runs of fifty to two hundred
copies. His favorite was a two-volume spiral-bound work on point and
figure charting in dark red faux-leather covers. He had paid $500 for it
in 1948 and reminded Michael more than once to be careful with it.

"Dad, these are yours when I go to the Spirit World," he told
Michael. After Charlie's death someone else drove from Denver to Eads
and took them. Michael still looks for that set online.
What it means. Charlie valued study. He paid $500 for two volumes of charts in 1948 and lent them like a treasure.
Try this. Choose one book or paper you have never finished and read ten pages today.

Introduction
to Goodman: Method, Probability and the Will of the Market (2022)

In this introduction I want to lay the ground before explaining
Goodman's theory itself. I start with the scientific method and with
probability, because a trader needs both. Then I show how human behavior
in markets formed, how it repeats, and how Goodman Wave Theory reads
that behavior bar by bar, swing by swing and Matrix by Matrix. I finish
with chance, balance, anticipation and managing the trade.

The Scientific Method and
the Trader

The kindness of scientists is a favor to every one of us. Because of
them, the path to success becomes easier. Their efforts make the
impossible possible.

A scientist has the ability to take a critical problem from
complexity to simplicity. He encourages people to learn and to do the
right thing at the right time.

The history of science is the story of the difference between dark
and light, between confusion and evidence. It is the story of
experiments and of observing phenomena. Scientists collect evidence by
day and in the dark of night, day after day and year after year. They
continue until the hypothesis is proven. Then the theory becomes clear
and easy to follow, and anyone can pick its fruit.
In brief, the scientific method has three steps:

1. Ask a research question and make a hypothesis.

2. Collect the evidence, either through an experiment or by observing the phenomena.

3. Analyze the results and conclude whether they confirm or disprove the hypothesis.

These three steps are the important ones. The path to success in
trading opens for the one who is willing to experiment and practice the
theory, as Mr. Goodman did with his many "bathtubs". Those who do not
want to exercise the theory fool themselves. They will never take a
single step on this path. There is no shortcut.

Our first job is to practice these steps. Without action there is no
result, and every action brings a result. Good or bad, the result helps
us. The result is the best teacher.
"I make it by my hand, I visualize it in my head, I collect the evidence, I test it, and never fail."

Probability: What Four
Trades Teach Us

In most experiments we can list the possible results before they
happen. Each trade has its possible outcomes:

Group of possibilities = {Win, Loss}; the probability of a Win =
1/2.

The group of possibilities means considering everything that can
happen before we experiment. Now let us repeat the experiment: we take
four trades.
Here I lean on James Bernoulli and his book The Art of Conjecturing:

"People create their own good or bad fortune by their conduct; for the most part, those who are wise leave the least possible to chance. We cannot know the future, but we can always in games of chance, and often in other affairs of life, know exactly how much more probable it is that something will happen in one way rather than another. Since these are the limits of our knowledge, we might at least reach them.

Everyone knows that when certainty is impossible, we should search for verisimilitude, [some degrees of which] are greater than others to infinity…"

"A player will enjoy a game more if he knows at each turn what his hope of winning or risk of losing is."

To summarize his theory, here are all the ways the wins can fall in
four trades:

• Four wins — 1 way: {W,W,W,W}

  • Three wins — 4 ways: {W,W,W,L}, {W,W,L,W}, {W,L,W,W}, {L,W,W,W}

  • Two wins — 6 ways: {W,W,L,L}, {W,L,W,L}, {W,L,L,W}, {L,W,W,L}, {L,W,L,W}, {L,L,W,W}

  • One win — 4 ways: {W,L,L,L}, {L,W,L,L}, {L,L,W,L}, {L,L,L,W}

  • No win — 1 way: {L,L,L,L}

In one experiment, a win has a probability of ½ and only one way to
appear. When we repeat the experiment four times, the wins have many
different ways to appear.

Four wins in a row has only one way to appear, {W,W,W,W}. It is the
least probable result in statistics, and yet it is what traders hope
for. Four losses in a row, {L,L,L,L}, also has only one way. It is just
as improbable, and yet it is what most traders fear.

One win out of four and three wins out of four both have four ways to
appear, so they are equal in probability. Only one result has the
highest probability, with six ways to appear: two wins in four
trades.

The benchmark for Goodman traders is 10-4-1. Statistics almost
confirm it as the high-probability approach, as the four-trade
experiment shows. So set the risk for ten trades, let the winners come
by themselves, and learn to trade the Line to increase the
probability.
Why a Trader Needs a Method

This short introduction is the base before I explain Goodman's
theory.

The theory is a process. It interprets the market's fluctuations as
phenomena, connects them with their original cause, and explains the
factors that govern them.

For the follower of this theory, it becomes the method he prefers to
apply in the market. The method solves the problems traders usually face
when they start to apply the theory. On this basis, I cannot imagine a
community of traders without a method to organize their activity in the
market.

Without any doubt, traders always want to choose the right method,
one that makes them more profitable and is easy to apply. But statistics
show that most traders lose and very few profit consistently. Do the
losers use a losing method? Or do they pick anything and call it a
method, without deep study?

The right method always has practical proof, or at least a true logic
behind it. That logic encourages the trader to use it, profit from it,
and trade with confidence because he accepts and believes it. A method
without confidence leaves room for doubt, and doubt always stops action.
No action, no success.

1.1
How Human Behavior Changed Through the History of Trading

Trading today plays a primary role in the economy. Human needs grow
as new and creative items come to market. Suppliers specialize in one
item and neglect the others, so that they can compete.

From this, people get what they need and the economy expands. Then
the economic cycle sets in: prosperity, crisis, depression. Crisis is
followed by depression, depression by prosperity, and prosperity by
crisis again.

Let me try to explain these cycles briefly. Any exchange happens in
one of two ways:

• Barter: exchanging goods directly.

  • A medium of exchange, such as money.
Barter

Barter is the oldest way: you simply exchange 10 kg of cotton for 10
kg of wheat. But the system cannot continue when someone wants fruit and
offers cotton, while the fruit seller does not want cotton.

In barter, buyer and seller exchange their benefits at the same time.
Both are satisfied in one transaction. Supply and demand stay roughly in
balance. People satisfy their own needs first, then exchange the
remaining cotton and fruit for other things they need, without inflation
in price.
Money

Human needs were the basis for exchange with money. With money, the
difficulty of exchanging fruit for cotton is no longer a problem. But
money brought its own difficulties, and as we moved from barter to
money, many things in economic history changed with it.

With money, both sides must agree on a market price. Each must first
sell to gain money before he can buy what he needs. So each plays the
role of seller to gain money, and then the role of buyer. That creates
the desire to collect money.

Buyers and sellers then found new ways to collect money. Instead of a
direct exchange, a buyer takes the item and pays later on credit.
Sellers also pay their suppliers on credit. Everyone seeks to collect
money instead of having a real desire for the items.

Money can also be saved and kept, while fruit is hard to keep for
long. And money can be borrowed and returned with interest.

So the relationship between production and consumption changed into
one between production and collecting money. The seller produces and
exchanges for money in order to collect more money. The buyer pays money
for items as an expense, not to re-produce or to satisfy needs.

This brought an imbalance between the quantity demanded and the
quantity supplied. Human behavior changed once money appeared. Instead
of exchanging for needs, one can now buy for a monopoly, to raise or to
push down the price, without any real desire for the item. The small
capital of small buyers and sellers is always the fish eaten by the
larger fish, whose purpose is to push small competitors out of the
market.
"Yellow coins and white money are able to destroy the will power."

In brief, this section shows how people in general behave and act:
they simply seek the maximum profit they can catch. This forms the basis
for anticipating the upcoming move.

1.2 The Repetition of Human
Behavior

Almost every time people find an opportunity to gain more money, they
take it together, in consensus. They continue until fear sets in with
the idea that this is the maximum profit the opportunity can give. Then
a decline follows.

On the contrary, when they cannot gain from the trade, they withdraw
gradually. Profit acts as a magnet and loss acts as a repellent. This
behavior repeats over and over.

Goodman's theory interprets the market. The applied theory
anticipates what will most likely happen, based on that interpretation,
and it provides a technique to manage the trade.
Interpreting One Bar
Suppose we have a daily bar. Our first job is to interpret it.

Figure: One bar read as a contest — the distance from Low to Close is
the buyers' gain, the distance from High to Close is the sellers' gain,
and volume expresses the will of buying.

Price rose because of an imbalance between demand and supply. In this
bar the buyers were looking for profit. At the close, measured from the
low of the bar, the buyers gained. Measured from the high to the close,
the sellers lost.

The distance from Low to Close (the buying side) is greater than the
distance from High to Close (the selling side). So the buyers gained
more in this bar. Volume shows the quantity of transactions the buyers
paid for. It expresses the will of buying.

Do not anticipate from one bar. Always look for a combination: an
Overlay. When buyers repeat their behavior and keep the will to buy for
more profit, from the first bar to many swings and Matrices, Propagation
starts. When you interpret bars, always remember that buyers and sellers
change their will power.

From Bars to Swings

From the low of bar 1 to the high of bar 7, the last high price, is

1. A few bars make a swing.

2. A few swings make a 1-2-3.

3. Each 1-2-3 is a Matrix.

4. A combination of Matrices is the lens of Goodman's theory.

1.3 Chances and the
Structure of the Matrix

Figure: Three Matrices with the same FPS and SS but different SPS —
the b-matrix covers the most boxes in the least time, so it has the
highest velocity.

In this figure the FPS and SS are the same in all three, but the SPS
has a different outcome in each. The difference between the a-, b- and
c-matrix lies in the number of boxes and, assuming some number of bars
for each SPS, in time:
a-matrix b-matrix c-matrix 2 boxes, 8 bars 3 boxes, 5 bars 1.5 boxes, 12 bars V = 2/8 = 0.25 V = 3/5 = 0.6 V = 1.5/12 = 0.125

What makes the b-matrix gain the most while the others gain less? Any
movement, even in price, can be interpreted with Newton's first law of
motion: there must be a cause (a net external force) for any change in
velocity, either in magnitude or in direction.

Velocity is V = Δx / Δt, where x is boxes and t is time. In words:
more boxes in less time means more velocity.

The greatest buying velocity is in the b-matrix. But what made the
buyers so aggressive there, compared with the other Matrices? There are
two possible answers, and they are mutually exclusive events: {chance, a
definite cause}.
Two Kinds of Chance
Let us discuss chance. There are two types:

• Absolute chance: an effect without any cause. Most philosophers do not accept this type. An example: someone throws a coin and, as an effect, gains $1,000,000.

  • Relative chance: an effect with a cause, but without repetition. A coin flip has only two possibilities, {Tails, Heads}. If someone keeps flipping, it cannot be that only Tails appear in every 100 throws. No cause makes the coin show only Tails. Sometimes Tails, sometimes Heads.

Another example: someone opens his door and suddenly finds his friend
in front of it. That is a chance with a cause, because his friend came
for some reason. But an event without repetition cannot become a rule.
We cannot say that every time he opens the door he will find his friend
there. It is a relative chance.
Relative Chance and the 3-C

Figure: In case A the SPS achieves the 3-C count; in case B it
suddenly stops short — a relative chance that we must observe.

At A the SPS achieves the 3-C count. At B, suddenly, the sellers
change their will or the buyers lose theirs. It is a relative chance.
Still, it is important to observe it when the SPS cannot achieve the
count, or when the SPS passes the over-count.
So what is the probability that buying passes the over-count?

Group = {buyers strong, buyers regular, buyers weak} = 3
possibilities. The probability = 1/3 = 33.3%.

If there is no absolute chance in the world, and none in the market,
can we build a Matrix combination that removes "buyers weak" from the
group? Then the group is {buyers strong, buyers regular}, and the
probability = 1/2 = 50%.

Everything — Propagation, Intersection, 3-C and the other advanced
Overlays — is an experiment that removes "buyers weak" from the group of
probabilities when we buy. Every Overlay is part of the whole; every
principle is part of the whole.

Our job is to find the path where the opposite will is weakest, as in
the b-matrix. That lets us gain more profit.

Remember: Goodman's theory is a holistic approach. Every concept is
part of the whole.
Balancing the Concepts

Balance aims to bring all the concepts into one system of measures
that can eliminate the unwanted probability events. It does this through
either a joint or a disjoint relationship, which I explain below. We can
induce that balance from our own experiments:

Probability of buying strong = (number of experiments showing strong
buying) / (total number of experiments, buying weak or strong).
Anticipating the Future

After explaining how to interpret the market, let us discuss how to
anticipate the future.

The future is something coming to us. It is the probability of a set
of relative chances. What future comes from flipping a coin? {T, H}. And
what future comes from trading Goodman?

• Buying strong — the effect is a winning trade.

  • Buying regular — the effect is at least breakeven.

  • Buyers weak — the effect is a losing trade.

1.3a Matrix Combination

Every Matrix describes a concept, and there are two types of
concept:

• General concept: understanding the facts as an abstraction that applies to many objects. Example: the buyers in the SPS meet the EP of the FPS.

  • Partial concept: understanding a fact that applies only to one definite object. Example: the SPS struggles as it meets the EP of the FPS — it is a Knot.

Figure: The general concept (the SPS meeting EP-FPS, where buyers
stand among the Goodman points) and the partial concept on a lower time
frame (buyers and sellers moving into a Knot).

Combined, these concepts reveal the condition of buyers and sellers:
strong or weak, even in a sideways market. The partial concept is always
part of the general concept. Between them there is a relationship:
1. Joint: the Knot develops into a Propagation that continues the SPS of the general concept. Here the combination reveals a strong buying picture.

Figure: Joint relationship — the lower-time-frame Knot resolves
upward and continues the SPS.
1. Disjoint: the lower time frames reveal that sellers are strong.

Figure: Disjoint relationship — the lower time frame breaks down at
the 50% level and shows sellers in control.

The relationship can also change, from joint to disjoint or from
disjoint to joint.

1.3b The Cause Behind Each
Swing

The market is a game of chances. The best way to show how price moves
is to imagine two players. One plays for the group on the buying side,
the other for the group on the selling side.

Each has limited capital, but neither knows the other's capital. This
is the unknown factor. On each turn, each player decides only the lot
size. Lot = expectation, and both have free will to choose it. The
remainder is the amount left over after each turn.

• Win rule: whoever puts in the larger lot (expectation) wins after the remainder.

  • Loss rule: whoever puts in the smaller lot (expectation) loses after the remainder.

  • Equal: equal lots leave no remainder, so no one wins or loses.

Turn Price What happens 1 Sideways No remainder. 2 Declines Sellers win by increasing their expectation from 100 to 500. Important selling: sellers strong, buyers weak. 3 Declines Sellers' expectation rises from 100 to 500 to 1,000, while buyers are controlled by fear. To win, buyers must absorb the remaining 1,000 shares. Buyers weak, sellers strong. 4 Advances For unknown reasons, the buyers' expectation jumps from 200 to 10,000. Important buying: they become greedy. Buyers strong, sellers weak.

The basic rule of the trend is to follow the remainder of the orders
coming from buyers and sellers. Watch for an unusual order, such as the
10,000 from the buying side. It shows that buyers have changed their
opinion by being willing to pay for large lots. It reveals their
expectation.

In brief: lots = volume = expectation. The greater the variance in
expectation, the more it points to important buying or selling.
1.4 Balance

Balance in the market means looking at both sellers and buyers to
find the remainder factor on the chart. Always keep in mind these
important changes in expectation: the players change their expectation
by being willing to offer or to pay. The same reading also applies to
the Goldilocks. Three cases, each with its selling and buying
mirror:

1. Important expectation in the FPS. Volume rises during the FPS, showing important selling (or buying), while the SS shows weak counter-activity with low expectation. Balance: most likely, sellers are willing to offer at a lower price (or buyers are willing to pay a higher price).

2. A regular Jumbo with a change in the FMX. The Jumbo has regular volume (no important expectation). The FMX shows a change in expectation compared with the Jumbo, while the BMX shows either low expectation from the counter side or high expectation at the reversal point. Balance: most likely, sellers will offer lower (or buyers will pay higher).

3. A regular Jumbo with exhaustion. The Jumbo has regular volume. The FMX changes from regular to very low expectation, and the BMX shows an even lower expectation — exhaustion at the high (or at the low). Balance: most likely, sellers will offer lower (or buyers will pay higher).
Bernoulli's Axioms

1. There is no place for conjectures in matters in which one may reach complete certainty.

2. It is not sufficient to weigh one or another argument. Instead we must bring together all arguments that we can come to know and that seem in any way to work toward a proof of the thing.

3. In matters that are uncertain and open to doubt, we should suspend our actions until we learn more. But if the occasion for action brooks no delay, then between two actions we should always choose the one that seems more appropriate, safer, more carefully considered, or more probable, even if neither action is such in a positive sense.
1.5 Anticipation

Anticipation is the process that follows the ability to interpret. It
sets the necessary conditions for deciding whether buying or selling is
advisable.
To anticipate that buyers are willing to pay higher, check:

1. The current Matrix relates to the larger and the smaller Matrix (general/partial concept) in a joint relationship.

2. Propagation is in the direction of the larger Matrix.

3. Important buying is confirmed.

4. The 3-C is cancelled.

5. There is an Overlay in the larger Matrix.

6. Expectation (volume) is joint in both Matrices.

7. Profit exceeds risk (the 3-C Setup target).

Figure: The buying checklist on a chart — joint with the larger
Matrix, Propagation, important buying, 3-C cancel, Propagation Overlay
and joint expectation in volume.
To anticipate that sellers are willing to offer lower, check the same list in mirror form:

1. The current Matrix relates to the larger and the smaller Matrix (general/partial concept) in a joint relationship.

2. Propagation is in the direction of the larger Matrix.

3. Important selling is confirmed.

4. The 3-C is cancelled.

5. There is an Overlay in the larger Matrix.

6. Expectation (volume) is joint in both Matrices.

7. Profit exceeds risk (the 3-C Setup target).

Figure: The selling checklist on a chart — the mirror of the buying
case, with important selling and a Propagation Overlay in the larger
Matrix.
1.6 Managing the Trade

The biggest problem traders face is taking a loss. When we deal with
chance, a loss or a win is just a chance. It takes a habit to stand firm
in front of a series of small losses. Do not hurry to increase the lot
size after a loss in the hope of profit. That action can destroy a
trading account immediately.
The secret of a winning attitude:

• After a series of losses: lower your expectation by decreasing the lot size, and review your feedback.

  • After a series of wins: raise your expectation by increasing the lot, slowly.

Professional traders use this attitude, and we can see it easily on
the chart. When buyers take profit from their expectation by riding the
FPS, they lower their expectation in the SS. Then they repeat: they
enter again at the EP of the SS, expecting to increase their profit.

Figure: Buyers ride the FPS with high expectation (volume), lower it
during the SS, then enter again at the EP of the SS.

The best way to apply Goodman's theory is through experiment and
investigation, and then to profit with confidence.

After which, the Probability of an assigned Chance, that is of some particular disposition of the Dice, becomes as proper a subject of Investigation as any other quantity or Ratio can be."

The Visionary
Trader: Connecting the Dots (2024)

In this short paper I describe one habit of mind I call being a
visionary trader. I explain the two steps behind it, and then I show it
on a real gold trade, from the daily Matrix Overlay down to a 5-minute
entry.
Know Yourself First

Every trader comes to recognize his emotional patterns, the good and
the bad. He learns what he needs to fix to trade better. A feedback loop
tells him, in detail, about his own process.

You do not need to be perfect. No one is perfect. You improve
gradually from your results. A deep understanding of "know yourself" is
the key to consistent success, and it is inside you.

The Visionary Habit: Two
Steps

One important and highly emotionally intelligent skill is to be a
visionary. It has two steps:

1. Collect facts from everywhere until they become very strong evidence that points to a way of winning.

2. Look for new facts that come to you and support that conclusion.

What do I see now? What do I want to see next? The two questions are
connected and fit together, like drawing a line through many dots.
Connect the dots! First you draw the line; then you watch forward for a
new dot, and draw it again.

Figure: The visionary habit as a loop — see now, expect next, then
redraw the line with each new dot.
