Market
Environments and the Propagation Lens (2025)

In this introduction I tell how I first met the market's swings and
how I found Goodman. Then I describe the four market environments, show
why popular strategies fail when the environment changes, and explain
why the Propagation lens sees what multi-timeframe indicators
cannot.
How I Came to Goodman

The first time I saw markets, I was struck by how the market moves in
a phenomenal structure. The chart always has upswings and downswings. At
the same time, it generates many smaller swings on a 1-minute chart.
When I look at higher time frames, like the monthly, I see many swings
too.

Then I asked: how are these waves generated by buy and sell orders? I
was trying to understand the noumenon behind them.

I started with a basic assumption. The secrets of these waves — how
they occur, why they occur, and the type of each swing — would be the
source code of the market.

As in any scientific field, we have more questions than real answers.
The more I dug, the more I found myself lost in the forest. What if it
is just a kind of chaos, random, without any real explanation behind
it?

I did much research, trying to catch any clue that reveals the market's secrets in a logical and predictive way. I found a book, The Spirals of Growth and Decay by Daniel T. Ferrera, one of the most expensive books I have seen. At the end of the book he writes: "Interesting article I recently found on Swing wave and the 50% rule". It was "Goodman's Swing Count System — by M. Duane Archer".
At that moment I felt I was finally in the right place.
The Market's Complexity
"The totality of things is almost certainly more complex than the human mind can imagine, much less understand."

It is very difficult to absorb facts because of the human ego. But
the market environment (ME) reflects the facts very directly, through
four primary clusters of directional movement (DM) and volatility
(V):

• High DM / Low V

  • High DM / High V

  • Low DM / Low V

  • Low DM / High V

The market is always in transition between these clusters, from Low
DM / Low V to High DM / High V.

Figure: The four market-environment clusters on a DM-versus-V grid —
steady trend, volatile trend, quiet range and violent chop.

Why Popular
Strategies Fail in Transition

Everyone is a genius in a bull market, especially in High DM / Low V.
But let us count the popular strategies that fail when there is a
transition.
1. High DM / Low V

Strategies that fail: mean reversion (RSI, Bollinger reversion),
counter-trend trading, stochastic reversals, grid trading.

The dominant psychology here is greed: people want to enter the
market as soon as possible. The result is very low volatility. The
failing strategies hope for a return to the average, but it never comes,
because the buying is aggressive.
2. High DM / High V

Strategies that fail: pullback trading, tight stop-loss trend
systems, moving-average reversion, fixed-size breakouts.

High volatility has a great effect on many strategies. A trader with
a tight stop finds himself out of the market while the market moves
higher without him. Violent volatility creates fear. Trend-following
strategies underestimate volatility and take losses without profit.
Unfortunately, the pullback strategy cannot deal with high volatility
and produces wrong signals.
3. Low DM / Low V

Strategies that fail: trend following (EMA cross, SuperTrend),
Donchian breakouts, momentum trading, MACD trend systems.

Never short a dull market. Traders gain false confidence because
volatility is low and the market seems so predictable. There are many
small breakouts but no follow-through. It is a trap.
4. Low DM / High V

Strategies that fail: all trend-following systems, breakouts (mostly
false), deep mean reversion (RSI below 20 or above 80), channel and
regression trading.

With low direction, traders do not know which direction to trust.
Overbought and oversold signals stop working. Traders see a "pattern"
that does not do what they expect. Trend followers lose in this play:
there is no trend, and fear creates high volatility.
"Systems fail because they were developed and optimised over ME skewed data sets, NOT because of any intrinsic deficiency in back-testing."

I see many traders make a nice profit for some months, then lose what
they gained, and they do not know why the strategy stopped working. The
market is more complex than traders imagine.
"There is a degree of indeterminacy and/or 'noise' in the market, making them much less than 100 percent predictable."

Matrices within
Matrices: the Propagation lens
"No matter how thin you slice it, there will always be two sides." — Spinoza

It is whole worlds inside whole worlds: Matrices within Matrices,
each at the same time part of larger Matrices. This is the Propagation
lens. Without it, we are walking on a dark and cloudy day; the lens is
the light in the dark. We cannot see what is going on in the market
unless we connect the Matrices in the best fit.

For example, a Setup is a Propagation with a breakaway from the
smaller Matrix that connects to the larger Matrix. This means a Setup is
a market-environment transition, far away from a system curve-fitted to
one ME cluster.

It works relatively well across all ME clusters. It does not depend
on the current ME; it anticipates and exploits the transition between
environments.

Figure: Multi-timeframe alignment is not the Propagation lens — only
the lens connects the smaller Matrix to the larger one and sees the
transition.

Multi-Timeframe Is
Not the Propagation Lens

Other systems fail even with multiple time frames, because they look
for:

1. Trend (moving averages)

2. Momentum

3. Signals

With multiple time frames there is a kind of alignment. But it does
not show the transition when the ME cluster changes. Such systems cannot
see the false spike signals of Low DM / High V. And they have no real
logic for connecting to the higher Matrix.
Multi-timeframe ≠ Propagation lens.

Examples of
Indicators Sending Wrong Signals
ME cluster: Low DM / High V

Indicators say Goodman Wave Theory says H4 shows big candles → "momentum building" H4 volatility spike = liquidation, not trend H1 breaks out of range → "trend starting" H1 breakout = noise expansion with Low DM RSI crosses above 50 → "bullish momentum" RSI is reacting to volatility, not direction MACD bullish cross → "confirmation" MACD cross = lag from volatility, no DM Volume spike → "institutional entry" Volume spike = stop run, normal in Low DM / High V They buy the breakout The ME shows no Propagation, no Matrix connection
ME cluster: Low DM / Low V

Indicators say Goodman Wave Theory says H1 shows higher highs → "trend forming" H1 movement is inside a tiny Matrix = compression M15 pullback to the EMA → "buy setup" M15 pullback has no energy → Low V RSI bounce from 40 → "trend continuation" RSI bounce = oscillation of chop, not trend MACD rising → "momentum" MACD rises because price drifts, not because DM increases Everything "aligns" across time frames No breakaway, no expansion, no transition They enter expecting a trend The ME shows Low DM, no Propagation into H4
ME cluster: High DM / High V (late trend)

Indicators say Goodman Wave Theory says H4 strong trend → "trend intact" H4 trend, but Propagation slowing (DM losing rhythm) H1 pullback → "buy the dip" The pullback = the trend weakening RSI oversold → "perfect entry" RSI oversold = end-phase liquidation MACD above zero → "bullish structure" MACD flattening → energy is leaving the Matrix Volume increasing → "trend support" High volume = climaxing, not continuation They enter expecting another upswing The trend is transitioning with no rhythm, not continuing
ME cluster: High DM / Low V

Indicators say Goodman Wave Theory says M15 breakout from a triangle → "entry" M15 triangle breakout = volatility behavior, no DM H1 candles expanding → "strength" H1 expansion = random volatility, unstructured RSI above 50 → "momentum forming" RSI rises because volatility rises, not direction MACD positive → "trend starting" MACD is fooled by price swings, not trend Two time frames align → "higher probability" Both time frames are stuck in High V / Low DM chaos They enter on the breakout No Propagation

Aligning multiple time frames with indicators does not show the real
psychological state. It distorts the vision. We must understand the
market through the market environment, the Propagation lens, the
Intersection and the 3-C.
"What do I see now, what do I want to see next." — Goodman

Rung 2 · Knowing: How Is
Truth Learned?
Charlie rarely explained. He showed, pointed and waited. Five chapters on why.

5. You have to find it on your
own
The night on the mountain pass.

Michael and Charlie were driving back from the dog track in Colorado
Springs, around midnight, over a mountain pass in Michael's new Datsun
280ZX turbo. Michael was worried the car would stall, as it had a couple
of times. Charlie spoke in the dark.

"In the late 1950s I met a young fellow who was learning to trade. He
looked like he had promise. I approached him and over several short
meetings I explained the basic 1-2-3, propagation, intersection, and so
on. He seemed a little interested but not particularly connected to it.
I lost track of him."

Several years later Charlie saw him at a brokerage house and asked
how his trading was going. The man was excited. "I've tried everything
under the sun! But I finally found something that works! The markets are
all 1-2-3 waves and they are interconnected, Charlie! I wait for one to
repeat then hop aboard!"

Charlie was stunned. It was exactly what he had told the man years
before.

"Dad, I realized he had to find it on his own. You couldn't tell it
to him, that was a waste of time. Finding something on your own means so
much more than having someone give it to you or explain it to you. This
is why each generation learns anew. Parents tell their kids things and
get ignored, but when the kids find it later on their own, it's
knowledge. That's why I teach you by example rather than a book
explanation like that thing you wrote!"

Michael later added a note for me: don't explain, use examples and
set an example. When it is time, a smart child will discover it alone.
"Patience, in the markets and in parenting."
What it means. Information can be handed over. Understanding has to be earned.
Try this. When you explain a setup to someone, show them two charts and ask what they notice before you say a word.

6. "What did you think I
meant?"
Why the best teacher in the room sounded vague.

Michael came to Charlie with a Western, rigid, scientific mind.
Charlie's teaching often frustrated him. Charlie would point to a chart
and say, "There's your return, Dad!" Michael would hurry home, go over
the charts, and try to work out where the Returns were. When he showed
his results, Charlie sometimes looked a little puzzled: "What did you
think I meant?"

There was a reason, which Michael learned later. In the late 1950s
Charlie had tried to teach a student in a Western, step-by-step
delineation style and failed miserably. A few years later he found out
the student had worked out much of it by himself.

"I just use examples because in the end you have to figure it out for
yourself; you have to find how it fits in your own mind."

Michael also notes that Charlie had something of an Eastern
mentality, which you can see in the Goodmanisms. His left brain and
right brain communicated extremely well.
What it means. A hint you work out yourself stays in your head longer than an answer you are given.
Try this. Next time you are stuck, write down what you think the chart is hinting at, in one sentence, before you ask anyone.
7. Christmas Day
The phone call that fixed a mother's anger.

It happened in Charlie's first or second year with Michael, around
1973 or 1974. On Christmas Day at about one o'clock Michael drove his
parents to Aunt Ruth's family party, a crowded house of twenty-five to
thirty relatives. His mother said she would call at four-thirty or five
to be picked up.

Michael went home, where it was quiet. The phone rang. It was
Charlie. "Hey, Dad, what are you doing?" He had an idea and wanted to
look at charts. Michael had a couple of hours before his mother would
call, so he drove across town to Charlie's Denver house.

He lost track of time completely. When he looked at his watch it was
past six. His mother had called and called, and was not happy. She
thought he had gone out raising hell with his friend Mark.

Charlie told him to go home and then call, and let him talk to his
mother. Michael's mother liked Charlie much more than Mark, who just
looked like trouble to her. Michael did what he was told. His mother was
very angry. He called Charlie. "I don't know what he said to her but
when she got off the phone she was fine and not at all upset with
me!"
What it means. Charlie took responsibility for the hours he had taken from his student. He solved the problem rather than letting Michael carry it alone.
Try this. When you ask someone for their time, make sure they leave better off than they came.
8. Think like Charlie
An accident outside the window.

Michael was at Charlie's Denver house one summer afternoon, looking
at charts. Charlie's roll-top desk stood by the window, and the vents
were open. They heard a crash and the crunch of metal. Someone had hit
one of Charlie's Corvairs, probably coming out of the alley across
Fillmore Street. The driver stopped, looked, and drove off before they
got outside.

The damage was a dented fender and a broken taillight. "What a jerk
for running off!" Michael said.

Charlie said: "Maybe. But it is possible the accident slowed him down
a few seconds and kept him from being killed by someone running a red
light on Colfax. We really don't know why such things happen and how
they play out eventually."
"Only Charlie thought like that!!!" Michael wrote.
What it means. A single event looks like an ending only because we cut the story short. Charlie always asked what else could be connected to it.
Try this. After your next stop-out, write down one way the loss may be protecting you from something worse.

9. Draw the box before the
setup forms
Abduction, Charlie's way.

In July 2025 Michael found an old chart and walked me through one of Charlie's methods. "After a Setup builds, the most likely consequent for an Under is the TP of the Jumbo." So Charlie would ask a question while the Jumbo was still forming: If a Setup formed here, at the current EP of the Jumbo, how large would it need to be, in vertical value and with its tail on the Molokai, for an Under count to land at the TP of the Jumbo? Then he drew a light box on the chart for that Setup space.

Figure: While the Jumbo is still forming, a light box marks the space
a Setup would need for an Under count to land at the Jumbo's TP.

As the Setup began to form, he could then predict how it would build.
Michael is careful: it did not always happen exactly like that, but it
made him extremely proactive with the charts. "I can tell you, many of
them work. Charlie drew a light LayDown and I watched over days and
weeks with my jaw hanging, like he controlled the market." He stresses
the time frame was weeks, not minutes or hours.

Michael collected eleven of these examples for an article on
Abduction in Goodman Wave Theory. That article and the Playbook, he
said, would be his final word on Goodman. "Everything else is for
you."
What it means. A forecast made before the pattern forms is a hypothesis you can test. A reaction made after is only a story.
Try this. On your next Jumbo Swing, draw the box where a Setup would have to form. Put the date on it. Check it a week later.
The Logic of Goodman (2022)

In this paper I want to show why traders need logic, and what I call
the logic of Goodman. Logic corrects the mindset. It moves us from
doubt, fear and hope toward clear decisions in a market of probability.
I then show how this logic reads the language of the bar chart, and how
indications on the chart tell the story of buyers and sellers.
Introduction

Traders want to win, because winning serves their goals. They work
for those goals and prepare in every way they can. But many of them lose
the road. They jump from one method to another, or they never fully
understand what their goals really require.

In the end they doubt their ability to succeed. Some become fearful,
others live on the hope of success. Either way, logic can show them the
real road.
Logic corrects the mindset

Logic guides traders toward success. It is a guide for anyone who
holds wrong premises that block success. It is also a guide for anyone
who carries a wrong belief that came from a bad conclusion or a fallacy
in reasoning.

Logic corrects our mindset, and through that correction it leads us
to success and to our goals. This is why the logic of Goodman matters so
much.

A mindset is a perspective: a set of assumptions through which we
look at an environment and make decisions. When the mindset is
corrected, the trader makes the right decisions. He goes long, goes
short, or sits on his hands.
Discipline is a lifestyle

Success comes if, and only if, one has the desire to correct the
mindset based on logic. It is not an easy process. In the end it depends
on your desire, and you must be consistent until you reach discipline in
trading.

Discipline has its own problem. Once a trader becomes successful, his
intensity drops slowly over the years. Then the door of failure can open
again. So we must refresh and correct the mindset by logic, again and
again. Yes, it is a lifestyle.
The aim of the mindset: truth

What is the aim of a mindset? It is to be the perspective that
explains the truth. It should not only be a valid argument; it should be
true in reality.

Knowing simply brings what already exists in the world into our
minds. Knowledge makes impressions of things that exist as facts for
us.
Two kinds of impression

An impression can be only an imagination. The chart represents buyers
and sellers, but that picture of buyers and sellers does not lead to a
decision to act. It is an abstract image of a fact that exists.

An impression can also lead to a decision to act with confidence. For
example, the chart shows a qualified Goldilocks Setup. That impression
is followed by a decision to act.

Whatever is followed by action, we are responsible for its result. In
the market there are only two actions, buy and sell, and both are under
our control. The market will never force you to enter a trade.

An impression held with confidence does not necessarily meet the
truth about the market's outcome. Sometimes confidence represents
certainty about the result. Sometimes it represents only the probability
of what is about to happen.

Four logical
cases: certainty, doubt and probability

Let us assume someone expects the Eurxxx pair to move up, and he
invites us to enter the trade. As I said, our actions are our
responsibility.

Logically, his assumption can only be true, if the move up happens,
or false, if it does not. Our job is to judge whether the assumption is
true or false. So we ask: can this person anticipate the market
correctly 100% of the time? There are four possible answers.

1. We decide yes, he can. Here we have certainty.

2. We decide no, he is 100% wrong. Here we also have certainty.

3. We decide he has a 50% chance to be right or wrong. Here we have doubt.

4. We decide he is possibly right that Eurxxx will move up, but because of uncertainty we hold delusions about a possible move down. Here we have only a probability that the outcome occurs, with some degree of delusion that it will not.

Figure: Four ways to judge a call: two kinds of certainty, doubt, and
probability with some delusion. Only the fourth meets the reality of the
market.

So confidence can come with certainty, or with probability, even with
some degree of delusion. Yes, this is the reality of the market.

Can a man be 100% certain about the outcome of the market? That man
does not exist yet.

When a
trader cannot decide: two kinds of ignorance

What about the trader who still cannot decide and cannot act? He has
ignorance, a lack of knowledge. Simply put, he has no impression to act
on. Here we must define the type of ignorance.

• Simple ignorance. He has no knowledge of the market. Or he has knowledge but cannot turn it into a probability of the outcome. This ignorance leaves no impression to act on. Such a trader should learn the logic of Goodman.

  • Complex ignorance. He can read the probability of the market, but he wants certainty about the outcome. He wants to trade with no delusions. This ignorance does not meet the reality of the market. It is complex because he feels he knows a great deal, and still he refuses to act without certainty. Some courage is needed!

By now it should be clear why it is necessary to learn the logic of
Goodman. It gives the trader the ability to decide in an environment of
probability.

1.1 Learning the logic of
Goodman

We learn logic so that we can stand in reality, between probability
and delusion, when we decide. The urgency to learn comes from one fact:
we cannot control what the market does. That inability exists for simple
reasons:

• The market does not exist by our choice.

  • Price will not move up or down because of our bias.

  • The market exists, but we cannot force it to move as we wish.

The market continues even if you feel frozen and cannot act. It
continues even if it locks you into a losing position and you panic. It
simply keeps moving normally.

Logic is our primary tool for becoming aware of this nature, which we
can do nothing about. It produces self-awareness: of the market's
existence, and of the limits of our own ability. So we must be
selective. We must be picky.
The process of deciding

When we face an unknown outcome, we stand between probability and
delusion. This is the furthest the learning curve can take us. There is
no certainty.

So we must move from the known to the unknown. The known are our
axioms, such as "everything is a 1-2-3". The mind takes this knowledge
and uses it to find the unknowns, and those unknowns are our probability
decisions. It is like algebra, where we use what we know to find X.

In practice, the trader looks at a timeframe where price is moving.
He knows the problem: will price move to SS or to SPS? Will this action
propagate? He asks several such questions to define the type of
unknown.

Then his mind starts to work on how to solve that type. He organizes
his knowledge and moves Outward or Inward. He tries to reach a logical
reason for the probable outcome. If, after this process, he can conclude
with confidence where the next direction will be, SPS or SS, the problem
is solved.
The five steps
The process has five steps:

1. Know the problem: the unknown.

2. Know the type of unknown. Many traders face the unknown but do not know what type of unknown it is.

3. Choose the tool. By organizing the type of unknown, we know what we need to use: the Overlay.

4. Build the evidence. Using what is known, the Overlay, we construct logical evidence for what is required to solve the unknown.

5. Meet the conclusion. We match the conclusion of our logical construction with the unknown.

Figure: The five steps of a Goodman decision, from knowing the
unknown to the conclusion; experienced traders start at step 3.

Experienced traders, with some intuition, start directly at steps 3,
4 and 5. For steps 1 and 2 they carry a kind of axiom.

So the logic of Goodman is a set of research on how to construct an
argument that solves the unknown. It defines the unknown and its type,
and it justifies the tools we use. It gives a reasonable ground for
balancing the Overlay to trigger the trade.

1.2 The language of the bar
chart

Understanding the language of the bar chart helps us receive the
chart's message. Every chart is unique and carries a different
message.

Logic connects directly with understanding that message. The chart is
only a language, spoken through its basic mediator: the bar, with its
OPEN, CLOSE, HIGH and LOW.

Figure: GBPUSD, 15-minute, 17–21 February 2022. Every bar is built
from four words, Open, High, Low and Close, and together they record
what buyers and sellers did.

Logic aims to use at least these four data points to understand the
message clearly. They play a very important role. They bring us the
activity of all buyers and sellers within a specific time.

The chart does for us something we cannot do. It shows buyers and
sellers from everywhere in the world, and the bar carries their meaning.
This is very deep. We could never watch every buyer and seller in the
real world at every moment. So instead of trying to find out who is
buying and who is selling, we take what the chart already gives us.

The chart registers all buyer and seller activity. Let me
summarize:
"The existence of any bar*, exist a meaning about buyers-sellers."
That meaning gives us an indication of the trend.

*In many cases a single bar does not reveal any significant
indication.
What is an indication?

When someone knocks on the door, the mind translates the sound into
an indication: someone is standing in front of the door. That indication
may be significant for us.

So an indication works like this. We know that something exists, a
sound or a bar. Then, through a process of the mind, it indicates that
something else exists: buyers or sellers.
A significant indication

In the next chart, a significant indication shows the existence of
buyers. Why is it significant? Look at the older bars. Here buyers
increase their energy for the first time. Did such buying energy exist
before? No. That is what makes the indication significant: the existence
of buyers with new energy.

Figure: EURUSD, 15-minute, 23–25 February 2022. After a long fall,
buyers show new energy at the low on heavy volume: a significant
indication of the future trend.
A significant indication works as evidence of the future trend.
Three types of indication

The existence of buyers or sellers can carry different meanings. That
is the type of indication. Each type may be significant or
non-significant. There are three types:

• Logical indication

  • Character indication

  • Structure indication

Figure: The three types of indication (logical, character and
structure), and the three kinds of structure: congruence, implicitly and
intrinsic.
Logical indication

A logical indication is one that has an inherence in existence that
comes from buyers and sellers.

Figure: EURUSD, 5-minute, 24 February 2022. At A sellers increase
their orders; at B they renew them in the same way.

At bar A the indication shows inherence to sellers: sellers increase
their orders. At bar B sellers renew their orders, just as at A. Both A
and B carry an inherence.
The six types of inherence

There are six types of inherence. Each applies to both buyers and
sellers. They can show their existence on the chart at any time by:

1. Entering orders into the market.

2. Leaving (exiting), that is, stopping to enter orders into the market.

Figure: GBPUSD, 5-minute, 24 February 2022. Buyers show their
existence by entering at the low; sellers show theirs by leaving.

1. Increasing their orders to the market.

2. Decreasing their orders to the market.

Figure: GBPUSD, 15-minute, 21–24 February 2022. Buyers increase, then
decrease; sellers increase, then increase more than last time.

1. Deciding when they want to enter orders into the market.

2. Deciding why they want to enter orders into the market.

Figure: Buyers and sellers show their existence by when and why they
enter: after the fall, sellers increase at its TP, and again when buyers
rally back to the same price level. Real data: AUDSGD, daily, 19 May
2017 – 13 April 2018. (Same symbol, timeframe and dates as the original
chart. The daily data file has no volume, so the volume panel is
empty.)

Inherences 1 to 4 also belong to the Character indication. Inherences
5 and 6 work as the Structure indication. In many cases they play
together.

Figure: Buyers increase at the TP of the rise, then sellers increase
at the TP of the fall, a sign of strong character and of a future trend.
Real data: AUDSGD, daily, 20 November 2017 – 23 March 2018. (Same
symbol, timeframe and dates as the original chart. The daily data file
has no volume, so the volume panel is empty.)

Here buyers increased with the character of greed. Then sellers
increased, which caused fear in buyers to enter more orders. That is a
significant indication of a future trend.
Character indication

A character indication is one whose inherence comes from the nature
of buyers and sellers: greed and fear.

"All through time, people have basically acted and re-acted the same way in the market as a result of: greed, fear, ignorance, and hope-that is why the numerical formations and patterns recur on a constant basis." — Jesse Livermore

Crying, for example, is an indication that someone feels pain. As I
said, character has four essential inherences. Extracting indications
from natural inherence is studied by different schools of psychology and
philosophy, and the door is always open to further study.

Entering and
exiting: the responsibility of choice
The first two inherences are:

1. They show their existence on the chart by entering orders into the market at any time.

2. They show their existence on the chart by leaving (exiting) the market at any time.

Both show that traders have a choice: to enter or to exit. They carry
full responsibility for those choices. Their choices run in the market,
where some win and others lose.

All choices move toward their destinations, sometimes under
predestination. In the end, our control is limited to the choice.
Everything returns to choices.

A good trade returns good profit. But that is not always the case: a
bad trade returns a loss. Because there are consequences, participants
want to make rational choices. Yet humans act non-rationally, through
their beliefs.

Figure: EURNZD, 5-minute, 24 February 2022. Buyers enter at the top
and many become losers; sellers enter at the bottom. Every move is the
result of a choice.

Increasing and
decreasing: hope and anxiety
The next two inherences are:

1. They show their existence on the chart by increasing orders to the market at any time.

2. They show their existence on the chart by decreasing orders to the market at any time.

When traders realize they are against the trend, they enter a state
of hope that they can still make some profit. That hope increases their
orders. Then anxiety from the losing side makes them decrease their
orders.

Figure: EURNZD, 5-minute, 24 February 2022. Above the line buyers
keep adding orders in hope, while sellers who sold the bottom grow
anxious.
Structure indication

A structure indication is one that has an element of inherence coming
from buyers and sellers. Arranging that element according to the
inherences gives buyers and sellers a structure.

The element:
greed, fear, excitement and sadness

The element comes from human nature. Humans have greed and fear. These forces give us the intensity to act on an opportunity: the when. They also give us the power to cause action: the why. But they follow one rule: NO EXTREME EXAGGERATIONS NOR NEGLIGENCE.

Extremes show the maximum desire of buyers and sellers. The reaction
to this process is excitement. In this game, the opposite of excitement
is sadness.

Humans are excited when they can hit their goal, and sad when they
cannot. This is the element.

Arranging the element by
inherence
The element is arranged according to the last two inherences:

1. They show their existence on the chart by deciding when they want to enter orders into the market at any time.

2. They show their existence on the chart by deciding why they want to enter orders into the market at any time.

Figure: One leg of buying told by the Goodman points: the BP where
buyers start, the 50% Tipping Point, and the EP where greed runs
out.

The Goodman points tell the
story
The Goodman points use this element.

• BP (Beginning Point) is the point that answers when buyers enter orders. Greed drives the force. Buyers act by entering orders to absorb the offers. This reflects courage to take the opportunity, and the excitement of hitting the goal.

  • Along the way, buyers do not allow any significant movement in the opposite direction (25%).

  • Greed* then rises to the extreme: EXTREME EXAGGERATIONS. There the EP (Ending Point) occurs. Buyers have exceeded their ability and cannot continue.
Every Goodman point tells its own story.

*There is nothing wrong with greed. Here it is simply a force to act,
different from its usual meaning.
Types of arrangement

There are three types of arrangement: Congruence, Implicitly and
Intrinsic.
Congruence

Congruence is an indication that matches the most recent story. It
gives a mirror story, or a high-performance mirror story.

Figure: GBPUSD, 5-minute, 1–2 March 2022. Buyers drive A to B,
correct to C near the TP, then drive C to D with the same force: CD is a
congruent mirror of AB.

The story starts at A, when buyers decide to enter orders. Their
maximum comes when they reach point B. They then correct their positions
at mid-way (TP). Then buyers enter again at C and move to D.

The story CD is a mirror of AB; it is congruent with it. This
arrangement shows that buyers in CD have the same force as in AB. The
trend is up, for simple reasons:

• Buyers can recover their strength from the correction.

  • Even after the correction, buyers can move with performance similar to their past extremes.
"Everything is a 1-2-3."
Implicitly

Implicitly is an indication that is implied by the most recent story.
It gives a sign of something about to occur.

Figure: Sellers lose force at C and again at E while buyers re-enter;
two implicit signs put the downtrend in doubt and point to the buying
force at F. Real data: USDCZK, daily, 27 October 2021 – 4 March 2022.
(Same symbol, timeframe and dates as the original chart. The daily data
file has no volume, so the volume panel is empty.)

Buyers enter at A with the force to carry price to the maximum at B,
mid-way of A (TP).

• First implicitly: sellers at C lose their force. This shows either that buyers are too strong or that sellers are too weak. The downtrend is now in doubt.

  • Buyers enter again at C and show their force, but there is no improvement in their performance at D.

  • Second implicitly: sellers lose intensity. Buyers enter at E with a logical indication, shown in the circle around the closing of the bars. T is a character indication.

Because the selling force loses its intensity at E (the second
implicitly), a buying force at F is implied. CD then forms a congruence,
a high-performance mirror story, with EF.

At the first implicitly at C, a buying force is also implied, which
makes DE an inside move within BC.

Implicitly works as a diagnostic tool to check the intensity of the
trend. Several implicit signs are needed to make the message clear.
Intrinsic

Intrinsic is a compound of Congruence and Implicitly. It is the most
important type of structure indication. It appears naturally as part of
a consequence of indications. The consequence cannot be separated from
the indications.

Figure: A 1-2-3 nested inside a larger 1-2-3, where A and B are
congruent and C is implicit; price returns toward the TP of the larger
(1). Real data: GBPSGD, daily, 17 June 2021 – 4 March 2022. (Same
symbol, timeframe and dates as the original chart. The daily data file
has no volume, so the volume panel is empty.)

Every 1-2-3 sits inside a larger 1-2-3. This happens naturally in the
market, and it cannot be separated. The market will follow this
structure.

Because it is intrinsic, it lets us predict: after a 1-2-3, watch for
a return to the same level as the TP of the larger (1).

Here A and B are congruent. C is implicit, and there the intrinsic
structure shows the way. The price itself does not matter. Price will
follow and move to the Goodman points: the bounces X, Y and Z.
"The markets can only go up or down." — Charles B. Goodman

The Problem of
Imperfect Induction (2022)

Imperfect induction is the kind of reasoning we use every day on the
chart. We see a cause work a few times and we expect it to work again.
In this short paper I want to show the problems it faces, as they appear
to me.

Problem 1: no proof of a
definite cause

The aim of induction is to establish a general law: every natural
phenomenon has a cause. But without proof of a definite cause, it is
probable that some other cause is at work. It is even probable that the
phenomenon happens without any cause.

When we consider these possibilities, it follows that a cause does
not necessarily produce its effect.

Figure: Old highs that looked like a definite cause for sellers to
stop the rise; each one failed, and price closed above them. Real data:
AUDJPY, 1-hour, 28 February – 4 March 2022. (The original chart was
AUDJPY, 1-hour, 4–21 July 2022; this one shows the same structure on the
same symbol, in the window the data covers.)

Problem 2: will the
cause work in the future?

The purpose of induction is to generalize the cause so that it works
in the future. It claims that every time the cause happens, it will
produce the phenomenon. So we must prove that the cause will keep
working in the future.

Figure: A high that stopped buyers this time; a cause observed in the
past does not promise the same effect in the future. Real data: AUDJPY,
1-hour, 21–24 February 2022. (The original chart was AUDJPY, 1-hour, 30
August – 16 September 2022; this one shows the same structure on the
same symbol, in the window the data covers.)

Figure: The two gaps of imperfect induction: an unproven cause, and
an unproven future.

What this means for the
trader

Every time one makes an imperfect induction, one will face these
problems. One must realize this, above all when something important
rests on it.

(2022)

In this AUDCAD study, I want to show how the Propagation lens makes
the chart clearer and easier to grasp. I also want to show how we can
add probability causes, one by one, until we can make an inductive
inference about a reversal.

The Jumbo and the first
positive cause

Figure: The Jumbo: YY, the X-Propagation from EP-Jumbo, and the
LS-Propagation back to the same low at A (here A holds 0.6 pip above the

(The original chart was AUDCAD, 4-hour, 15 June – 24 August 2022; this

The Jumbo is a flat decline. It is a propagation, a concentration of
selling force that comes from seeking profit in a downtrend. The selling
at YY is the fastest swing in the Jumbo.

An external purchasing force enters the market at EP-Jumbo. It tries
to concentrate its buying power by X-propagating the swings, from a
1-2-3 to a larger 1-2-3. The buying force appears able to concentrate,
taking all the shares until it meets selling at YY.

This gives probability positive cause #1. It suggests that the new external force from the X-propagation may change the velocity (speed and direction). When the next selling swing comes with contraction, that confirms it, and we add the cause. A positive cause raises the chance that the trend velocity changes from down to up.

Note that the LS (last downswing) Propagation comes with contraction
rather than expansion.

Abduction (2023)

Here are some ideas and applications I do not want to lose. As the
old saying goes: write it, or lose it!

The chart is like a cat: a different world, a different spirit, a
different mind. The trader needs to connect with that cat by watching it
and caring about it, until he knows what the cat most likely does in
different conditions.
The story behind the chart

I first read this on GBPCHF, daily chart; here the same structure is
shown on real EURUSD 1-hour data.

Figure: Price coiling under a falling line from the excess point and

Then the market coiled between a test point and an excess point, unable

My logical inference about these points is that they are obstacles.
Neither buyers nor sellers can breach them. Watch the volume in March:
many buyers and many sellers struggling at the test point. In April,
buyers could not breach the obstacle of the excess point line. A strong
bear bar changed the equation: a lack of buying momentum. This produced

This alternation from a buying swing to a selling swing and back to a

The core of every movement is a 1-2-3, or part of one. The current

Can buyers breach the
obstacle?

If buyers can propagate within the excess and test levels, how far
can price go? Is there the strength to breach the excess obstacle? The
logical answer is that we are in doubt. Buyers can withdraw from the
market when they struggle with the excess obstacle.

We need an Overlay that confirms the strength of buying when it faces

matrices

Goodman is based on matrices, not on time. It is very clear that
larger matrices produce buying. At the SS intersection with the TP,
buying wins. When the sellers' EP of the FPS meets the TP, the sellers

A smaller propagation sits within a larger propagation, and the trend

By trading on the side of propagation, we let the probability of

Deduction, Induction and
Abduction

Looking back at these papers, I see that I was really studying one
question: how does a trader reason from what he sees to what he does?
Logic gives three answers, and I used all three.

Deduction goes from a rule to a result. If everything is a 1-2-3, and I see a 1-2 Setup, then the 3 must follow. The conclusion is certain, but only as certain as the rule. My four logical combinations work this way: when the daily and the 1-hour agree on an extreme, the signal follows from the rule.

Induction goes from many cases to a rule. In the AUDCAD study I added probability positive causes, #1, #2 and #3, until I could infer a reversal. This is how we learn the market. But, as I wrote in "The Problem of Imperfect Induction," the rule is never proven. Another cause may be at work, and the cause that worked yesterday may fail tomorrow. Induction gives probability, not certainty.

Abduction goes from a surprising result to the best explanation. GBPCHF coiled between a test point and an excess point. Why? My best story was obstacles that neither buyers nor sellers could breach. Abduction is how we read the story behind the chart, the way one learns what a cat usually does. It is only plausible, so it must be tested by an Overlay before we act.

Figure: The three kinds of reasoning use the same parts, rule, case
and result, in three different directions.

A good trader moves between all three. Abduction proposes the story.
Deduction tells him what must happen if the story is right. Induction,
case after case, tells him how often it really does. Goodman's words fit
here: the deeper you dig, the fewer possibilities you derive. Each kind
of reasoning removes some possibilities, and what remains is the
trade.

Rung 3 · Seeing: What Is a
Market?
Charlie did not predict prices. He read people. Five chapters from the Peavey and Bache years.
10. Silver and soybeans
Why two unrelated markets moved together.

Michael was watching the markets at Peavey and noticed that every
time silver rallied or fell sharply, soybeans followed. He worked out a
wild theory to explain why and told Charlie, a little proud of his
analysis.

Charlie smiled and chuckled. "No, Dad. The silver and soybean pits
are squeezed right next to each other. When there is a lot of action in
silver, it spills over to the soybean traders. They see action and want
some of their own. It is just human psychology!"

Figure: The silver and soybean pits stood side by side, so action in
silver spilled over to the soybean traders.

And then the line Michael has repeated for fifty years: "You can
figure the dogs, but you can't figure the human race!"
What it means. Before you build a theory about why two markets are linked, ask who is standing next to whom.
Try this. When two charts move together, write down one human explanation before you write a mathematical one.

11. The man with inside
information
A contrary-opinion story from 1974 or 1975.

A man in a very nice suit, carrying a fancy briefcase, walked into
the Peavey office one morning. The manager, Pete Rednor, asked if he
could help. "I have inside information on tomorrow's soybean report. It
is going to be very bullish. I want to purchase ten contracts!"

Everyone listened. Pete explained that inside information on crop
reports is all but impossible to get, but of course he would take the
business. The man filled out an account card and wrote a check for the
margin. "I am told soybeans will be up the limit at least two days. I
will come back tomorrow before the market opens to hear the report."

After he left, Michael, Pete, Charlie and two other traders looked at
the soybean chart. Nobody saw anything bullish or bearish. They asked
Charlie what he thought.

"If this guy who knows nothing about the market has this information,
then it is all over the street and prices are only up a few cents today.
Everyone who wants to buy will buy today. I predict a strong close,
maybe a slightly strong opening, then a sharp sell-off. The report will
be bullish but already in the market."

He suggested watching the point and figure chart at the opening, on
the minimum tick, for a sell signal. The market closed a little strong.
The man came back early. The report was very bullish, and he smiled at
what he thought was a $2,000-per-contract profit on ten contracts. Then
the market opened up two or three cents, moved sideways, collapsed, and
closed limit down. "Never see man again," Michael wrote.
What it means. News is worth what the market has not already paid for it. When everyone has the same tip, the tip is already in the price.
Try this. Before you trade a headline, ask: who already knows this, and what have they already done?

12. The train that did not
jerk
The Simplot potato scandal, 1976.

Michael says it helps to search for the Simplot potato scandal of
1976, but that none of the accounts is entirely accurate, and he was
there.

The May Maine potato contract was nearing delivery. Everyone said
Simplot, a big grower who was heavily short, did not have potatoes to
deliver, so a squeeze was on. Michael traded the "pots" because the
contract was small and its moves were small. He was long three
contracts. Normally May potatoes moved two to four cents a pound. Now
they were moving seven.

Big longs were also buying up rail cars so Simplot could not ship
potatoes to Chicago. The story ran on the evening news for days. Then
one night the news showed a big train of sixty or seventy cars rolling
into the Chicago yards, all stamped SIMPLOT. Simplot had found potatoes.
Sell, sell. The squeeze was over.

Charlie called Michael at home right after the news. "Dad, don't sell
your potatoes. Those rail cars are either empty or just partially full.
When they open them, the potato contract goes to 15 or 20 cents. Hold
your position!"
"How do you know that, Charlie?"

"Dad, the commodity house in Garden City, Kansas, where I traded as a
young man, was right across from the rail yards. We used to watch the
trains come in as a distraction from slow markets. When boxcars are
heavy with a load, they buck and jerk, because momentum makes them push
and pull. Those Simplot cars are running too steady. I see no jerking or
bucking. They are either empty or just partially full."

Figure: Loaded boxcars buck and jerk; the Simplot cars ran too
steady, so Charlie judged them empty or partly full.

Charlie was right. Potatoes soared. Then the New York Mercantile
Exchange declared force majeure and settled the contract at about 8
cents. It killed the potato futures contract. Michael wrote that people
thought, "I can't win even when I am right, why play?" A new contract
was tried two years later and no one would touch it.
What it means. Charlie's edge was a lifetime of watching small physical details, and the patience to remember them for forty years.
Try this. Keep a notebook of small things you notice about how a market moves that are not on your indicators. Review it monthly.

13. Everyone was bearish at
the bottom
The 1974 low and the market letters.

The Dow came off a seven-year bear market and bottomed at about 575
in October 1974. Charlie and Michael used to go to Bache and read all
the market letters: Dines, Schultz, Russell, Holt, Myers and others.
They were all doom and gloom. Charlie joked, "You read these, you feel
like going home and blowing your brains out."

Around 600, Charlie told the Bache brokers to buy, because the market
had bottomed. Only Jerry Peters believed him.

Figure: The Dow bottomed near 575 in October 1974 while every market
letter was gloomy; Charlie said buy around 600.

From 1975 to 1980 Michael managed stock accounts for two brokers
while the Dow climbed from 575 to about 800. Charlie had given him a
fundamental ratio, and Goodman plus the ratio served those clients very
well. "Charlie hated technical ratios but seemed OK with some basic
fundamental stuff."
What it means. When every newsletter agrees, you are looking at a crowd, not at information. Charlie bought where the crowd could not.
Try this. Count how many analysts in your feed share your view. If it is nearly all of them, reduce your size.

14. Short
sayings that cost nothing and saved a lot
Six Goodmanisms from the trading room.

• "If I had been a greedy man, my method would not have worked and I'd be broke!" Someone had told him, in the early 1970s, that a greedy man could have made millions more.

  • "We'll do something even if it's wrong!" Michael's reading: doing something just to be doing something is probably wrong. You need to plan and prepare.

  • "Just go for the high percentage sitting ducks, Dad!"

  • "Remember, light shines brightest in a dark room!" He said it in about 1975, when Michael had made four or five bad trades in a row and wanted to quit and go back to school. "Hang in there, Dad, this is where the learning takes place and the boys are separated from the men."

  • "You put enough lines on a chart, one of them is bound to be right!"

  • "Information is so plentiful as to be nearly worthless. Knowledge is when you combine information for something useful, practical. Wisdom is rarest. It is when knowledge is combined to achieve truth."

Figure: Charlie's ladder from plentiful information to useful
knowledge to rare wisdom.
Try this. Pick one saying and write it on a card above your screen for a week.
Market Anatomy (2021)

In this paper I look at the anatomy of the market: who really decides
that price may go higher or lower. My answer is not "buyers" or
"sellers" alone. It is a shared culture that manages price, and it
judges by experiment.

Why price rises without
buyers

Many people believe that when price is very high, it must fall
because buyers are missing. Yet if you watch closely, the market often
moves from one new high to the next even when buyers are few. The reason
is simple: sellers refuse to sell lower than that price.

I call this the harmonic culture of sellers. They agree together not
to accept a lower, unacceptable price.

The King: a picture of
harmonic culture

To make this easier to see, imagine that this harmonic culture rules
like a King. The King does not create price. He only manages it.

• When the price of goods is very low, sellers want to push it higher and higher. The King knows that buyers could pay more, but only by falling into poverty. So he stops the sellers' greed and sets the price as a floor.

  • When the price is already very high, the King judges what his people can afford. If buyers can pay with abundance and without poverty, he allows sellers to raise the price further.
This explains two things that confuse many traders:

1. Price can make a new high even with fewer buyers, because the King judges that buyers can still pay with abundance.

2. Price can make a new low even with fewer sellers, because the King judges that paying a higher price would bring buyers into poverty, even if they could technically pay.

How the King reverses a
trend

• When the King judges that buyers can now pay a higher price with abundance, he changes his judgment. He allows sellers to sell to a new high. This is a reversal from down to up.

  • When buyers show poverty at the current price and cannot pay with abundance, the King judges that sellers must move down. This is a reversal from up to down.

The King judges by
experiment

The King learns his people's ability by experiment. First he tests
how buyers react when they are in poverty; then his judgment refuses to
change the price. A later experiment shows buyers who can pay with
abundance; then his judgment agrees to raise the price, based on that
last experiment.
So there is a King who manages price. He only manages it.
Note: "King" is only a descriptive word for the harmonic culture belief, the power of culture belief.

Figure: The King judges by experiment: each test of buyers at a price
leads to an inference and to the King's justice. Abundance allows a
higher price; poverty forces it lower.

Smaller 1-2-3s
are the blood of the larger 1-2-3

Every justice that comes from an experiment supports one of two
things: the larger FPS or SPS, or the larger SS. It is always a 1-2-3
inside a larger 1-2-3.

• A smaller 1-2-3 either supports the larger one or stops supporting it. When the smaller 1-2-3 stops supporting the larger, the next move is the SS.

  • A larger 1-2-3 without support from smaller 1-2-3s will move in the opposite direction.

  • The smaller 1-2-3 plays as blood to the larger 1-2-3.

When justice works to support a larger 1-2-3 (a larger timeframe, in
real time), it means fresh blood is flowing in a new direction.

Figure: Smaller 1-2-3s are the blood of the larger 1-2-3: while they

Energy boxes and the

The energy of every larger 1-2-3 is simply divided among its smaller

Each box shows how blood, the Propagation, flows to the larger box to

Market Circulation (2021)

Every day has 24 hours. A week has 7 days, a month about 4 weeks, a
year 12 months and 4 seasons. Life moves in cycles, and so does the
market. In this study I want to show how much a trader can gain by
reading the cycle in the market. I define that cycle simply: a swing
from extreme happiness to extreme sadness, and back again.

Part 1: Cycles, energy
and the Crosspoint

Projectiles and potential
energy

In physics we study projectile motion. The greater the velocity, the
further the projectile travels, just like directional movement in price.
Each projectile has a different velocity.
Here is an example from the market.

Figure: Each leg is a projectile with its own angle, and the circled
lows are where the market stored energy before the next launch. Real
data: EURGBP, 1-hour, 14–28 February 2022. (The original chart was
EURGBP daily, March to October 2019; this one shows the same structure
on the same symbol, in the window the data covers.)

Each projectile, or vector, has a different angle, and the angle
shows its strength. The market can only go up or down. Everything else
is the market in a "hash", charging its battery. In physics this is
potential energy.

When the market sits in a time hash, it is only building potential
energy for the next move, down or up. That proves what Goodman says.
When we deal only with down and up, the market looks very simple, and it
really is simple.
Where to board the bus

I have spent a lot of time thinking deeply about all the Goodman
setups. Where is the safest point to board the bus? It is easy: where
the bus is in potential energy, at the top of the hill before it rolls.
That is how the 6&6 and the Goldilocks work. Each of these
potential-energy states leads either up or down.

Figure: A down leg, then a box of potential energy where a 6&6
forms, then the up leg that releases it. Real data: EURGBP, 1-hour,
16–25 February 2022. (The original chart was EURGBP daily, February 2014
to May 2015; this one shows the same structure on the same symbol, in
the window the data covers.)

In Goodman we call this a station point: the place where a down trend
or an up trend reduces its speed until its velocity reaches zero and it
stops, like a car at a police checkpoint.

In brief, we use the Overlay to find a station point that can turn
the current trend, shown by a 6&6 or a Goldilocks. From this we know
what we want to see. That is the most important question:
What do I want to see next?

Without it, we trade without seeing anything. There is no real
purpose; it is random.

In Goodman trading, success means spotting 4 out of 10, with at least
1 line. That one line can sometimes cover all 6 losses. This is a very
important TTL: 10-4-1.
Many trends at once

Many trends can conflict with each other. The 1-hour chart may trend
differently from the weekly chart, or from the 5-minute chart. This is
why the market is so difficult. It is only up and down, but with many,
many up and down moves running at the same time.

A friend once called me. He was long EURUSD and asked if I was long
too. I told him I was short. We both made a good profit. The difference
was that I ran a station point on the 15-minute chart, and he traded the
daily chart.

That is why it is a very bad idea to take market advice from anyone.
They may tell you where to get in, but can they tell you where to exit,
where to take profit, or when to raise your stop? It is better to start
with one timeframe and stay with it until the current trend stops.
Patience.
Cycles within cycles

Things can become more complicated: cycles within cycles. Think of
the Earth's seasons around the Sun, and the Moon's cycle around the
Earth. Dealing with cycles helps us work out which season we are in
(what do I see now?). From that cycle we can observe the next season
(what do I want to see next?). Sometimes we also look at other cycles
related to the same chart.

A chart is the same: we read it horizontally, through time and
cycles. Some currencies move with others in the same cycle, the general
economic cycle. No one in the world can govern the market and fight the
economic cycle. We can also compare cycles with each other, as
scientists do with the Earth's climate over thousands of years.

The rules of the cycle are
few

1. For the current uptrend to continue, it must propagate a 1-2-3.

2. For the current downtrend to continue, it must propagate a 1-2-3.

I treat a complete 1-2-3 as a complete cycle. To measure the strength of the cycle, I use a Crosspoint: a line drawn from the BP of the FPS to the EP of the SPS. When the cycle completes, this line crosses the SS and shows a full cycle.

Figure: A complete 1-2-3 as a complete cycle: four batteries of
potential energy, joined by the Crosspoint line from BP-FPS to
EP-SPS.

How does this 1-2-3 relate to "the market can only go up or down"?
There is no difference. Each rectangle is a battery of potential energy
that can launch a move. The red rectangle holds only 3 bars, which is
why the move stopped at the Tipping Point.

The market only moves up and down. But to make a trend, one wave of
passion must have less energy and the other greater energy. Look at the
SS: it has a smaller battery, less "hash". That is why we work with the
1-2-3. Up and down without structure is not directional movement.
Seeing the battery

Why can we not see the battery? It shows very clearly on point and
figure charts, as a congestion area with a small reversal box. Or simply
zoom in to a lower timeframe: the congestion area, the potential energy,
appears clearly, often with a setup inside it.

Figure: A 1-2-3 with its four batteries at points 0, 1, 2 and 3. Real
data: GBPCHF, 15-minute, 24–25 February 2022. (The original chart was
GBPCHF H4, date not shown; this one shows the same structure on the same

Anyone can spot these areas: little to lose and much to gain. The
market can only go up or down, but always within a 1-2-3.

Using the Crosspoint to
find EP-SPS

Instead of drawing the Crosspoint from BP-FPS to EP-SPS, we can use
it to find the EP-SPS in advance. Draw a line from BP-FPS through the
middle of the SS and extend it. You will see that it finds the EP-SPS
almost exactly. It works better with a 3-C.

Figure: A Crosspoint line from point 0 through the middle of the SS
reaches almost exactly the EP-SPS. Real data: EURUSD, 15-minute, 24–25
February 2022. (The original chart did not show its symbol or date; this
one shows the same structure.)

The Crosspoint is also a very good tool to show the velocity of the
projectile launched from a battery.
Angle Propagation

The Crosspoint is connected to the BP-FPS, so let us look first at
the angle from the BP-FPS. This angle is just a slope in two dimensions,
price and time, where x is time and y is price: y = mx + b, where m is
the slope and b the y-intercept.

When the market recovers from the SS, the SPS tries to move faster
than the SS: price accelerates in much less time. All buyers now want to
move faster than in the FPS. Why? It is the Dagger concept: elastic
energy. That is why the cycle works.
Elastic energy: a tug of war

When the market holds potential energy, it is elastic potential
energy, like a spring. It comes from impression force on two sides,
buyers and sellers, inside a very small range. This creates a war, with
both sides seeking maximum profit: a Nash equilibrium.

The reaction in the SS is not a reaction without real effort. It is
decisive. Buyers from the FPS act like a magnetic field that tries to
stop the whole SS through impression force.

Impression forces come from many origins: emotions, pressure, pain.
An impression is "an idea, feeling, or opinion about something or
someone, especially one formed without conscious thought or on the basis
of little evidence."

In Goodman, the SS at 50% means half sellers, half buyers. Buyers in
the SS are losing 50% of their old profit; sellers want 50% more profit.
That is the Dagger story. Buyers want to hold their gains, so they use
impression force and increase their orders, fighting the sellers for
control.

Like a compressed spring, when impression force puts the spring under
high pressure, it releases very quickly. One side must win the war, and
the stronger the impression force, the greater the success. The cycle
continues until the impression force changes its passion, its opinion
about price.

We must go with the winner, the fresh flag. It is a pity, but that is
the market. It is a game, a Monopoly game.

Tick volume as impression
force

The amount of trading reveals how strong the impression force is in
the SS. In forex there is no central volume, only tick volume. A tick is
a market's smallest possible price movement. For example, if a market
moves in increments of 0.25, a change from 450.00 to 451.00 is four
ticks, or one point. "The tick volume study simply counts the number of
ticks during the interval specified."

Tick volume differs between brokers, but I checked several and find
about 70% of it agrees. When the mass of traders presses on a price,
that pressure counts as ticks. The mass is the mass at every broker. So
when price changes a lot, I ask why. It shows a tug of war, an
impression force pushing up or down. Measuring ticks helps show how
strong that force is.

1. Many ticks mean a new impression force: new traders with great emotion. When a salesman promises a crowd a deal they believe in, many rush to buy, and the rush carries the price.

2. Few ticks mean no great war: the impression force is low. Ask a child, "Do you want chocolate or carrots?" With no passion for carrots, we know the real passion is chocolate. That is how the mass plays. In the end, they are just human.

Any new impression force, especially when the market is in the SS,
confirms the elastic energy in the market.

Figure: The SS comes back to the TP, where new traders bring a new
impression force and vote for the uptrend. Real data: GBPJPY, 15-minute,
24–25 February 2022. (The original chart was Bitcoin, timeframe and date
not shown; this one shows the same structure.)

New traders vote for the uptrend: "Yes, we want the market to move
up." That is why elastic energy is proven in the market. At 50%, old
buyers seek new profit, or at least to hold their old gain. Sellers fear
the 50% station point and no longer want to fight. When that happens,
buyers take the flag and dominate.

Cycles govern volume and
price

I find that the Crosspoint (Angle Propagation) and the Spread Triple
give a clearer picture than volume. Cycles govern volume, and price too.
You may not believe it yet, but the show is just beginning. The market
can always teach us, and it can also shock us.

The Earth's cycle governs the weather everywhere. It governs the
temperature (its "price"), and it can govern the mass "volume" too.
Rain, flooding, snow, fog and mist, hail storms, smoke from bush and
forest fires, strong winds, extreme cold and heat: all of these can stop
the traffic (the volume) on the road.

So why does so much volume appear at 50%? Because of the station
point, the Intersection. Price makes volume; cycles make price.

When a setup fails, we are in bad weather in the market. Enjoy your
stop order and be thankful, because losing capital is the worst idea.
Some think, "I will miss that trade." Even if you do not miss it, you
cannot trade 100 lots, so you miss plenty of profit anyway. Cry for the
big banana you could make with 100 lots, little humble man!

Angle Propagation
and the stretched spring

Back to Angle Propagation. It is Propagation by time: time forces new
buyers to recover old profits quickly. Old buyers feel better because
they won the war. Their first target is to recover what they lost. No
one gives up something without a fight, not even animals.

When the market is in elastic energy, after the EP-SS it moves
quickly away from the Dagger. Momentum increases, the angle steepens,
and a new impression force takes position. A simple experiment shows
this clearly: the response is like a spring that stretches.

What I try to do is measure that stretch with the Crosspoint. The
Crosspoint gives me the total result of all energy, volume plus Nash
equilibrium, its maximum, and the next target. By following the
Crosspoint in every 1-2-3, I can see when buyers are weak or strong. It
is an overall indicator. In my opinion, it is the best indicator a
trader can have.
Reading the Crosspoint
Measure where the Crosspoint line crosses the SS:

1. A bad response, less than 50% of the middle of the SS: the impression force is weak.

2. A good response, more than 50% of the middle of the SS: the impression force is strong.

3. The Crosspoint very near the EP-SS: the impression force is extremely weak.

4. The Crosspoint very near the EP-FPS: the impression force is extremely strong.

Figure: Reading the Crosspoint: where the line from BP-FPS crosses
the SS, from extremely strong (near EP-FPS) to extremely weak (near
EP-SS).
Examples

this down 1-2-3 is weak; price then rallies. Real data: GBPUSD,
30-minute, 21–25 February 2022. (The original chart did not show its
symbol or date; this one shows the same structure.)

Figure: The Crosspoint passes right by the EP-FPS, so the impression
force is extremely strong. Real data: USDJPY, 5-minute, 22 February

shows the same structure.)
We can also use it to qualify a Goodman setup.

Figure: Qualifying a setup: the buyers' impression force is weak,
while the sellers' is strong. Real data: NZDUSD, 30-minute, 21–24
February 2022. (The original chart did not show its symbol or date; this
one shows the same structure.)
Advanced: the corrupted cycle

When Mr. Market does not give me a 1-2-3 at all, the Crosspoint shows
that the force is extremely, extremely weak. A 6&6 setup can confirm
this.

Figure: Sellers very, very extremely weak: the down move stalls at
support, no down 1-2-3 completes, and the uptrend resumes. Real data:
NZDUSD, 30-minute, 28 February – 4 March 2022. (The original chart did
not show its symbol or date; this one shows the same structure.)

When the sellers' SS stops near the BP-FPS, it shows no energy. It is
the same concept. When it happens, there is no complete cycle, no 1-2-3.
I call it a corrupted cycle.

Think of pulmonary circulation. For any reason it can stop, and we
know that when it stops it means big trouble. When Mr. Market cannot
give me a down 1-2-3, there is no complete cycle, and that means big
trouble for the sellers. I am happy; I will go with the buyers. No new
lows, no downtrend. What is new?

The Crosspoint measures how far the down cycle got before it stopped.
It can be used for a second-chance 6&6, when supply is extremely
weak.
Note: this is only knowledge that helps us answer a question, so that we gain confidence.
Spread Triples

A Spread Triple connects three (or more) Return Points, the EPs of
the SSs, in a Propagation. It is the chain between all the 1-2-3s. It
shows the steps: watch the market in every 3 steps, 3 jumps.

Figure: The Spread Triple: a line through the Return Points chains
the 1-2-3s. Each jump recharges there; a jump that cannot clear the old
high ends the uptrend.

In each jump, where is its maximum point, where V = 0? We know that
each EP-SS is a point of elastic potential energy. So it is a simple
connection with the EP and the Crosspoint. Each time the market reaches
an EP-SS, it recharges its energy and tries to jump higher than before,
like a child on a trampoline.

This shows the quality of the capacitor, the battery. As physics
says: "Charging the capacitor by using potential energy source or
voltage source through a frictional media such as the electrical
resistor will cause losing the electrical energy into friction, since
the current passing to charge the capacitor will meet friction in the
resistance."

When the market cannot jump higher than the old Propagation, the
uptrend is over. It resumes only when it can jump over the old points.
Each time the market recharges, it suggests some loss of energy.
What time really means

Time is one of the dimensions in physics. Do we use time to
understand what happened in the past? No. We use time to answer
questions about the current moment, the critical point. Ninety percent
of human memory exists because of time.

When a capacitor loses energy over time, no trend can go on forever.
The biggest gains in history came when no one expected a collapse, as in
2008. In some way, that trend was already losing energy.

We can build a real sequence of events from these forces. The sequence is like an action movie, always fighting. Our job is to understand the movie and know who the hero is, who can save the lady. So let us watch and decide with confidence who the hero is. Sometimes it is very hard, as in a mystery like The Da Vinci Code.

Examples with
the Crosspoint and Spread Triple

February – 1 March 2022. (The original chart did not show its symbol or

Figure: Each jump reaches less far: over time the market loses energy

28 February – 1 March 2022. (The original chart did not show its symbol
or date; this one shows the same structure.)

What happens here is exactly a loss of energy every time Mr. Market
jumps, like a capacitor discharging over time.
Mr. Market's house

The market can only go up or down. To give that a structure, we look
at the 1-2-3. What creates the FPS, SS and SPS is potential energy.

Mr. Market's house has three rooms: FPS, SS and SPS. By watching the
chart, we can see which room he is in. When he lives in the FPS, we know
the next room is the SS, and that is all.

So what do I mean by circulation? It is how Mr. Market flows through
the 1-2-3. We know his state from his old jump and from the Crosspoint:
fast or weak, or extremely strong.

Figure: Reading circulation: a strong impression force, then weak
jumps, an extremely strong force at A that marks a climax, a weak push

Part 2: Market noise
and the Goodman Box
Is the market predictable?

The market can only go up or down, yet every timeframe has its own
trend, which confuses everyone. At every single price there is a
different opinion, a different impression force. To make this clear, let
us look at a few bars, on any timeframe from 1 minute to 1 month.

Figure: The same bars read four ways: a strong up bar, shifting
energy, a lie in shifting, and a temporary pause.
One bar

The first bar tells me without doubt that the market opened very low
and buyers bid it up to close near the high. Instead of taking that as
true, I ask: is this bar honest enough to promise me the next bar? Is
the energy to move up real?

What caused the bar is the energy inside the buyers. The bar itself
is only noise. The question is whether that energy can carry price to
the next level or not. In most cases, a chart cannot describe the real
energy behind each move. The chart is only a tool that shows the noise
of that energy.

Shifting energy, and
the lie in shifting

The energy can shift. When it does, we know at least that there was
no real energy in the first up bar. Here we have shifting energy.

Even the down move can be false. There is real shifting, but it is
false. I call it a lie in shifting: a fox movement. So where is the
truth? Someone may say the truth comes after the false move, with the
next up bar. Maybe right, but wrong.

The effect of the false move remains: it looks like a new low, which
shows that real energy is still there, somewhere at the new low. That
false move also acts as a magnetic field for all sellers who want to
sell. I call this a temporary pause in energy: the real energy is still
unstable. That is why it is so important to qualify a setup. Is there
real energy behind that up bar, or is it just a false move made by
profit-takers?
General versus specific

Here I see the general against the specific. The specific is the
close at the high. The general is the downward movement of the larger
trend, outside the picture. The close shows some energy to move up, but
not enough to fight the higher timeframe that wants to push price
down.

When those buyers fail, we know that all buyers who could pull the
market up a little after a false breakdown hold a delusional belief.
That up move is noise; it does not show the real energy that lasts. One
picture is not enough. There is also what I call controlled energy,
which no one can deny: the last down bar shows who dominates the
market.
Six cases in the market

So is the market predictable? Most of the time, no, until we know the
real energy that lasts and go with it. Much movement is delusional and
cannot describe the energy that will dominate for a long time. I find
six cases:

1. The current movement may tell the true energy, or may not.

2. There is a false move and a true move, but even the true move may be delusional and may or may not describe the true energy of case 1.

3. Energy can shift from buying to selling and back. That shift may or may not describe the absolute true energy that dominates for a long time.

4. There is the general against the specific. Sometimes the specific changes the general, when the general is too weak to fight the current movement.

5. There is a sign no one can deny that describes the real energy.

6. Sometimes buyers or sellers are in a delusional area.

All six cases apply to every 1-2-3 in the market, and to every
Crosspoint and Spread Triple.
The Goodman Box (G-box)

A Goodman Box is a box drawn around successive 1-2-3s, or around the
BP and EP of a Propagation. It helps show the dominant trend, where the
real energy is. We must always redraw the box.
We can use the box for tests and exceeds: tests happen near the BP, exceeds near the EP.

• Test: a confirmation tool. No one can deny where the real energy is. A down 1-2-3 inside a small G-box that cannot exceed it is also a test.

  • Exceed: shows the true energy behind the current move. It can be evidence that price will break the bigger G-box and propagate into a larger box.

Zoom out: G-box, then Larger G-box, then Jumbo G-box. Zoom in: Jumbo
G-box, then Larger G-box, then G-box. I recommend giving each a fixed
colour and name.

What happens when the market stays a long time inside a box? It is in
energy mode, charging the battery. The G-box can be used as an Overlay;
a Jumbo box at the BP or EP acts as a Mo Overlay, and there you may find
a setup. It is very useful to combine the Spread Triple and the
Crosspoint with the G-box to detect where the real energy is. The G-box
also helps with volume, to measure the response of real energy, and to
measure a jump from one level to the next, as with the Spread
Triple.
What if a G-box breaks out falsely at the EP or BP? Then we measure the general energy to decide. Always redraw the box from smaller to larger.
