A
Short Study in Overlay Combination and the Concept of Bounces
(2022)

In this short study I introduce the idea of bounces and show how
balancing a combination of propagations can sharpen our view of what
buyers and sellers are able to do at an Intersection.
What is a bounce?

By studying charts for a long time, you realise that every movement
in the market can be divided into bounces. A bounce is simply a price
level that generates momentum, either down or up. Price can only go up
or down.

• A bounce that generates momentum up is a bull bounce.

  • A bounce that generates momentum down is a bear bounce.
This concept is very similar to the triple spread.

Figure: Bull bounces along a rising line, where each EP of
propagation is higher than the last.

If a bounce generates a higher EP of propagation compared with the
last EP, it means a bull propagation. Conversely, a lower EP means a
bear propagation.
Balancing a combination

The chart is a combination of different propagations: bear
propagations, bull propagations, timehash or Knot.

Figure: When the second propagation makes a lower EP, it is only a
reaction, and the next lower high reacts to it.

In cases like this the bounces are weak, both bull and bear. They are
mostly in equilibrium: a tug of war where no one succeeds.

By balancing these propagations, their bounces and their EPs, we see
whether the move is bull, bear or just a Knot. This enhances our vision
of the ability of buyers and sellers. Will they generate a bull bounce
that breaks the Intersection, or just move away from it?

A visionary idea: the wood
wall

Think of the Matrix Overlay, in outward analysis, as a wall of MDF
wood.

Figure: Bull propagations pushing toward the Matrix Overlay wall,
then turning into a bear propagation as buyers fail to hold the
price.

Is this combination of propagations most likely to break the MDF
wood? Or is the combination too weak to break it? The change from bull
propagation to bear propagation shows weakness: buyers are simply unable
to hold the price.
Chart example

Will the Intersection of AA with BB produce more sellers, down to the
EP of the Jumbo? Or will price just move away from the BB line?

Figure: The outward chart: after the fall and the Jumbo up, the
falling line AA meets the horizontal line BB. Real data: GBPUSD,
15-minute, 24–25 Feb 2022. (The original chart was probably EURNZD, 23
Dec 2022; this one shows the same structure.)

Now watch the inward chart, reading the combination of propagations
and their bounces.

Figure: The inward chart: the bear propagations fade as price reaches
BB, with no bear propagation through it, and new orders at BB turn price
up. Real data: GBPUSD, 5-minute, 25 Feb 2022. (The original chart was
EURNZD 1-minute, 23 Dec 2022; this one shows the same structure.)

After the Jumbo came a series of bear propagations. Now the new
orders at BB change the matter to the buying side, after a 6&6.

Matrix Overlay with Volume
(2021)

In this paper I show how volume, read through Goodman theory, can
confirm a Matrix Overlay. I treat volume as energy, divide the box into
Goodman levels, and watch where energy is spent and whether price
transits to the next level.
The Matrix Overlay in brief

A Matrix Overlay is when buyers or sellers return to the original
point after a substantial move. It is stronger when the return to the
original point comes by 1-2-3 movements. When those 1-2-3 movements are
cancelled by a 3-C, it gives more confidence to enter the trade. Of
course, we trade in the direction of the Matrix Overlay.

The 3-C is evidence that the move against the MO trend has no energy.
Volume can help confirm that the counter-trend move has no energy, or
that the MO trend has more energy than the counter-trend. It is relative
energy.
Caution: without a proper construction of the MO and the 1-2-3, volume will mislead you about the true energy.

Here are several examples. Each one explains an important
concept.
Example 1: EURUSD, 1-hour

Figure: Price returns to the origin point in the buyers' zone after a
1-2-3 up; the last down move is cancelled by a 3-C. Real data: EURUSD,
1-hour, 22 Feb – 1 Mar 2022. (The original chart was EURUSD 1-hour, 6–11
October; this one shows the same structure.)

On EURUSD the price returns to the origin point, in the buyers' zone.
This MO has two 1-2-3s and a cancel in the last 1-2-3. It looks exactly
like a 6&6 Setup. But here I want to quantify the MO. On its own,
the volume shows nothing but columns with no specific meaning. That is
why interpreting volume with Goodman theory is so important.

Figure: The same chart with the MO propagated into boxes. Real data:
EURUSD, 1-hour, 22 Feb – 1 Mar 2022. (The original chart was EURUSD
1-hour, 6–11 October; this one shows the same structure.)

Let us propagate within boxes and split the boxes into levels to
track the energy. I divide each box into Goodman points as horizontal
levels, then watch the volume in that frame. It looks hard, but it is
only at the start, to show how volume works. Later we do not need the
levels; they are just for visual purposes.

I draw a horizontal line for each Goodman point in the 1-2-3. Our
focus is the first box.

Figure: The first box with a horizontal level drawn at each Goodman
point and the energy (volume) at each. Real data: EURUSD, 1-hour, 22 Feb
– 1 Mar 2022. (The original chart was EURUSD 1-hour, 6–11 October; this
one shows the same structure.)
Energy levels
The first box reminded me of energy levels in an atom.

"Atomic electron transition is a change (or jump) of an electron from one energy level to another within an atom or artificial atom. It appears discontinuous as the electron "jumps" from one energy level to another, typically in a few nanoseconds or less. It is also known as an electronic (de-)excitation or atomic transition or quantum jump." (Wikipedia)

Figure: An electron absorbs energy to jump levels; price spends
volume to transit between Goodman levels.

Figure: A close-up of the first box with its four levels and the
volume beneath. Real data: EURUSD, 15-minute, 24–25 Feb 2022. (The
original chart was EURUSD 1-hour, 6–11 October; this one shows the same
structure.)
Energy can be measured by E = hv; on the chart, E = Volume.
Concept 1: what the volume shows is the quantity of energy spent (absorption) at every level.

Calories: the closest
example to volume

Let us discuss the behaviour of energy through its closest example to
volume: calories.

• The input for calories is food.

  • The output for calories is body consumption, or activities (sports and so on).
In the same way:

• The input for volume is the transactions of buyers and sellers at a known moment.

  • The output for volume is activity: the absorption forces that transit price to the next level.

A Harvard study lists the calories burned in 30-minute
activities.

Figure: Calories and volume compared as input and output of energy,
with the Harvard figures for 30-minute activities.

Volume, like calories, is relative energy: the energy spent from one
activity (absorption) level to the next. So let us study the energy at
each activity level.

Reading the first box
level by level

Figure: The first box with four numbered levels and the volume at the
first arrow. Real data: EURUSD, 15-minute, 24–25 Feb 2022. (The original
chart was EURUSD 1-hour, 6–11 October; this one shows the same
structure.)

We have 4 levels of activity, and the volume shows the energy spent
at each one. At the first arrow, energy increased at level 1. This is
the beginning of the MO, the BP. That energy shows sufficient buyers at
level 1. To confirm it, buyers must make price absorb the next visual
level, 2.

Figure: A successful transition to level 2 on less volume. Real data:
EURUSD, 15-minute, 24–25 Feb 2022. (The original chart was EURUSD
1-hour, 6–11 October; this one shows the same structure.)

The energy (volume) is less at level 2, but with a successful
transition and absorption.

Figure: A small sideways box where volume rises but fails to reach
level 3. Real data: EURUSD, 15-minute, 24–25 Feb 2022. (The original
chart was EURUSD 1-hour, 6–11 October; this one shows the same
structure.)

Then the market moves sideways in a small box. Energy and price are
in some conflict, with no clear sign. Volume increased at the last arrow
but failed to transit to the next level, 3.

Figure: Price leaves the small box as buyers raise the energy toward
level 3. Real data: EURUSD, 15-minute, 24–25 Feb 2022. (The original
chart was EURUSD 1-hour, 6–11 October; this one shows the same
structure.)

At the last arrow, price moved out of the smaller box as buyers
increased the energy to level 3.

Figure: The red arrow marks the buyers' failure to move above level
3. Real data: EURUSD, 15-minute, 24–25 Feb 2022. (The original chart was
EURUSD 1-hour, 6–11 October; this one shows the same structure.)

The red arrow shows the buyers' failure to move to the next level,
higher than 3. When that happens, look at the price and the arrow: this
energy will return price to level 2. If the chart stopped here, the
price action would suggest a Nest setup.
The Nest

Figure: The Nest setup: a 1-2-3 down on rising energy (red) and a
last rally on falling energy (yellow). Real data: EURUSD, 15-minute,
24–25 Feb 2022. (The original chart was EURUSD 1-hour, 6–11 October;
this one shows the same structure.)

Here the chart shows the Nest setup. First a 1-2-3 down with
increased energy. At the yellow arrow, energy decreases. This behaviour
suggests buyers are scrimpy. A 1-2-3 down on increased energy, and a
last rally on decreased energy? The tendency is for sellers: lower low,
lower high.

How is it a 1-2-3? Its SS has broken the BP of the FPS. The aim of
any 1-2-3 is to show progress, the ability to move, when the smaller
1-2-3 propagates into a larger 1-2-3. The larger 1-2-3 proves the
smaller one. As the red SS shows, the downside propagates into a larger
1-2-3.

Figure: Red, yellow and green arrows: rising, falling and rising
energy that fails to push below level 2. Real data: EURUSD, 15-minute,
24–25 Feb 2022. (The original chart was EURUSD 1-hour, 6–11 October;
this one shows the same structure.)

After the increased volume at the red arrow, the yellow shows
decreased energy, and the green arrow shows an increase to transit below
level 2. Instead of moving lower, the chart gives a nested setup.

Figure: At the green arrow, volume rises but cannot transit to the
lower level. Real data: EURUSD, 15-minute, 24–25 Feb 2022. (The original
chart was EURUSD 1-hour, 6–11 October; this one shows the same
structure.)

Just enter on the lower time frame, before the bar closes. The level
by itself shows nothing. What matters is the new behaviour at the green
arrow: volume increased but could not transit to the lower level.

Figure: Black arrows: energy lifts price above level 3, then hugs it
as a Dagger forms toward level 4. Real data: EURUSD, 15-minute, 24–25
Feb 2022. (The original chart was EURUSD 1-hour, 6–11 October; this one
shows the same structure.)

At the first black arrow, energy increased and price transited above
level 3. At the second black arrow, energy decreased but hugged level 3,
and price moved into a Dagger and broke out close to level 4.

Figure: The full first box with all the energy arrows from level 1 to
level 4. Real data: EURUSD, 15-minute, 24–25 Feb 2022. (The original
chart was EURUSD 1-hour, 6–11 October; this one shows the same
structure.)

From this it should be obvious that volume shows the energy behind
these levels.
Guidelines
To summarise into guidelines:

Figure: Points A, B and C, where rising volume produced the FPS, the
SS and the SPS. Real data: EURUSD, 15-minute, 24–25 Feb 2022. (The
original chart was EURUSD 1-hour, 6–11 October; this one shows the same
structure.)

• At A: energy increased relatively, which produced an FPS.

  • At B: increased volume, as the setup shows, produced an SS.

  • At C: volume increased to produce an SPS.

To use this in real time, read the behaviour of energy within the
FPS, SS and SPS. Then watch where volume increases but, instead of
moving in the same direction, price shows a tendency to move the
opposite way.

Caution: do not look for divergence between price and volume; it is a misleading way to deal with volume. Focus on decreasing and increasing energy together with the momentum of price. Whenever there is no momentum, be on alert.

Figure: Coloured bands mark how volume collected and spent energy at
A, B, C and the last new high. Real data: EURUSD, 15-minute, 24–25 Feb
2022. (The original chart was EURUSD 1-hour, 6–11 October; this one
shows the same structure.)

• At A: energy increased, and price action shows sufficient buyers to move it higher. The purple line shows price collecting energy.

  • At B: energy increased, but with a tendency to move lower, as the 1-2-3 shows. The blue line shows the market in the correction phase of the FPS move.

  • At C: energy increased, but the tendency was to move higher rather than lower, as the nested 1-2-3 setup shows.

  • The last yellow line: an abnormal increase on a new higher high, then a move to equilibrium on low volume at the last line.

Volume can help detect tipping levels when we watch the relative
increase. At B, the energy at level 3 shows buyers unable to move
higher. At C, the energy at level 2 shows sellers unable to move lower.
Both show no momentum to transit to the next level.
Two more examples

Figure: Volume points 1, 2 and 3 around the creation of the MO origin
point. Real data: EURUSD, 1-hour, 22 Feb – 1 Mar 2022. (The original
chart was EURUSD 1-hour, 6–11 October; this one shows the same
structure.)

At 1, the down move comes on decreased energy. At 2, energy increases
with a tendency to move higher; this creates the MO origin point. At 3
there is energy, but price moves sideways instead of falling fast as at
1. In the last few bars (blue line) the market moves by its own weight,
on small energy. Whichever energy wins in the sideways move can control
the market.

Figure: At X, energy rises and price transits to the next level with
good momentum. Real data: EURUSD, 5-minute, 2 Mar 2022. (The original
chart was EURUSD 5-minute; this one shows the same structure.)

Look at X: energy increased and price transited to the next level
with good momentum. Does this behaviour show a tendency to move down, or
up? There is no question: the tendency is up, the SPS.
Thank you.
Volume (2021)

In this paper I tell the story of my long struggle with one word:
volume. I want to show how I moved from confusion to a simple, logical
definition I can trade with. At the end I show how I read volume inside
the 1-2-3, with a real EURUSD example.
What I Thought Volume Was

I still remember the first time I heard the word in trading. I was
surprised. To me, volume meant sound. I used to work with sound editors
such as Adobe Audition.

Figure: A sound wave in an audio editor — the louder the sound, the
wider the wave.

Anyone can read such waves easily. When the sound increases, the wave
expands its range. When the sound is very low, the wave narrows. It is
very easy to understand.

I am also not a native English speaker. When I played sound on my
computer, my brother would shout at me: "Could you turn the volume down?
I'm trying to sleep." So I set the volume to 20%.
Figure: The volume I knew before trading — a slider set to 20.
That was everything I knew about "volume".
Meeting Volume in the Market

When I came to the market, I felt something bad inside myself:
misunderstanding.

Figure: A row of market volume bars — at first it meant nothing to
me. Real data: EURUSD, 1-hour volume, 21–25 February 2022. (The original
was a volume strip cut from another chart; this one is drawn from real
volume.)

What on earth was that? The technical books I read made this unknown
thing a top priority. Did anyone tell the truth about volume? I was
greedy. I wanted to know the next direction. I wanted a nice car. Was
the truth hidden somewhere here?

But I could not see any of that dream truth. What could I learn from
columns that all looked the same? My aim was to find the next direction,
and my mind kept showing an error. Was this important at all? Perhaps it
was more logical to forget volume and look somewhere else.
Stories without evidence

In the following weeks, I found books that spoke about manipulators
hiding in the volume. Wow. But I do not believe anything without
evidence. I am not in court; anyone can make a claim. Without evidence,
I cannot accept it. Even if such a story sank into my unconscious mind,
how could I profit from it?

Other books built equations to analyze volume. My answer was: first
tell me what volume is, then play with all the magical equations. They
showed lucky charts with divergence — buy here, sell there. Even if that
game paid me a million, I would not allow myself to play it.

Very experienced people created other indicators: the Force Index, On
Balance Volume, and more — delta, gamma and so on. To me these are only
a second translator of volume.
Finding my own path

So I tried to find my own path. I do not care about pool traders who
control the market; I am happy for them. You can detect them easily in
very small stocks. It is probably easier to make a deal with them than
to recognize them from volume. But what about Forex, or futures in the
past? There is no central volume. Is there a big ghost controlling the
market? Maybe the big banks.

When I found myself in no man's land, that confusion itself told me
something. I needed a path that was more logical and easier — one I
could at least be confident with. So I went back to simple logic:

• Behind one door, when it opens, there is a lion.

  • Behind the other door there is at least a safe path that suits my ability.

I am happy for those who can play with indicators and fight the lion.
I will not choose that path. In the end, success in the market means
trading with confidence, and confidence depends on each person's
character — "to each his own".
Expectation Versus Reality

Finding your own path takes patience. One of the hardest questions
is: what do you want? The second is: what is the aim behind it? I love
the work of Socrates.

At this point I stood between two paths: comfort and reality. The
comfortable path may simply not exist. Sometimes we are happy with a
beautiful but false image, while reality is very far from our
expectation.
My first expectations about volume were like my dream car:

1. If I understood volume, I could anticipate the next direction.

2. If I knew nothing about volume, I could not trade, because the truth lives in the volume.

3. My greed could cover my eyes, so I would not believe what the market says about itself.

In this state it is easy to fall and give up. But I could do it.
Anyone who begins to see the facts from outside starts to learn deeply.
Why? Because he finds that what is inside him is unreal. Thank God, our
minds can change as easily as our hands can move, with a little
practice. Otherwise I would stay ignorant forever.
"A man should look for what is, and not for what he thinks should be." — Einstein
The Rule of Signs

In simple logic, is there any sign that a path exists? There is a
strong rule: anything that exists has a sign that correlates with it.
Anyone can say he owns a car, but the car must show up somewhere. If the
car is nowhere and there is no sign, it does not exist.

For a joke: one student in my school was a big liar. Every day he
claimed he came to school by helicopter. There was never any sign. That
is the mark of a liar — claiming something that does not exist.

So I follow this logic: wherever there is a sign, one sign is enough
for me. Let us start the journey to discover a simple path.

"It's not that I'm so smart, it's just that I stay with problems longer." — Albert Einstein

"A thousand roads lead a man forever toward Rome."

Defining Volume from the
Ground Up

Where could I start? Any first sign would help. I began by analyzing
the dictionary definition. The Oxford dictionary says volume is "the
amount of something". That was enough for me. I wanted a simple model to
work with before I added any more parameters.
I asked two simple questions:

1. What benefit do I get from knowing the amount of something?

2. What type of amount is it?

The benefit of knowing an
amount

I remember a physics class about units. Before modern units, people
used very old tools to measure amounts.

Figure: Old units of land measure (oxgang, virgate, carucate) — every
age measured amounts with its own tools.

The benefit of knowing an amount is obvious: it lets us put things in
the right place. How? An amount gives a differential picture. From that
difference we can find the level or boundary. It is a matter of
judgment: who is taller, who is shorter? Our ability to judge depends on
our experience and knowledge.

Take chemistry. Which atom has the largest atomic radius? Potassium.
We do not know everything, so we cannot judge everything. Sometimes we
need a special tool to measure. For example:

"This is possible because carbon atoms occur in heavy and light forms or isotopes, and measuring the relative amounts of each can reveal the source of the carbon. Using carbon isotopes in this way is not a new idea, but it requires extremely precise—and expensive—measurements."
My simple conclusion
From this analysis I drew four points:

• The main benefit of knowing an amount is to put each thing at its proper level or boundary.

  • Some types of amount are easy to judge; others are hard.

  • Judgment aims to place the amount inside its boundary — no more, no less. Sometimes the judgment is relative, as with carbon.

  • The ways of measuring differ: different units, different tools, different devices.

I use this simple conclusion as the ground on which to build
something bigger. The word "volume" alone is not enough. We must dig
deeper, because the model works only according to what we put into
it.
Measuring Humans

In the stock market, the reason behind every movement is humans, and
only humans. I know of no monkey or animal that buys or sells. If anyone
denies it, I welcome the discussion 😊.

So the critical question is not "how do we measure the number of
humans?" It is "how do we put human action into levels or
boundaries?"

Old wisdom shows how hard this is. Socrates said: "I know that I am
intelligent because I know that I know nothing." There, intelligence
goes with knowing nothing. Today it is the opposite: intelligence goes
with the one who knows everything. The old teacher said: "I cannot teach
anybody anything. I can only make them think." Today we say: go to
school and take a certificate. I am not judging which is right. I only
want to show how difficult it is to build a unit that measures human
action or habit. From here my other ideas were born — energy, passion
and others.

Still, some human things are easy to judge, such as love and hate.
Someone who loves another will not kill him — that is 99% sure. So in
some cases we can judge with high confidence.

But can we measure it with an equation? It is impossible. Can anyone
write an equation that tells whether there is love in his marriage? We
have tools inside our brain that measure the amount of love easily. Can
any equation replace testosterone? A monitor may tell you how healthy
your testosterone is, but reading a description is not the same as
living the feeling. This is why I do not believe in indicators. I may be
100% wrong, but I cannot fight my own analysis without a sign that
proves me wrong.

My Definition:
The Amount of Selling at a Price

So what does volume in the market measure? It measures the amount of
change in property. Mr. Goodman was right: price causes volume. In every
market, the amount of selling depends on what the price is.
My definition is therefore: volume is the amount of selling, depending on the price. When the market is at price X, it generates an amount of selling Y.
What the amount tells us

What is the benefit? In every market, the amount of selling tells a
story about price:

• When the amount of selling increases, the price will probably rise.

  • When the amount of selling decreases, the price will probably be discounted.

  • When the amount of selling runs at average, the price will probably follow whoever dominates.

  • When the amount of selling is abnormally high, the price is probably at a critical point.

  • When the amount of selling is abnormally low, the price is also probably at a critical point. No business can live without customers — the real boss of every business is the customer.

Figure: Reading the amount of selling: what increasing, decreasing,
average and abnormal volume probably tell us about price.
A big note

One bar is not enough to tell the story, and the same is true of
volume. We must work Inward and Outward to understand the amount of
selling in each hour, day and week. Sometimes the market moves up on a
very low amount of selling simply because it has just come from an
abnormal amount. This is a soft judgment.

Figure: Volume bars read as nothing more than the quantity of sales
in each period. Real data: GBPUSD, 1-hour volume, 28 Feb – 4 Mar 2022.
(The original was a volume strip cut from another chart; this one is
drawn from real volume.)

Reading Volume with the
Matrix

So all these columns follow one simple path: the quantity of sales.
By judging the quantity, we can put it in the right place. For example,
when the market moves up on a very low quantity of sales, we can easily
judge that the market will probably go down. It is just an Overlay.

How do we judge that the quantity is very low? It is not hard:
memorize the Matrix. Thank you, Mr. Goodman. I watch each Matrix,
memorize the change, and make my judgment behind it. Most of the time I
combine it with a judgment of time. Time represents control, like how
long a football team keeps the ball.

The change in the amount of sales in each FPS, SS and SPS can tell
the story.

Figure: Volume inside a down 1-2-3: the amount of selling under the
FPS, SS and SPS, and what each change means.
Example: EURUSD

Figure: A 1-2-3 down with the volume under each leg marked 1, 2 and
3. Real data: EURUSD, 4-hour, 17 Feb – 2 Mar 2022. (The original chart
was EURUSD daily, July–August 2021; this one shows the same
structure.)

1. FPS (1). The volume fits the range of the wave very well; everything is fine. The amount of sales at 1 shows how the down move travels at an average pace. I memorize that.

2. SS (2). But everything can change. At 2 the amount of sales is clearly lower than at 1. It shows only a correction. The time is very short, so there is no control.

3. SPS (3). Here we have an indication. The volume is abnormal for the range and for the time held. There are a lot of sales and the market is at a critical point. Because sales increased on a down SPS held for very little time, it shows many buyers want to enter the market.

4. After the SPS. As soon as the SPS ends, the quantity of sales rises above the SS at 2. More buyers want to bid the market. Reading this, I know the right place for this amount: it is to raise the price. Buyers have a lot of energy to pull the market up.

I know this is tick volume, but it works well with judgment behind
the Matrix. Reading volume without the 1-2-3 will mislead you a lot.

That is my very simple study of how I read volume — the quantity of
sales. Thanks for reading.

Qualifying Trades by
Using Volume (2023)

In this short study I show how I use volume to qualify a trade. I
start from one simple rule — price makes volume — and build a three-step
routine around the 3-C cancel and the Matrix. Then I read two examples,
and finally walk through a full chart bar by bar.
Price Makes Volume

The market is a voting machine. New buyers come when price rises, and
new sellers come when price declines. Price makes volume.

Once price rises above the last top, volume may increase. That shows
new buyers are joining the move. As more new buyers arrive, the move
goes much higher, because the previous sellers withdraw from the market
and become interested in the new move.

Three Steps to Qualify a
Trade

1. Start with the 3-C cancel. Use it as the reference point for studying volume.

2. Look for a Matrix Overlay at the same point.

3. Do the Inward analysis. Watch for significant changes in volume. A significant price level makes volume. Look for volume increasing on the upswing and decreasing on the downswing that makes a higher low.

Volume can only increase or decrease, and both tell us something. If

picture clearer.

Compare the selling with what the Dagger line produced. Selling

Volume Today: When
Everyone Agrees (2025–2026)

My first two papers on volume asked a narrow question: does volume confirm the trade I already see? In 2021 I read volume against the matrix. In 2023 I used it to qualify a trade in three steps. Today I ask a different question: how many people agree right now? When almost everyone agrees, the move is finished. Volume consensus is exhaustion. If everyone is selling, it means buy. If everyone is buying, it means sell.

From confirmation to
consensus

The change did not come from volume alone. It came from years of
reading sentiment beside it. In September 2024 I wrote to Michael what
my own testing had shown:

"Anyway my back testing shows the best Sentiment indicators are Bullish consensus, second OI, third Volume. What i find when BC above 90. This reflects in Volume, because everyone is buying at that price level. (There is a willing to let money on the table) every one bet. This is a real sign of turning point. But in my test, many false signals from volume if not confirmed with BC." (26 September 2024)

So volume was third in the ranking, and alone it gave false signals.
What made it useful was the same thing that makes Bullish Consensus
useful: the extreme. A reading of 90 means the crowd has already placed
its bet. A volume extreme means the same thing, measured in ticks
instead of opinions.
In the same letter I explained what open interest adds:
"Price at 100, but OI increase it shows new buying (willing). Same Price at 100, but OI Decrase, shows buying out of the market." (26 September 2024)

Two weeks earlier I had watched silver change character exactly this
way:
"As I anticipated, the market changed in volatility from Aggressive Selling into a lack of selling a kind of consensus." (9 September 2024)

Aggressive selling first, then nobody left to sell. That is the shape
of a consensus extreme: the crowd agrees, acts all at once, and then has
nothing left.

Why raw forex volume
cannot be trusted

Most of my trading is forex, and forex has no central exchange. The
volume your platform shows is tick volume: the number of price changes
on one broker's feed. It is not the number of contracts traded. I said
it plainly in November 2025:

"Most of the volume in the market. It's artificial volume. Type of scam. Just money rounds and rounds. I think the cumulative volume. Its a good idea. Volume by time losing thier value." (21 November 2025)

Two ideas sit in that note. First, one bar of volume means little; what counts is volume accumulated along a move. Second, volume measured by the clock loses value; the move should decide where a count starts and stops, not the hour.

At the end of 2025 Michael found his old folder on the Descartes
Index, the last big project he did with Jim Bickford. He described it as
an attempt to "tease out new information from price/range/oi/volume" (30
December 2025). I had tried to program it in Pine Script years before,
using open interest. The next day I wrote:
"The descartes raito. I did some to let it work on forex. Tick volume mixed with ATR. I think there is relationship between voltiltiy and volume." (31 December 2025)

This is the same problem again. Forex has no open interest and no
true volume, so every tool built for futures must be adapted.

Our indicator:
Continuity + Consensus Extreme
The answer I built is my own TradingView indicator, Continuity + Consensus Extreme (Time-aware), which I call ContExtT, or simply "our indicator". It does three things.

1. It classifies every bar by structure, not by colour. A bar with a higher high and higher low is a bull bar. A lower high and lower low is a bear bar. An inside bar or an outside bar is undecided. The close is used only to break the tie on an outside bar.

2. It counts continuity volume. While bull bars follow each other, their volume is added into one buyer column. While bear bars follow each other, their volume is added into one seller column. Inside and outside bars do not break the count. Their volume waits in a pending pool. If the same direction resumes, the pool joins the streak. If the direction truly reverses, the pool is discarded. This is the "cumulative volume" of my 2025 note: the move, not the clock, defines the count.

3. It marks the consensus extreme. When a streak ends, the indicator compares its final total with every completed streak of the same side in the lookback window (50 bars by default). If it is a new record, a gold dot is placed on the last bar of the streak. That dot is the fold point: maximum one-sided commitment, immediately before the reversal.
In short form the logic is:
for each bar:
if inside or outside: pending += volume

elif bull bar: buyers = (last == up ? buyers + pending + volume :
volume); sellers = 0; pending = 0

elif bear bar: sellers = (last == down ? sellers + pending + volume :
volume); buyers = 0; pending = 0

if seller streak just ended and its total > highest seller streak
in lookback: mark SELLER CONSENSUS EXTREME (look to buy)

if buyer streak just ended and its total > highest buyer streak in
lookback: mark BUYER CONSENSUS EXTREME (look to sell)

The signal is contrarian on purpose. A record seller streak does not
say "sell". It says the sellers have all sold.

builds into one unbroken streak on 24 February; when the streak breaks
at 13:00 it is the largest seller streak of the window (gold dot). Price

Many feeds, one vote:
composite volume

One broker's tick volume is one broker's clients. So I added a
multi-broker composite to the indicator: several forex feeds combined
into one volume series. It works better than any single feed, because a
real extreme shows on every feed at once, while a feed's own noise does
not.

The open question is how to combine them. The mean lets one loud or quiet feed pull the whole composite. The median follows what most of the feeds say and ignores the single outlier. I am still weighing the two.

This does not cancel what I wrote earlier, that adding platforms
cannot give the true market volume because one liquidity provider often
serves many brokers. That is still right. I am not trying to measure the
whole forex world. I am measuring agreement. In 2021 I found that about
70% of the ticks agree between brokers; the composite asks the same
question every hour: do the feeds agree that this is an extreme? Their
overlap is part of why they agree, and the median keeps one odd feed
from deciding the vote. The idea did not change; it grew.

The next plate is an illustration of the idea, not the indicator
itself. It applies the same thinking across pairs instead of brokers.
Each USD pair's tick volume is divided by its own five-day median, so
every feed is on the same scale. The bars are the median of the
three.

(lines), combined by the median of the three (bars). The composite peaks

Note what the median did here. AUDUSD was the quietest of the three,
at 2.36 times normal. The mean was pulled down to 3.30 by that one feed.
The median stayed with the two feeds that agreed, at 3.76.
Two currencies, two votes

Volume can show me the selling too, not only the buying. When I read
a pair at its two currencies, the volume is literally opposite. One side
shows rising bars. The other side shows falling bars.

To see it, I put two pictures side by side: the dollar index (DXY)
and the euro index (EXY). When EURUSD is about to turn, one index is
being bought and the other is being sold. If both are at maximum volume
at the same time, that is an excellent signal.

First, let me be clear about what makes EURUSD rise. There are three
possibilities:

1. Strong buying in the euro, and weak buying in the dollar. Both are bought, but the euro is bought more.

2. Strong buying in the euro, and no change in the dollar. The euro does all the work.

3. No change in the euro, and strong selling in the dollar. The dollar does all the work.

Figure: Three ways EURUSD rises. In each case the euro gains on the
dollar, but the force comes from a different side.

None of these is what I wait for. The strongest case is consensus.
Consensus is when I have two contradictory forces, both at their
climax.

In the dollar I see a buying climax. Everyone has bought the dollar,
so the dollar will fall. In the euro I see a selling climax. Everyone
has sold the euro, so the euro will rise. Two exhausted crowds, pulling
in opposite directions, and both of them act on the current pair.
Together they push EURUSD up.

This is the rule of this chapter, seen from both sides at once. A
climax is exhaustion. When everyone is buying the dollar, it means sell
the dollar. When everyone is selling the euro, it means buy the
euro.

Figure: The double climax. A buying climax in the dollar index
(record up-wave volume, so it will fall) against a selling climax in the
euro index (record down-wave volume, so it will rise). Both arrows meet
at EURUSD up. Index = equal-weight, median volume (not DXY weights).

There is one problem. DXY does not express the real strength of the
dollar. It is built with weights. The euro alone is more than half of
it, so DXY is mostly the euro read upside down. It cannot give me a fair
second opinion on EURUSD.

So I changed it. I build the index myself. For each currency I take its seven pairs and count every pair equally. Each pair's volume is divided by its own average, so a busy pair does not shout over a quiet one. Then I combine the pairs with the median, not the average. The euro pairs will vary: EURJPY can be wild while EURCHF sleeps. The median keeps one noisy pair from deciding the vote. Where the currency is the quote, as the dollar is in GBPUSD, I read that pair upside down, because the index must use all of its pairs.

In 2026 I put this into one tool, which I call NetGate. It draws the pair on top, and the two currency indexes below it. It cuts each index into swings by Goodman's rule: a swing ends only after a 25% correction, as Michael Archer teaches in The Goodman 6 & 6. It adds up the volume of each wave. A wave is a record when its volume is above the last N waves. A double climax needs both currencies to print a record wave on at least 3 of their 7 pairs, closing against the move. It is counted inside the setup window, after the prior move. And the waves must have ended. Only then do I wait for my trigger. NetGate never tells me up or down. Direction belongs to the method.

Here is one real example, built the same way from the data I
have.

Look at 24 February. From 22 February 16:00 the euro index was sold
in one long wave of 54.3x, the largest since the prior move. From 23
February 15:00 the dollar index was bought in one long wave of 44.5x,
nearly three times its largest of the last eight waves. At 10:00 to

wait for the waves to end. The euro selling wave ended at 12:00. The
dollar buying wave ended at 17:00. At 18:00 EURUSD printed its low at

One extreme is a hint. Two contradictory climaxes is the signal.

How the three papers fit
together

• Volume (2021): volume is read inside the matrix, never alone.

  • Qualifying Trades by Using Volume (2023): price makes volume; a trade is qualified by the 3-C reference, the Matrix Overlay at the same point, and an Inward reading of the volume flow.

  • Volume today (2025–2026): volume is sentiment. It is accumulated along the move, combined across feeds, and read at its extreme, against the crowd.

The earlier rules still hold. A consensus extreme is not a trade by
itself; it is a warning that one side is finished. I still want the
overlay, the 3-C and the setup. What changed is where I look first. I no
longer ask whether volume is high. I ask whether everyone is on the same
side.
The rule

When everyone is selling, it means buy. When everyone is buying, it
means sell. The crowd is never wrong about the move that has already
happened. It is wrong about the next one.

The 6&6 Under the
Microscope (2021)

There are several types of 6&6 Setup, and each one affects the
profit we can make. In reality some of them will produce a loss, and it
is hard to know which type gives the maximum profit. In this paper I try
to find the way to the most profitable type.
Method and Logical Model

A target this large needs a strong diagnostic tool. I use Game
Theory, and especially the Nash equilibrium, to examine the 6&6
types.

My logical model is simple. Some cases produce a successful 6&6
and others produce a failed one. Our aim is to find the cause that gives
a success instead of a failure. So I study the cases and their causes,
and ask why each one succeeds or fails.

Mass Behavior and
Constant Conjunction

The 6&6 pattern is just a reflection of mass behavior. Every case
of the 6&6 reflects a different type of mass behavior. We do not
need to know the "why" behind that behavior. As Hume put it:

"Reason alone cannot be a motive to the will, but rather is the 'slave of the passions'."

"We never actually perceive that one event causes another but only experience the 'constant conjunction' of events."

By experiencing the constant conjunction of events behind mass
behavior, we can induce a logical response. That logical response can be
framed as a Nash equilibrium.

Why the Nash Equilibrium
Matters

"However, one doesn't need to be a wayward genius to understand the idea of a Nash equilibrium. We have seen that the payoffs in a game are chosen to make it tautological that rational players will seek to maximize their average payoff. This would be easy if players knew what strategies their opponents were going to choose." — Ken Binmore

In a Nash equilibrium, rational players seek to maximize their
profit. A professional trader who makes a living from trading wants
exactly that. He looks for a great target and a great movement.

The evolutionary reading of this is very clear at the Intersection.
When the market breaks out of the Intersection, the old losers try to
maximize their profit. They take trades in the direction of the
breakout, which generates more movement.

Supply-demand
equilibrium versus Nash equilibrium

The old supply-demand theory says the market always seeks an
equilibrium value between supply and demand. Buyers and sellers each
look for the equilibrium price, so the future price can be found from
that balance. That is what university teaches about the market:

"Why is the equilibrium price the best deal available for both buyers and sellers? The equilibrium price reflects that the highest price consumers are willing to pay for that amount of the good or service and is just equal to the minimum price that suppliers require for delivering it." — McConnell, Brue and Flynn, Introduction to Microeconomic Principles, Chapter 3

But the equilibrium price is not the best deal. In my opinion, the
market follows the Nash equilibrium for a simple reason: it is a very
competitive environment. In any competitive game, the Nash equilibrium
is the best choice for all players.

The Components of the
Market Microscope

Trend, maximum profit and
climax

Old market wisdom says the trend is "the path of least resistance",
and an experienced trader follows it: "the trend is your friend". It is
your friend because it puts the maximum gain in your pocket. But traders
follow it only until they take their maximum profit — the Nash
equilibrium.

That is why the market always looks for oversold and overbought
conditions:

• Oversold: the maximum point sellers can achieve.

  • Overbought: the maximum point buyers can achieve.

Adding this to my Energy model creates a new concept: each swing
measures the pulling force that drives it to its maximum. The impression
forces carry a lot of passion and emotion, pushed by the pulling force
toward maximum gain. The market is always looking for the Nash
equilibrium price.

What happens when the market reaches its Nash equilibrium (oversold
or overbought)? It retreats and corrects. The energy inside the pulling
force drives the impression force until it reaches maximum gain, and
then the energy is at climax.
The battery model

It is exactly like a battery. The market charges the battery, and the
battery carries the trend until it runs out. When there is no battery
left, the trend shuts down and the next phase is correction — just like
a smartphone going from 100% to 0% and shutting down.

This is relative energy. When the swing reaches its Nash equilibrium,
traders have their maximum profit at that price. They take it, and that
is how a climax forms. Traders are happy, their passion is satisfied,
and the market moves into its correction phase.

Every swing has a maximum. By studying the old swings, we can measure
how energy responded in each one. Some phones run three days on one
charge, others seven. The battery's response depends on how the phone is
used and on the quality of the battery.

In the same way, every swing, up or down, shows its own energy and
response:

• One swing moves 100 pips and its battery is at 0%.

  • Another swing moves 1,000 pips and its battery is still at 50%.

By studying the quality of each swing and its response up to its
maximum, we can see on which side — up or down — the pulling and
impression forces are greater. It is like a simple test of two phones to
see which battery has more power.

Figure: The battery model of a swing: energy runs down to the climax.
A 100-pip swing at 0% against a 1,000-pip swing still at 50%.
Shifting energy

How do we know the battery is finished in a swing? It is not
difficult. A phone's battery is finished when it cannot run an app, or
the app shuts down and cannot restart. In a swing, we compare it with
the old pulling force when it worked perfectly. If the difference is
large, there is no relative energy left.
I call this shifting energy in the swing. By watching shifting energy, we can see which side has more pulling power from the impression force to reach its maximum.

How shifting energy
affects mass behavior

1. It changes mood and passion. When a phone battery dies, the owner feels torn between sadness and anger. That energy pulls him into action — he goes to find a charger.

2. It shows the path of least resistance. We see the shift by comparing the maximum of each up and down swing. The side with the greater pulling power and passion is the path of least resistance. No one can fight real passion ("slave of the passions").

3. Passion shows in the response. Comparing the upswings and downswings shows their response, which measures pulling power and passion. As Steve Jobs said: "People don't know what they want until you show it to them." When the market shows its offers, we see the mass response to them.

4. The response is everything. Jack has $100 in his pocket. A computer shop tries to sell him a $1,000 laptop, and he cannot pay. A hundred meters on, a real-estate salesman wants to sell him a $200,000 house. Can he sell it? Of course not — Jack could not even buy the laptop. Anything can happen; maybe Jack gets a loan, as in 2008. But the response tells us what to expect. This is "constant conjunction" — induction.

To summarize: the market is a salesman, and the mass shows its
passion for each item. Professional traders study that passion and
response, then trade with it — up for a positive mood, down for a
negative mood.
Why the 6&6?

The 6&6 shows mass passion in a position of conflict. It is the
most destructive pattern, and it shows clearly how a shift in energy and
passion happens. By studying its two Matrices, the FMX and the BMX, we
can measure directly where the most passion and energy sit.

Applying the Model to the
6&6

Here I look at which pattern carries more passion, or energy, to the
upside. I build the picture step by step.
Step 1: The Jumbo
Figure: Step 1 — the Jumbo down wave.

This energy field stops the negative passion, or at least reduces it
to a minimum. The reason is that the market has reached its Nash
equilibrium. The market now corrects the passion to check whether the
last Jumbo can survive and grow with a new down Propagation, or whether
it stops. That correction creates new energy with a positive passion to
bid the offers.

Figure: Step 2 — the first up wave after the Jumbo, the newest
passion to the upside.

We always look for a shift in passion. This point shows the newest
passion in the up wave. If the next wave corrects by less than 50%, the
negative passion has stopped and the positive passion is growing
stronger.
Step 2: The Knot

The down wave is very small relative to the Jumbo. It shows there is no passion left for the down move. This is clear deduction: there is a shift in energy, confirmed by the Nash equilibrium of the downswing. Its maximum target is tiny. There is no energy left to pull the market down. In Goodman this is called a Knot.

Figure: Step 3 — the small down wave after the first up wave forms a
Knot.

When the market moves above EP1, it confirms the passion for an
uptrend. The path of least resistance is now up. The market is ruled by
good emotion and new energy.
Figure: Step 4 — a sharp break above EP1 confirms the up passion.

More pulling power produces more breakaway, which shows a stronger up
passion. Whenever we see that, the uptrend is confirmed. When the
movement is sharper, the passion is very strong — buyers are extremely
happy. The Nash equilibrium at EP3 is larger than at EP1, and it arrived
faster. That is a positive shift in passion; the passion is growing.

Why does a down move come after such new energy? Some hidden negative
passion remains from the Jumbo, and some sellers temporarily overcome
the buyers.
Step 3: Testing the passion

When there is no breakaway and the angle is a little slower, the
passion is close to a retracement. The market tests whether the good
passion can survive, and at what price it can hold its gains. A test
means: is the passion strong enough to create a pulling force that beats
all sellers in a real struggle? If the positive passion wins, the test
is successful.

In this case the market gives a very unreliable target. When the
passion is strong, it must make a good breakout of BP1.

Figure: The rally fails to break BP1 well (orange line) — an
unreliable target.

Here I measure the speed of the impression force with a slope line
drawn through two anchor points. The line shows how fast positive
passion responds to the next correction.

We now have the FMX. This Matrix acts as a centripetal force — like a
magnetic field that attracts positive passion from all over the world.
This magnetic field cannot be destroyed. It is a major sign of a
potential shift in energy.

Figure: The slope line (green) through two anchor points measures the
speed of the positive passion.

When the market gives only a small Nash equilibrium — a very low
maximum profit — positive passion is taking profit very quickly.

Step 4: Testing the magnetic
field

When the next negative passion reacts behind the slope line, some
impression force wants to grow the passion upward, and the market
responds faster.

Figure: A negative reaction behind the slope line, followed by a
quicker response.

But when the next response has too little energy to make a new Nash equilibrium, there is no interest or passion to move the trend up. The trend is over, yet the magnetic field remains. I call it hidden positive passion; it can generate more positive passion later.

Figure: Yellow arrows mark where the passion stops relative to
EP1.

If the passion stops above EP1, the market can hold its gains. If it
cannot move above EP1, the weakness is greater. Both are weakness, but a
rally that cannot exceed EP1 is the weaker; the energy is gone very
quickly.

• Note 1: The weaker the market now, the better it tests the positive passion. In such a struggle we need to know that positive passion wins, so that sellers cannot come back. Then we have a strong shift in energy.

  • Note 2: When the weakness is very low, and the positive passion still cannot continue the trend after 50%, it shows more weakness than positive passion.

Big Deal Notes: Two BMX
Conditions
Let us assume two conditions:

1. The clearance sale. The market wants to sell all its stock. It is like a shop full of old items at a big discount, eager to clear them. Here the BMX is very sharp, because they want to remove all sell orders and take profit from the FMX effect (the magnetic field). After that, no one wants to sell any more.

2. The sticky price. The FMX creates a conflict in passion. Imagine a shop that offered a big discount for a long time (the Jumbo). In summer it raises its prices (the FMX). When summer ends, it does not want to return to the old price quickly, because it thinks customers accept the new one. Here the BMX forms slowly and takes a long time.

Which is better? I think the first, because they know the depression
is over and recovery (expansion) has begun.

Testing the
Centripetal Force of the FMX

Let us test the centripetal force from the 1-2-3 FMX. The break of
BP2 is the first test of whether the uptrend can survive again. As we
can see, this sign shows negative passion. Why? In the old wave, at the
first yellow arrow, the Nash equilibrium is very low relative to the
second arrow. The newer wave shows a better Nash equilibrium — though of
course still less than the Jumbo's.

Figure: Yellow arrows compare the Nash equilibrium of the old wave
and the newer wave after the break of BP2.

If the next rally shows a good Nash equilibrium, the market can move
up again. If it shows only a very small one, expect it to move down
more.

Figure: Three arrows track a shrinking Nash equilibrium in the
rallies — buyers accept ever smaller targets.

Here the positive passion has only a small Nash equilibrium, so the
market weakens further until the weakness is satisfied and the energy is
lost. The downtrend resumes with very negative passion, and we test the
FMX magnetic field. The market wants to dump all its offers in front of
the buyers.

The third arrow shows how quickly sellers dump on the buyers, and the
buyers accept a small Nash equilibrium. The buyers are weak and the
sellers are strong. The next breakdown confirms the downtrend. Comparing
the first, second and third arrows shows the shift in passion: the
impression force is weak, the pulling power is weak, and demand is very
weak.

When that happens, shifting energy can change the trend from up to
down. To confirm it, price should break down through EP1 of the BMX.

Figure: The last down wave reaches a smaller Nash equilibrium than
the first down wave from EP1 of the BMX.

In the last down wave, the Nash equilibrium is smaller than in the
first down wave. The response of negative passion is much weaker than at
its origin at EP1 of the BMX. The negative passion is struggling against
the FMX positive passion. In other words, this is the final test: does
any negative passion want to go further? The FMX effect makes the market
look, from another perspective, like a double bottom.

Which 6&6 Is the Most
Effective?

The answer: the one with more pulling power to move. Let me set out
the evidence for measuring which side has the greater pulling power.

Figure: Points 1, 2 and 3 used to compare the Nash equilibrium of
each side.
First evidence

1. At 1, the Nash equilibrium is very, very large — the Jumbo.

2. At 2, a fresh positive Nash equilibrium — good positive passion.

3. At 3, a very small Nash equilibrium — bad negative passion. Supply is very weak and easy to break.
Second evidence

The SPS of the BMX shows a worse response than the FPS. The Nash
equilibrium of the SPS of the BMX is smaller than that of the FPS of the
BMX. The negative passion stops at the ESPS.

Using the slope: the left green arrow shows an impression force whose
Nash equilibrium runs to the left red arrow. But at the second,
right-hand arrow the impression force shifts and produces a smaller Nash
equilibrium than on the left.

Figure: Green arrows mark the impression force and red arrows the FPS
and SPS of the BMX — the SPS gains less, in less time.

The time at the left red arrow (FPS) is longer than at the right red
arrow (SPS), which shows a shift in negative passion. The FPS gained a
larger Nash equilibrium — more gain, more profit. The SPS had less gain,
less profit and less time dominating the market, so it reverses
easily.

There is also no breakaway in the BMX. All this evidence shows that
the FMX caused the shift in energy.
Implications

This study also helps diagnose something a little odd — the second
Big Deal condition. The shop gave a big discount for a long time (the
Jumbo), raised its prices in summer (the FMX), and then did not want to
return quickly to the old price, believing customers accepted the new
one. The BMX then forms slowly and takes a long time, with no growth in
negative passion and no more energy in the BMX.

Figure: The slow BMX: after the fast Jumbo, the BMX drags on for a
long time without new negative energy. Real data: GBPUSD, 1-hour, 23 Feb
– 3 Mar 2022. (The original chart's symbol and dates are not known; this
one shows the same structure.)
Conclusion

In the 6&6, the FMX and the BMX each play an excellent role in
showing how — and why — the market changes its course from down to up.
This study is only one part; there is a lot more to explore.
Spread Triples (2023)

In this study I look at Spread Triples: lines that connect three
Return points. I show how to draw them, what the spacing between the
Returns tells us about selling, how the lines work as a magnet for
Returns, and how they measure the pace of Propagation. I finish with a
full story on CADCHF.
What a Spread Triple Is
A Spread Triple is the connection of three Return points.

Figure: Three intermediate Returns, A, B and C, joined by Spread
Triple lines as the market spreads lower. Real data: EURJPY, 4-hour, 14
Feb – 4 Mar 2022. (The original chart was AUDCHF weekly, Oct 2020 – Jul
2023; this one shows the same structure.)

Here we have three intermediate Returns, A, B and C, that produce
several weeks of down movement. These lines show how the 1-2-3 spreads.
The best approach is to draw them only on intermediate and major Return
points. That filters out any minor moves.
Measuring the Rate of Spread

Now put a dot on each Return as it falls, vertically — like measuring
the speed of a ball falling to earth.

Figure: A dot on each Return, A, B and C, to measure how fast the
Returns fall. Real data: EURJPY, 4-hour, 14 Feb – 4 Mar 2022. (The
original chart was AUDCHF weekly, Oct 2020 – Jul 2023; this one shows
the same structure.)

Do these points tell us something? Do they always have a rate of
spread? My reading:

• The farther apart these points are, the more selling there is in the market.

  • The closer together they are, the less selling there is.

Figure: Three Returns on one Spread Triple line are critical points;
when price exceeds them, watch for a new Return around them. Real data:
EURNZD, 1-hour, 14 Feb – 4 Mar 2022. (The original chart was GBPCAD
weekly, Oct 2017 – May 2023; this one shows the same structure.)

These points are also very critical for the market. When price
exceeds them, watch for a new Return around them.

Figure: After price exceeds the red line, new black lines are drawn
for the new sequence of counter Returns. Real data: GBPUSD, 1-hour, 22
Feb – 1 Mar 2022. (The original chart was USDCAD weekly, Aug 2019 – Jun
2023; this one shows the same structure.)

When price exceeds the red line, draw new lines for the new sequence
of Returns, as with the black line.

Lines That Set the Pace
of Propagation

One advantage of these lines is that they define the pace of the
Returns that make the Propagation.

Figure: The red Spread Triple line marks short Setups and the green
line marks long Setups. Real data: NZDUSD, 1-hour, 23 Feb – 4 Mar 2022.
(The original chart was EURSGD weekly, Oct 2020 – Jul 2023; this one
shows the same structure.)

The red line marks high-probability short Setups, and the green line
marks high-probability long Setups. The logic is simple:

• Along the green line there is no 1-2-3 down.

  • Along the red line there is no 1-2-3 up, so any long Setup will fail.
The magnet for Returns

These lines also usually act as a magnet for Returns. The Returns are
drawn to them when they meet the TP.

Figure: Each Return reaches the TP of the leg before it and stops on
the Spread Triple line ("Spread + TP"); the last Return fails to reach
its TP. Real data: EURUSD, 4-hour, 14 Feb – 4 Mar 2022. (The original
chart was NZDUSD weekly, Oct 2020 – Jul 2023; this one shows the same
structure.)

These TPs tell the story when they meet the Spread Triple lines. At
the TP the sellers lose 50% and the buyers gain 50%. The sellers must
also keep their pace of Return; the buyers must not exceed it.

Figure: Buyers exceed the orange line; the first counter Return holds
above the 50% TP of the first leg up, and buying Propagation grows. Real
data: USDJPY, 1-hour, 21–28 Feb 2022. (The original chart was USDJPY
weekly, Oct 2017 – May 2023; this one shows the same structure.)

Here the sellers are not willing to increase their offers. The first
Return occurs when price exceeds the line, and then buying Propagation
grows larger and larger. "Knowing others is wisdom."

Adding the EP Line of the
Propagation

Next, draw a line on the EP of the Propagation after the Spread
Triple Return line.

AUDCHF weekly, Oct 2020 – Jul 2023; this one shows the same

The green line shows where sellers lose their power, reach

that the market moves from equilibrium to disequilibrium, and so on.

Now watch how these lines affect the Propagation.

A Full Story (first read on
CADCHF)

Figure: The red Return line above and the green EP line below, with
the current price at the EP of the Propagation. Real data: EURJPY,
1-hour, 15 Feb – 4 Mar 2022. (The original chart was CADCHF weekly, Aug
2015 – Apr 2023; this one shows the same structure.)

Figure: Points A to F: the EP at A, the Return at B, the red Return
line, D speeding up, E breaking the pace, and F meeting the line through
A and C. Real data: USDJPY, 1-hour, 14–24 Feb 2022. (The original showed
CADCHF H4 and weekly side by side, 2019–2023, with the G and H lines on
the H4; this one shows the weekly A-to-F structure on one chart.)
The weekly picture

1. The story starts with the EP of the Propagation at A. It ends with a wide spread and an abnormal surge in volume.

2. The Return comes with a cancel at B, the EP of the SS. New selling arrives, shown by a wide-spread reversal bar with abnormal volume. No buyer is willing to pay a higher price at B.

3. Selling dominates the trend along the red Spread Triple line. Sellers are able to propagate lower, and no one is interested in taking their offers.

4. At D the pace of Propagation speeds up, but buyers break the pace at E.

5. Price re-propagates from E along the red line — the Return line — trying to make new lows at F. F meets the Matrix Overlay exactly, at the EP of the Propagation at C and A. The market is now in hesitation.
The H4 picture

On the lower time frame, H4, we have the Spread Triple line G and the
EP-of-Propagation line H. The black circles show that sellers fail to
make new lows, and buyers are willing to take the offers. The quality of
these buyers comes from three sources:

1. A, or the Matrix Overlay.

2. Sellers who shorted at B and now have a good profit to take.

3. Buyers who profited from the last Propagation and now want to re-enter the trade.
The real test

When the buyers gain more quality and break the G line, expect a
selling reaction. The sellers will also try, from the E Spread Triple
line, to continue the Propagation lower. This will be the real test of
whether the buyers can make a genuine move.

Following the Propagation
(2023)

In this paper I show how to follow the Propagation on a lower time
frame to judge a higher-time-frame Setup. I use six schematic examples
of 5-minute action inside a 1-hour SPS, then a real AUDCHF trade, and I
close with a two-step summary.
Reading a Dead Chart

A chart by itself is only a description of a shift in motion. When we
read the history of a bar chart, we are on the past axis — it is dead
motion. To make an intelligent decision, we must interpret that history
so that it builds an intelligent conclusion, based on a reasonable and
factual process.

Anyone who knows Goodman knows that the core of all price action is
the 1-2-3. That action has many implications from which we can draw new
conclusions.

Here is an abstract 1-2-3 inside a larger 1-2-3. Which one has the better odds of completing the 1-2-3 elements? In each example below, there is a Goodman Setup on the 1H, and the question is the same: what does the 5M action imply, and are the odds in favor of this being the EP of the SPS on the 1H?
Six Examples
Example 1

Figure: Example 1 — choppy 5M action with no fresh lows inside the 1H
SPS.

Is this 5M action more bullish? It is very clear: we have a Goodman
Setup on the 1H, and this is most likely the EP of the SPS on the
1H.
Example 2

Figure: Example 2 — 5M action that keeps making new lows, with the
last swing showing selling tiring.

This looks more bearish than bullish. Price can always move to a new
low without any hesitation. The only problem is the last swing: it
suggests the selling is temporarily tiring.
Example 3

Figure: Example 3 — a clean, low-volatility down Propagation on the
5M.

This is the most bearish example: a down Propagation with clear
direction and low volatility. The odds of this being the EP of the SPS
are very low. We can only treat it as a Jumbo and wait for more bullish
development.
Example 4

Figure: Example 4 — a breakaway low, then an up Propagation and a
last down Propagation that fails to make a new low.

Here the market has a breakaway. Sometimes this produces panic
behavior. Then the market tries to propagate up. The message of the last
down Propagation is that sellers are unable to make a new low — there is
a lack of sell orders. The odds are higher that this is the EP of the
SPS on the 1H.
Example 5

Figure: Example 5 — buyers try to end the down move (a weak sister),
but sellers re-propagate lower.

The buyers try to propagate and end the down movement, but the
sellers re-propagate for a further down move. This usually happens when
the 1H has no 3-C cancel, or a bad Overlay combination.
Example 6

Figure: Example 6 — a balancing Knot, with buyers and sellers
struggling to dominate the Matrix.

This is balancing — Knot behavior. Buyers and sellers struggle to
dominate the Matrix.
What the examples teach

These examples give an idea of what happens on a live chart: the most
bullish, the most bearish, where selling is only struggling, and where
the Setup may fail and sellers re-propagate. They are based on many real
charts.

Simply watch the up Propagation inside the down movement. Then
measure its effect on buyers and sellers: how do they react?

A Real Chart (first read on
AUDCHF)

Figure: A steady downtrend: is the latest low the EP of the SPS? Real
data: EURNZD, 4-hour, 14 Feb – 4 Mar 2022. (The original chart was
AUDCHF daily, July 2022 – May 2023; this one shows the same
structure.)

Is this the EP of the SPS? Let us watch how buyers and sellers play
on the lower time frame (the 4-hour in my original).

Figure: For the first time, buyers are able to propagate against the
downtrend. Real data: GBPJPY, 1-hour, 28 Feb – 3 Mar 2022. (The original
chart was AUDCHF H4, March–May 2023; this one shows the same
structure.)

This is the basic Goodman Setup. For the first time, buyers are able
to propagate against the downtrend. When price returned to the zone, I
entered at the Dagger — just like Example 4.

Goodman points are very critical: "something may happen". When they
intersect with a Propagation, they guide the direction at that point. It
is most likely to explode.
Summary

1. Define the Goodman point on the chart.

2. Follow the direction of the Propagation on the lower time frame.

Practice on the 3-C
Principle (2023)

In this practice I apply the 3-C principle to a real market, White
Sugar on the weekly chart. I take the count of a 6&6 as a box and
stack copies of it upward, to see where the up Propagation reacts and
where it finally halts.

Price as the Meeting of
Desires

At any price level there are many people who want to buy or sell. The
chart shows, as waves, their desires to fulfil their objectives. As in
life, every product has a price that depends on how much demand there is
and how much the supply costs. The price of a product represents the
current situation of BOTH demand and supply.

There are times when the activity of demand increases, such as
holidays. There are times when the activity of supply decreases, such as
war. This is always reflected in the price level.

I see the 3-C principle as a description of the situation of buying
and selling, together with their activity.
Practice 1: White Sugar
Building the boxes

Figure: The base count taken as a box and duplicated upward as levels
C1 to C4. Real data: AUDUSD, 2-hour, 14 Feb – 4 Mar 2022. (The original
chart was White Sugar weekly, 2018–2023, with levels C1 to C5 from a
6&6 count; this one shows the same structure.)

In Sugar we have a 6&6 Setup with a nice Jumbo (not shown on this
chart). I take the count of the 6&6 as a box. Then I duplicate the
same box many times, until the upward Propagation halts inside one of
these boxes. This gives the levels C1, C2, C3, C4 and C5.

Figure: The 6&6 count taken as a box and stacked upward as the
levels C1 to C5.
C1 and C2

Figure: The first up Propagation — EP-FPS above C1, the SS below, and
EP-SPS above C2. Real data: AUDUSD, 2-hour, 14 Feb – 4 Mar 2022. (The
original chart was White Sugar weekly, 2018–2023; this one shows the
same structure.)

Here the principle of Propagation plays an important role. At C1
price makes the EP of the FPS. Then it reacts and develops the EP of the
SS. Watch again how C1 plays an important role in building the SS, which
ends with the EP of the SPS exactly at the C2 price level.

Figure: Propagation from C2 — EP-FPS, then the EP-SS falling back to
the TP of the first FPS, near C1. Real data: AUDUSD, 2-hour, 14 Feb – 4
Mar 2022. (The original chart was White Sugar weekly, 2018–2023; this
one shows the same structure.)

At C2 price makes the EP of the FPS (Propagation 1). The EP of the SS
ends at the TP of the FPS, above C1. I apply the 3-C principle as a
projection for the SPS.
C3: Under and time hash

Figure: At C3 price moves into a trading range — a time hash. Real
data: AUDUSD, 2-hour, 14 Feb – 4 Mar 2022. (The original chart was White
Sugar weekly, 2018–2023, where the range formed exactly at the Under;
this one shows the same structure.)

When price hits C3, exactly at the Under, it moves into a trading
range — a time hash — without any reverse Propagation. It can also be
read as a minor Propagation (the green lines), and we can take a count
from it.
C4 and C5: The buying climax

Figure: A breakaway count out of the range, ending with EP-SPS at C4
on high volume. Real data: AUDUSD, 2-hour, 14 Feb – 4 Mar 2022. (The
original chart was White Sugar weekly, 2018–2023, running from C4 to C5;
this one shows the same structure one level lower.)

1. After the time hash, price hits C4 with a strong close-up bar. There is no hesitation, and things move very fast until price is very near C5.

2. I add a breakaway count and a minor Propagation count to support the picture.

3. The development ends with the EP of the SPS on high volume, which agrees with the breakaway count. This is a buying climax.

4. Buyers are unable to break the C5 level. This is the EP of the SPS of the Propagation, so we expect a large reaction for the EP of the SS.

5. Watch for the sign of a break down through the C4 level, with a down bar closing on its low.
Conclusion

I conclude that the duplication of counts, as in this practice, stays
valid for a long time — here from 2019 to 2023, and it is still
active.
Is That a Setup? (2023)

On a 5-minute chart I saw a nice Goldilocks. But is it a trade
candidate? In this short paper I test that question the strict way, by
placing the pattern inside its 1-2-3 on every time frame before I

The Rule: A Setup Lives
Inside a 1-2-3

Rung 5 · Acting: How Do
I Manage the Trade?
From the entry to the exit: protecting the trade, then letting it run.
Trading the Line (2021)

This paper is about Trading The Line (TTL). I want to show why the
current moment is all a trader really owns, and how to manage a trade
from one moment to the next. Then I walk through a real trade, raising
the stop with every new propagation. I first traded it on EURUSD; the
charts here redraw the same structure on real AUDUSD 1-hour data.
There Is No Future, Only Now

Every chart has a past and a current price. Time never stops, so the
current price soon becomes the past. Even the happiest moment on a chart
becomes past.

What about the future? There is no future. The future is only a
sequence that starts from the current moment. What is important is NOW,
the current moment.
Run fast or do not run at all.
I write it like this:
Future = Current Moment + Current Moment + … + Current Moment

When I let the current moment slip out of my control, I blame the
future. But there is no future, only the sum. The future is just a
compound of many past current moments. That is why a grandfather or a
father can anticipate his child so easily. Most of the time he is
right.

Figure: Only the current moment: the past is gone, and the future is
only the sum of the moments you manage.
A Protected Plan

That is why we need a protected plan, a kind of economic plan. Think of the film Cast Away with Tom Hanks. He could eat everything in one day, but he knows there is no guaranteed future. So he splits things: enough for today, the rest for the next day.
"Don't put all your eggs in one basket."
This is a logical way to manage the current moment.

Every market moment is unique. We never get a duplicate current
moment. It is like a passport number: it cannot be duplicated, it must
be a unique ID.

We do not need to know the future of a chart to make a profit. We
only need to know the current movement and manage it.
Driving on a Foggy Day

The market is exactly like driving on a very foggy day. We can see
only about 100 metres ahead. That is how markets look.

Anyone who drives in such conditions must be very careful and
cautious. Accidents can happen at any time. Trading the Line is like
driving carefully on a foggy day. It is risky, but with good management
one can reach the goal.

We manage the Line by concentrating and staying alert to anything
that happens to it. When we drive a Line, we do not want an accident
that causes damage. There is no right or wrong in such conditions; it is
a dangerous case, and we must protect ourselves.

Our goal is to avoid damage. When we cannot, we make the damage as
small as possible: a very soft accident.

Mr. Goodman does not accept any huge accident. Trading without a
stop-loss can lead to a large loss. Cut it quickly. Run fast.
"If you break even, you live to see another day." – Michael Archer, my mentor

More control on a foggy day is better than arriving quickly with huge
damage.

Anyone who wants to support a family by treating trading as a
business should not care about the destination. Care about the moment,
and drive slowly.

The Tool That Keeps Me
Focused

One tool keeps me very concentrated when I trade TTL: watching the
Line.
"Follow the Lines and the Tests/Exceeds."

It simply follows the BP and EP of each leg. When I operate TTL, my
goal is to save my position as much as I can, or at least to exit with
small damage. I do not like accidents. I take advantage of stop orders
to manage the trade.

The Goodman rule is clear: each time the market makes a new 1-2-3 in
the direction of the trade, and assuming you have not been stopped out,
bring your stop-loss to the most current SS EP. In short: with every new
propagation, raise the stop.

Figure: The Propagation Jumbo: each new propagation is larger, and
the stop (STP) is raised under each one.

Figure: The TTL stop routine: with each new 1-2-3 in the direction of
the trade, move the stop to the latest SS EP.

Real Driving: One Trade,
Step by Step
1. The breakaway

Here the market breaks away with increasing volume, and the Line
starts. The operation begins after a Dagger, at the first
propagation.

Figure: The Dagger bar at the low, the breakaway bar on rising
volume, and the first propagation (1-2-3) where the operation starts.
Real data: AUDUSD, 1-hour, 14–18 February 2022. (The original chart was
EURUSD 4-hour, March–April 2021; this one shows the same structure.)
2. The first stop raise

When the market breaks the EP of the first propagation, I raise the
stop to the same level as the buy order. We are not yet at break-even,
but at least we are protected.

Figure: The buy triggers above 1 of the first propagation, and the
stop (STP) moves up to its point 2. Real data: AUDUSD, 1-hour, 14–18
February 2022. (The original chart was EURUSD 4-hour, 2021; this one
shows the same structure.)
3. Watching the next 1-2-3

The next step is to watch the next 1-2-3, using Lines with their Test
and Exceed levels. Here there are two Lines, green and dark purple. When
the small dark-purple propagation finishes, I move my stop-loss.

Figure: Two Lines, the first (green) and the second (purple), with
the Exceed level of the first propagation marked. Real data: AUDUSD,
1-hour, 14–21 February 2022. (The original chart was EURUSD 4-hour,
2021; this one shows the same structure.)
4. The time-hash

Through the time-hash our trade still makes good profit, so we
continue the drive. The green propagation grows larger.

Figure: The time hash: price works sideways between the Exceed and
Test lines, and the stop is raised beneath it. Real data: AUDUSD,
1-hour, 14–22 February 2022. (The original chart was EURUSD 4-hour,
2021; this one shows the same structure.)

5. A new count for each
propagation

I suggest making a new count for every new propagation. It helps
measure the energy behind every PTS and makes us more conservative about
the next target. When the market breaks away for the PTS 2 target, it
moves sideways.

Figure: PTS1 and PTS2 counts; a new count for each propagation helps
find the next Line target. Real data: AUDUSD, 1-hour, 14–22 February

6. Propagating the bold green
Line

Here the bold green Line propagates with the smaller one inside it,

February 2022. (The original chart was EURUSD 4-hour, 2021; this one

7. Above the Under

When the market moves above the Under, I take the breakaway count

February 2022. (The original chart was EURUSD 4-hour, 2021; this one
shows the same structure.)
8. Booked profit

Up to here the trade shows a solid open profit: 127 pips at the
high.

Figure: The trade in solid profit: the larger Line clears its Exceed

AUDUSD, 1-hour, 14–23 February 2022. (The original chart was EURUSD
4-hour, 2021; this one shows the same structure.)
9. The PTS target reached

The market propagates into a larger structure and arrives exactly at

February 2022. (The original chart was EURUSD 4-hour, 2021; this one
