10. New propagation, new stop
Let's play with the new propagating 1-2-3 and raise the stop.

I raise the stop-loss again; the blue (powder) Line gives me a
1-2-3.

We play the last propagation, but the market's move is over. Price

13. Looking for a Setup in
the downturn
Now let's find a Setup in the downturn.

Figure: After the top, the market turns down through the last stop,

What This Study Shows

From this study we kept a profit from the uptrend: on this data the
stop was caught at +64 pips, against 70 pips of first risk. The open
profit had reached 127 pips, and the raised stops saved half of it. The
move followed the same shape as the Propagation Jumbo shown earlier.

The study also shows what Trading the Line adds compared with only
taking the Under. Our first protection came at the breakaway (see the
first chart), and the trade finally stopped out at the end of the last
propagation. The same Lines then gave the sell in the downturn, which
ran 126 pips.
Here is the whole operation using TTL:

Figure: The full TTL operation: entry after the Dagger, stops raised
through each 1-2-3, the 6x6 top where the stop is caught (on this data
+64 pips against 70 pips of first risk), then 126 pips from the sell.
Real data: AUDUSD, 1-hour, 14–25 February 2022. (The original chart was
EURUSD 4-hour, 2021, where the stop was caught for 3,897 pips of profit
against 500 pips of risk; this one shows the same structure.)

Trading with TTL is effective because it protects what the market
gives. Here the uptrend part was modest, yet the same routine kept the
risk small and turned the top into a 126-pip sell. On my original EURUSD
chart, the same routine kept 3,897 pips against 500 pips of risk.

Three
Swiss Franc Trades: When the Overlay Is Not Ready (2025)

In this paper I review three short-term trades I took in the Swiss
franc pairs (AUDCHF, EURCHF and USDCHF) in March 2025. Each one starts
from a Jumbo. The charts are redrawn on real 2022 data from other pairs,
named in each caption, with the same structure. The lesson is about the
Overlay: the Setup chart can be clear while the Overlay chart is not
ready yet.
Trade 1: AUDCHF
The idea

This was a nice Jumbo. I was looking exactly at the arrow, hoping to
find a short-term trade. The logic behind it: this is the EP of the
Jumbo, and the first 1-2-3 will occur here.

Figure: A large Jumbo down; the arrow marks where I expect the EP of
the Jumbo and the first 1-2-3. Real data: GBPUSD, 1-hour, 21–25 Feb
2022. (The original chart was AUDCHF 4-hour, published 5 Mar 2025; this
one shows the same structure.)
On the 15-minute chart there was a nice 3S Setup.

Figure: The 1-2-3 up from the EP of the Jumbo, then the 3S Setup and
the buy point. Real data: GBPUSD, 15-minute, 24–25 Feb 2022. (The
original chart was AUDCHF 15-minute, 4–5 Mar 2025; this one shows the
same structure.)

The
difficulty: finding the EP of the Jumbo in the Overlay

What made this trade difficult? Finding the EP of the Jumbo in the
Overlay chart. Let us look at the daily chart (redrawn here on 1-hour
data).

Figure: The Matrix Overlay (MO) above the Line and the breakdown
below it, marked by the arrow. Real data: GBPUSD, 1-hour, 15–25 Feb

It is an MO, and I suspected the EP might occur earlier than this

What actually happened
My first idea was here.

The hint I should have seen

One hint: the 1-2-3 was too small compared with the Jumbo. This is a

This is the 4-hour structure (shown here on a 1-hour chart): a nice

A nice Jumbo again. One can follow the lack of follow-through when

USDCHF 5-minute, 5 Mar 2025; this one shows the same structure.)
How I Manage a Trade

Charlie taught me to read the market. Managing a trade is the part I
had to build for myself, one email at a time. When I look back at what I
wrote to you, Michael, I see the same few ideas coming back, each time a
little cleaner.
The first aim is breakeven

In May 2021 I wrote to you about breakeven, and I still stand by
every word: "The importance of BreakEven. if I am right the meanings of
break-even the level trades start to show a profit. if I protect the
breakeven and the market doesn't play against me I will Take The line."
And then the sentence I would put on my wall: "GoodMan this is the first
aim to traders." (May 10, 2021)

I used football then, and I still like the picture. Once the trade is
at BE, my goal is safe. The other team cannot score against me. Now I
can attack. My money, my experience, and the price of testing my idea
are all protected.

Breakeven is not a target for profit. It is a target for safety. A
trade that reaches BE can no longer hurt the account, and a mind that
knows this can think clearly about the rest.
Nests inside the big play

By September 2022 I had added a second layer. I would see a setup on
the hourly or daily chart, but I would enter on a smaller Nest, on the
5-minute chart, often from a Dagger. The quick trade had one job: to pay
for the risk of the big one.

I wrote to you after one such trade: "so I entered in 5 min and my
aim was to cover the risk of playing with 1 hour - daily chart. my idea
is simply to play anything that covers the origin risk of BIG PLAY."
(September 20, 2022)

This is a simple idea, but it changes how the trade feels. Once the
small trade has paid for the risk of the large one, the large one is
free. I can let it breathe. I am no longer staring at every bar.
Under, Over and Line

Every trade I take ends in one of a few places. It goes to BE. It
reaches the Under. It reaches the Line. Or it goes Over and I am out at
a loss. Later I started to label every trade this way, and I will tell
that story in the next chapter.

For management, the rule is plain. Protect at BE. Take part of the
trade at the Under. Let the rest run to the Line. If I close everything
early, my average win shrinks and my whole system weakens. If I never
take anything, the market takes it back. The Under pays the bills; the
Line pays for the years.

Figure: The path of one managed trade, from the Outward scan to the
Line.
The order of qualification

In July 2024 you sent me a sequence for deciding on a trade. I kept
the steps, but I changed the order to match how my own mind works. I
called it my "Top -Down approach":

"1)Do Outward analysis (Propagation Chart) if nothing interesting
look for another chart." (July 3, 2024)

Then I identify a basic 6 & 6 or Goldilocks setup. Then the
Parameter analysis on a clean chart. Then Inward analysis. Then I decide
if the setup is qualified enough for me. Then I consider the Risk-Reward
Ledger. Only then do I watch for an entry.

The first step is the important one. If the propagation chart does
not interest me, I do not force it. I move to the next chart. Most of my
protection comes from the trades I never take.
Money-management profiles

By December 2024 I had put the whole method into a short list for
myself: setup, parameters, entry, outside analysis, and money
management. For money management I named five profiles: "Money
management : Walts ,Samba ,Bert,tiny dancer ,Fixed ." And under it I
wrote: "It's simple , more systematic . but Require Each of them
separate profiles ! . each profiles Fits as a Risk Strategy model ."
(December 25, 2024)

Each of these is a different way to split and manage a position: how
much at the Under, how much for the Line, when to move to BE, how much
to add. Fixed is the simplest: one size, no changes. The point is not
which profile is best. The point is that I choose one before I enter,
and I know which risk model I am running. I do not invent the management
in the middle of the trade.
A trade I was not proud of

I want to include one trade where I broke my own rules, because it
taught me more than ten good ones.

In August 2024 I bought AUDCAD. I made money. But when I looked at
the numbers, I was not happy: "117p Risk : 59p Reward , which is a bad
raito . almost 1 RISK TO 0.5 Reward". The lesson I wrote that day was
short: "Entry is important , Risk /Reward . such mistakes aren't
suitable for PRO! ." (August 29, 2024)

A profit does not make a trade good. If I keep risking two to make
one, the arithmetic will catch me sooner or later, even with a high win
rate. This trade was a win on the statement and a loss in the
process.

Questions before I accept a
risk

In February 2026 I tried to make my risk decisions more formal.
Before I accept a trade, I ask a few questions. How could this setup
fail? Which Overlays am I relying on, and which am I ignoring? What is
the impact if I am wrong? Is there whitespace, and is the chart
clean?

Then I wrote the rule for acceptance: "Logically the risk accept when
1) the impact of risk its very low impact that it's fine to live with.
2) the risk is very low compare to profit." (February 2, 2026)

The next day I added something I did not expect to write: "the
smaller risk if avoided will generate larger risk! . don't think about
profit , profits that's what we want , but if not protect the process
will lead to big loss." (February 3, 2026)

A trader who refuses every small risk will one day take a large one
out of frustration. Accepting small, known, livable risks is how the
process stays alive.
What ties it together

Looking at these five years, I see one movement. In 2021 I only knew
that BE came first. In 2022 I learned to make the small trade pay for
the big one. In 2024 I put the qualification in my own order, named my
management profiles, and was honest about my mistakes. In 2026 I turned
risk acceptance into questions.

None of this replaced Goodman. It is the frame around Goodman. The
Measured Move tells me where the Line is. Management decides whether I
am still in the trade when price gets there.

Rung 6 · Measuring: How
Much Do I Risk?
The arithmetic that keeps a trader alive long enough to be right.

Thirty Souls: The
Arithmetic of Survival

I have always believed that trading is a business, and that the
hardest problem in any business is cash flow. I told you this in my
early letters, Michael: I came to the market from account management,
and managing money is the part I enjoy. Over five years my rules about
size changed shape many times. The core never changed. I decide what I
can lose first, and only then do I look at the chart.
2021: the strict plan
In February 2021 I sent you my plan. It was short and strict:

"1) I never risk more than 1.5 for every trade . or i am gamble 😂 2)
I never open trades more than 6% of all my balance . 3) I never increase
my lot until I double my balance" (February 22, 2021)

There was more. After 10 trades, if the result was not right, I
reduced my lot. I never entered without a risk/reward. And if a trade
was good but too expensive for me, I let it go and waited for the next
one. I wrote then that I did not care about single trades: what matters
is who wins at the end of the game.

Reading it now, I see a young rule set. It was about limits. It did
not yet ask where the limits come from.
2022: the Green and Red signals

In October 2022 I tried to connect size to psychology. A trader can
be conservative, aggressive, or urgent, and each needs a different
allocation. Above, there is a greedy zone; below, a danger zone. I did
not want to move between them by feeling, so I made a rule:

"Green, Red signal policy.each critical points 5% lose 10% profit."
(October 22, 2022)

A green signal, after 10% profit, allows the size to grow: for
example, 1% of 100,000 plus 1% of the last 10% profit. A red signal,
after a 5% loss, does the opposite. It forbids the losses from
expanding, and the size comes down.

Figure: The Green / Red signal policy. Size changes only at critical
points.

2023: divide the drawdown by
thirty

By April 2023 the rule had turned around. I no longer started from a
percentage per trade. I started from the drawdown I was willing to live
with:

"I have always decided, on my max DD, then I divide it into 30
trades. if my capital is 20,000 . and I want only to risk 5%DD . the max
loss is 1000, I divide it into 30 trades opportunity . so the max risk
for every trade is 33 USD." (April 13, 2023)

Then every 10 trades I review and study the Overlay combinations. One
to five trades a week. That was the whole plan.

This was a real change. In 2021 the per-trade risk decided my
drawdown. In 2023 the drawdown decided my per-trade risk.

2023: the Golden Ratio and the
labels

In August 2023 I began labelling every trade: BE, Under, Over, Line,
and for the losses, mistake, bad entry, or lack of discipline. "Now each
of the trades from 300 has a specific label. These labels for sure
changes the game." (August 11, 2023) Once a trade has a name, a losing
streak is no longer a fog. I can see whether it came from the market or
from me.

In October 2023 I called the control of risk the chassis of a system,
like the chassis of a race car, and I put the Golden Ratio inside it:
the percentage of winners in each 10 trades, and the average win against
the average loss. "Golden Raito is standing behind the Probability of
Ruin." (October 6, 2023) By December I was calling it the "Blood heart"
(December 12, 2023).

In May 2024 I wrote down how to read it: "If my winning trades less
than 4 out of 10. Its suggest ether have issue in one of psychology
pattren. Or my choice in Market environment dosnt fit well." And if the
average win falls below 1:2, "I know i make very bad judgment. I did not
take under nor going for lines." (May 25, 2024)

So the ratio is not only a score. It is a diagnosis. It tells me
where to look.
2025: expect the worst

In January 2025 I described four kinds of equity periods: a rare best
streak, a worst streak of maybe 10 losses in a row, a rare run of trades
near BE, and the normal days, the stairs of one step up and a little
down that Charlie called 10-4-1. If I want a maximum drawdown of 2.5%,
the simplest way is to size so that 10 losses in a row still fit.
"Knowing the boundaries decreasing the surprising element .. its about
surviving first . The goal is BE.!" (January 24, 2025)

A few weeks earlier I had written something that sits under all of
this: "I know there will be many time i lose money. Its threat to the
capital . But i believe in methodology, its the edge i have . So its
kind of balance rather than trying to eliminate risk from the equation."
(January 4, 2025)
2025: thirty souls
In March 2025 the idea found its final form, and its name:

"Keep in mind we are trading the money not the market. so, every
trade is part of 30 trades, find the best or simply no action. you do
not have many souls in the market, have only 30 souls! take the best to
survive after 30 trades." (March 5, 2025)

Thirty souls means each trade spends one life. I do not spend a life
on a setup I only half believe. The first goal of the series is to
survive it, at least at breakeven. Profit comes from the probability
being on my side over the whole series, not from any one trade.
Figure: How my sizing rules grew from 2021 to 2026.

What the arithmetic
actually looks like

I wanted to see my rule run, not only describe it. So we simulated
it. The edge is the one I used as an example in my letters: 40% winners
at two times the risk, 60% losers at one. The size is my rule: a 5%
maximum drawdown divided by 30, which is about 0.17% per trade.

Over 10,000 simulated series of 30 trades, not one touched the 5%
limit. The median series ended about 1% up. Around three in ten ended
slightly down, which is honest: 30 trades is a short road. But nobody
died.

Then the same edge at higher sizes, over 100 trades. At 1% per trade,
a drawdown of 20% from the peak happened in about 2% of runs. At 1.5%,
in about 16%. At 2%, in about 41%. At 3%, in about 79%. Same system,
same win rate, same reward. Only the size changed.

Figure: A simulation of my max-DD/30 rule (illustration, not a
forecast), with simulated risk of ruin at higher sizes.

This is the whole chapter in one picture. The edge is the engine. The
size decides whether you are still driving when the edge pays.
Expectancy as momentum

In July 2025, after our talks about Molokai, I tried to write the
same thing as a line. There are two kinds of curves close to
compounding: "Y = kx" and "Y = k/x." In one, things multiply and riches
come to the door. In the other, things divide and poverty comes to the
door.

With my example edge: 0.4 times 2, minus 0.6 times 1, gives 0.2. "0.2
is the factor. K . While x is money." And then the advice to myself:
"You don't need to modify the factor. Just keep it consistently. But add
more money slowly" (July 18, 2025)

Keep k steady by keeping the Golden Ratio healthy. Grow x slowly. In
December 2024 I had already said I like to trade at a risk of ruin of
around 0 to 5% in my simulations. The momentum line is the same idea,
seen from the other side.

The Market
Environment as money management

My latest step, in August 2025, was to see the Market Environment
itself as part of money management. "Flat jumbo + setup . Is less risky
than a propagation jumbo with a setup." And: "Make each a setup its a
part of money managment. Each setup may play a rule . Maybe for a more
gains . Or a hedge , or a decrease the risk." (August 30, 2025)

Size is one lever. Choosing which environment to trade, and combining
setups from different environments, is another.

FireStarter: a separate
strategy

I must say clearly that one rule in my letters belongs to a different
strategy. FireStarter is quick trading on the 5-minute chart or less,
with PTS, Goldilocks and 66, and the Overlay mostly PO and Nest. It has
its own money management, and it does not replace anything above.

"Divide the capital into 30 or 50. Never change the size either in
losses or either in profit. NEVER." (March 5, 2025)

In FireStarter I do not adjust the size, and I do not watch the
drawdown closely, because the trades are quick and the win ratio does
the work. I also wrote that the mind cannot run two profiles at once:
"Firestarter, or nothing." When I trade it, I trade only it.
What I learned

From 1.5% in 2021 to thirty souls in 2025, the rules grew more
patient and more humble. They moved from "how much can I risk?" to "how
much can I survive?" The arithmetic is not exciting. It is what lets the
exciting part happen again tomorrow.

The
Error-Proof Trader: Poka-Yoke in Trading (2026)

Thirty Souls is about the arithmetic of survival. This chapter is
about the engineering of it. The arithmetic tells me how much I can
lose. The engineering makes sure I cannot lose it by mistake.

Mistakes are an operations
risk

On 2026-04-03 I wrote to Michael that trading needs three things
aligned: the dynamic market, the trading system, and yourself.
"If have a system not aligned with market means losing. If have a good system deals with market but unable to be discipline with means also losing. Making mistake is a operations risk to the system."

My background in risk work taught me to separate risks by where they
come from. Market risk is the price going against a good setup. I accept
it, because it is part of the 10-4-1. Operations risk is different. It
is the trade without a stop, the lot typed wrong, the revenge entry
after a loss. Years ago I defined it simply: "Mistakes = any
controllable action in wrong time." Market risk I manage. Operations
risk I should remove.
Finding the causes first

Before you can block a mistake, you have to know where it comes from.
On 2026-02-03 I wrote:
"the smaller risk if avoided will generate larger risk! . don't think about profit , profits that's what we want , but if not protect the process will lead to big loss. i like fishbone diagram"

The fishbone diagram is a quality tool. You write the problem at the
head, a bad trade, and draw the bones behind it: method, mind, size,
market, review. Each bone holds the causes. When I draw it for my own
losses, most of the bones are not about the market at all. They are
about me.

The day before, on 2026-02-02, I wrote the questions I ask before I
accept a trade:

"1)how could the setup fails? 2)at which overlays i rely and what the sign's tell me wrong about the combination. Then 3) what the impact when i am wrong. Its too high? 4) where is the causal factor? Have whitespace? Its clean?"

And the rule for acceptance: "Logically the risk accept when 1) the
impact of risk its very low impact that it's fine to live with. 2) the
risk is very low compare to profit." This is a risk register for one
trade. The failure modes are named before money is at stake.
Measuring the mind

A mistake starts in a state of mind, so I measure the state. On
2026-03-17 I sent Michael a table for rating emotion from 1 to 10 at
each checkpoint: before the trade, at entry, during it, at exit, after
it, and at random moments when I am only watching. The scale is simple.
1–2 is very angry or frustrated. 3–4 is nervous or uncomfortable. 5–6 is
calm and in control. 7–8 is confident and energized. 9–10 is too excited
or overconfident.

The point is in the two ends. A 9 is as dangerous as a 2. The best
trading happens in the middle, at 5 or 6. As I wrote under the table:
"Monitoring your emotions helps keep them under control."

Poka-Yoke: make the error
impossible

Poka-Yoke is a Japanese engineering principle. It means
mistake-proofing: a mechanism in a process that prevents, corrects, or
draws attention to a human error as it happens. A plug that fits only
one way is Poka-Yoke. Nobody needs discipline to plug it in
correctly.

On 2026-09-17 I told Michael I had used the idea for years and
finally turned it into a trading expert for MetaTrader 5:
"I converted it into a trading expert that almost guarantees what most traders fail to achieve: letting me trade easily, focused only on the setup, with less thinking on "money"."

The idea behind it is that most traders do not fail from poor
analysis. They fail from one disastrous event: a trade without a stop,
revenge after a loss, overconfidence after a streak, doubling down to
recover. So the expert does not touch the analysis. It guards the
failure modes.

Figure: The twelve protection layers of the Poka-Yoke Guardian, each
one a guard against a named failure mode, grouped by where the error
comes from: size, mind, method, market and review.
The twelve layers
The layers fall into five groups.

Size. Layer 1 calculates the lot from the real stop distance, which I set by dragging a line on the chart, so there is no guessing. Layer 2 fixes the maximum drawdown for a 30-trade cycle and locks it until the campaign ends. This is my Thirty Souls rule, made into a lock. Layer 3 watches floating equity and closes everything if the daily limit is breached. Layer 4 is anti-Martingale: after losing days the size steps down, 100% to 75% to 50% to 25% and then a full stop, and it returns to 100% after a winning day. Layer 8 caps the total risk open across all trades.

Mind. Layer 5 is a cooling-off period: after a loss, no new trade on the same pair for a set time. Revenge trading simply cannot happen. Layer 7 will not execute a trade until I write a clear reason and record my state: calm, excited, frustrated or tired. Layer 11 asks for extra confirmation after a series of wins, because overconfidence is the 9 on my emotion scale.

Method. Layer 6 is the Propagation Lens in five stages: Propagation, Intersection, 3-C Count, Overlays, Dagger. The stages cannot be skipped, and cancelling one invalidates all the stages after it. This is the 1-2-3 of my reading, enforced.
Market. Layer 9 is the Correlated Exposure Barrier, which stops two trades on the same currency. Layer 10 filters high-impact news before and after the event.
Review. Layer 12 calculates the Golden Ratios every 10 and 30 trades and keeps a permanent log, with chart snapshots at every entry and exit.
Every layer follows one principle: "When in doubt, block—don't allow." If the news filter cannot verify the calendar, it stops trading rather than assuming it is safe.
What it cannot do

I was honest with Michael about the limits. "The system manages your analytical edge; it does not create one." If the analysis is weak, it slows the bleeding but does not stop it. Fixed size grows slower than compounding, and that is a choice, not a flaw. And it depends on my honesty when I type my reason and my state. It stops automatic rule-breaking, not deliberate lies.

I wrote that it is "good for beginners and those who have lack
discipline." I would add: it is good for experienced traders on their
bad days. Fifty years did not make me immune to a 9 on the scale.
What I keep

• Market risk is accepted; operations risk is removed.

  • Find the causes with a fishbone before building the guard.

  • Ask how the setup can fail before asking what it can make.

  • Rate the mind. The middle of the scale is where good trades live.

  • Do not rely on willpower under pressure. Build the guard once, and let it hold.

Rung 7 · Doing
Right: How Do We Treat Each Other?
Charlie believed what you do to others returns to you with interest. Six chapters, including Michael's favorite.
15. The oboe
A story Michael calls long, with a short lesson.

Walter was a Vietnam veteran in poor shape. Michael believes he had
been close to a landmine when it exploded. He had many mental problems
and was slow to think and to move. He had once been considered a top
oboe scholarship prospect, but chose the Army because his father had
been a military man.

Charlie suggested Walter take up the oboe again, mostly as therapy.
Double-reed instruments are not cheap, so Charlie gave him about two
hundred dollars to find a decent used one.

A few days later Walter came back with an oboe, and for him, because
his emotions were very muted, he was excited. He had answered a
newspaper ad from an old woman who lived alone. The oboe was a
professional-quality instrument worth several thousand dollars. His plan
was to sell it, buy a cheaper one and pocket two or three thousand.

Charlie questioned him. The woman was very poor. Her husband had been
a professional musician, and she clearly suffered from some form of
dementia. Charlie explained that Walter could sell the oboe, buy an
inexpensive one, and take the rest of the money back to her. "Oh, no,
Charlie! I can do a lot with the money."

Charlie told him he would never take such money. "The longer you
wait, the worse things will get, Walter. At some point the universe has
to re-establish a balance by punishing you. And it charges interest.
Something might happen to you years from now and you'll have no idea
why, but it will be for taking advantage of an old woman years before.
There are infinite connections among things in this world and we should
not disturb them if we can avoid it."

Walter did not listen. He sold the oboe, bought a cheap one and kept
the money. In the next few weeks, as Michael remembers: the cheap oboe
had a crack in the body and was worthless; he got a flat tire on the
highway; the doctor he liked at the military hospital moved away and the
new doctor would not give him a medicine he needed; and a pipe broke and
flooded his small apartment. Each time something happened, Charlie said,
"Take the money back to the old woman, Walter."

Finally Walter decided to return the money, but admitted he had spent
some. Charlie gave him the difference. He took the money back. On the
way home he stopped for something to eat and met a really nice
girlfriend, who helped him with the things he found difficult.

Charlie reminded him that if he had never returned it, it would have
been a black cloud over his life, and some day it would rain very hard
on him.
What it means. A wrong you leave unrepaired grows. Charlie's rule was practical: pay it back early, while it is small.
Try this. Think of one thing you owe someone, a reply, an apology, a few dollars. Settle it today.

16. Never think about
getting paid back
The Corvair that went to a young mother.

One morning Charlie called Michael and asked for a lift to the bus
station. Michael joked: "They finally caught up with you and you have to
leave town!" Charlie laughed. He only wanted to take the bus down to
Eads.

Two days later he called again. When Michael arrived, Charlie had
brought another Corvair to Denver and was washing it. "What's the deal?"
"I have a gal who needs a car to go to a new job and take her baby to
day care, so I'm giving her this car."

Michael said, "That's nice of you, Charlie! You'll get paid back for
the good deed."

"Dad, when you do something for someone you NEVER think about getting
paid back. You do it because it is the right thing to do. Thinking you
will be rewarded spoils the gift!"
What it means. A gift with a hidden invoice is a trade. Charlie wanted to be clear about which one he was making.
Try this. Do one favor this week that no one will ever know about.

17. The fifty-dollar
investment
Charlie at the dog track, explained like Socrates.

Charlie liked to play the dog races for relaxation. Sometimes he and
Michael went every night for a week or two. During one of those
stretches a younger man at the track befriended Charlie. Michael did not
like the man but said nothing. After several nights the man asked
Charlie to lend him $50, which he would pay back a little at a time
whenever they met.

Michael was surprised to see Charlie hand it over. It was fairly
clear that the man had been setting Charlie up. Of course they never saw
him again.
"Didn't you know he was just setting you up?" Michael asked.

"Of course I did. He invested a lot of energy over several days to
get that job done. It was well planned. Because he expended so much
energy, the misdeed of stealing $50 will stick to him like glue until he
does some act to undo it. It's different than if he just picked
somebody's pocket on the spur of the moment. He won't be able to shake
loose of it. Either he will die with it or it will turn his life around
eventually. So I invested $50 in him."

Michael adds that after fifty years he cannot give the words
verbatim, but they are close.
What it means. Charlie treated a theft as an investment in another person's conscience. It cost him $50 and did not cost him his peace.
Try this. The next time someone wrongs you in a small way, ask what the wrong will cost them before you ask what it cost you.
18. The lake and the bathtub
A Goodmanism Michael had forgotten for fifty years.

Michael remembered this while walking one of his dogs around a small
lake, when he saw a man with a metal detector searching the shore. "I
have not thought of this for a LONG time. That tells me there are
probably still some Goodmanisms and Charlie stories locked up in my poor
old brain!"

One morning at Peavey, one of the younger traders was having no
success. He had tried this and that and now announced, "Charlie, I've
decided instead of studying all these markets I'm going to concentrate
on just two markets!"

Charlie replied: "If you can't find water in a lake, how do you
expect to find it in a bathtub?"

Figure: If there is no water in the lake of all markets, narrowing to
a bathtub of two will not find any.

Michael wrote that he laughs on and off for half an hour every time
he thinks of it. When someone at home asked why, he said, "Fifty years
ago I can still hear Charlie's voice and see his smile. It makes me
happy and brings peace to my mind!"
What it means. Narrowing your focus does not fix a method that does not work. First find an edge, then narrow.
Try this. Write down what you believe your edge is, in one sentence. If you cannot, simplifying will not help.

19. When we enter someone
else's house
Olives in the spaghetti.

Michael introduces this one as impossible to unpack until you hear
the story. One of Dave Downs' bankers was giving a birthday party for
his granddaughter, who wanted a big party. He told Dave to bring
friends. So Dave invited Michael and Charlie and brought his own
ten-year-old granddaughter. The four of them drove to Cherry Hills
Farms, an area of big houses on large lots. The banker's house was at
least 12,000 square feet on two acres.

They peeked into the kitchen, which was the size of a small house
itself and a frenzy of activity. Near them someone was mixing a can of
olives into a large bowl of spaghetti. Dave's granddaughter whispered,
with great certainty, "Grandpa, you don't put olives in spaghetti!"

Charlie took Michael aside and said, "When we enter someone else's
house, we are all children."

Michael's first reading was that you must be deferential in someone
else's domain. "Close, but Charlie's take was much deeper." Each of us
learns to do routine things in a certain way and forgets there are other
ways to do the same task. The girl had never seen olives in spaghetti,
so she thought it was wrong. We do the same when we meet a different way
of doing things, and reject it out of hand.

Decades later Michael heard a child say, "That's not the way you make
bread!" and the phrase came straight back to him.
What it means. When you meet a method, a culture or a person that does it differently, be a student first.
Try this. This week, when you disagree with another trader's approach, ask them to show you one trade from start to finish before you say anything.
20. Do you wrap up your poop?
The Petroleum Club, 1970s.

Jerry Peters, the Bache broker, took Michael and Charlie to lunch at
the Petroleum Club in Denver, a plush penthouse for oil men. It was the
1970s oil boom and everyone was making easy cash. At the next table,
three or four oil men were splitting the proceeds of a deal. They began
arguing loudly about how much each should get.

Charlie said: "They act like they are going to take it with them when
they die. Money is the last thing you want in the next world! Do you
wrap up your poop and take it with you on vacation?"

Michael calls it one of his favorites. He says Charlie had a special,
unique mind.
What it means. If you cannot take it with you, then how you hold it matters more than how much you hold.
Try this. Ask yourself what the money in your account is for. Write the answer on the first page of your trading journal.
Our Conversations on Value

Charlie's stories about doing right were never only about Charlie.
Over six years of letters, Michael and I kept returning to the same
question from different doors: what is knowledge worth, who should pay
for it, and what does a teacher owe the world? Michael had a short, sad,
funny name for the problem. He called it "Pearls -> Pork Chops." You
give pearls; people treat them like a plate of pork chops, or walk past
them altogether. This chapter collects our exchanges on that theme. I
have put his words first, then mine, and then what I think now.
Pearls -> Pork Chops

Michael, 2024-05-07, as he began posting free articles on
Substack:

"Years ago I asked to give full seminar on Goodman. I prepare two weeks, long ppt I think close to 200 slides!... About half-way through first session on Basic Principles everyone has blank look on faces. I hear Charlie, 'Dad, these people are here for a free lunch and you just told them there's no such thing as a free lunch!' Think same with SubS but try for a few weeks."

A week later, 2024-05-15: "Half-way done with this 'experiment'...
Pearls -> Pork Chops. :( Golden Ratios post should have 10k read
ahaha."
My reply on the Golden Ratios article, 2024-05-09:
"Amazing article. I read it many times to absorb. Golden ratio assessment every 10 trades. Average win / average loss. Play as a probability of anticipation for the next 10 trades... Wow."

Reflection. The number of readers was small, but the depth of the reading was not. I read that article again and again, and it changed how I review my own trades. A teacher counts heads; a student counts what stayed in his head. Both counts are real. Michael's disappointment was honest, and I never tried to argue him out of it, but I hope this book is one small proof that the pearls did not all land in the mud.
Free Versus Paid
Michael, 2024-06-20, planning the Playbook:
"Will not be free like SubS. I learn long ago if people don't pay they don't take it seriously, see value. 'Free' they think is junk."

And again, 2025-07-31, about his work on Abduction, which he shared
with only a few students. He passed on advice he had been given years
before:
"If you give free people will think worthless, not respect it. The more you charge the more they appreciate it! Good advice."

My answer came months later, 2025-12-22, when we were planning how to
offer the material:

"A mini course? Only if you have time for a few students, with a note 'by a reservation, only for serious students.' ... I am happy to be a Goodman mentor; teaching Charlie's ideas make me alive. Lucky I get a credit from you to teach the wisdom that I receive."

Reflection. A price is not only money; it is a filter for seriousness. The student who pays, in money or in effort, has already decided that the thing has value, and that decision is half of learning. Michael did not become less generous when he chose to charge. He became more careful about where his generosity would grow. I took the same lesson into my own courses: give the door freely, but ask for commitment before the inner rooms.
Greed and the Method

Michael, 2023-12-09, closing a funny story about money he had hidden
and lost:
"Greed eventually make you very poor. :)"

"Still I remember Charlie, when he say: If I am greed the system will not work, and I lose."

"Yes. Greed equal to poor."

Michael returned to it from another angle, 2025-07-28, on what
changed in trading in the 1970s:

"The 'free lunch' movement in trading began in the early to mid 1970s... The technical analysis work before then always also required some work and judgement... It started the trend of just plugging numbers into equations and expecting profits to get spit out the other end."
My reply the same day:

"Trading is process starting from understanding the risk that relates with the setup, then the importance to be focus to find a high-percentage setups. Then sitting, manage the trade until claiming the rewards. Finally don't count the chickens; instead do many bathtub analysis for every 30 trades."

Reflection. Greed and the free lunch are the same hunger seen from two sides. The greedy trader wants more than the market offers; the free-lunch trader wants it without the work. The Goodman method asks for the opposite on both counts: take only what the setup gives, and do the work of reading the chart yourself. That is why it cannot be sold to someone who wants a slot machine, and why it rewards the patient so well.
Generosity
Michael, 2021-08-24, sending me a box of old material:

Rung 8 · Feeling: Where
Do We Trade From?
Charlie said the market is mostly about the state of the person in front of it. Eight chapters, from the deepest to the funniest.

21. Relaxed and excited at
the same time
Charlie on love, and on trading.

Around 1978, when Michael was a young man still unsure about the girl
he was seeing, one day he and Charlie were at Charlie's Denver house
looking at charts. "Well, Dad, is this the one? Are you in love with
her?" Michael said he did not know. How do you know you're in love? He
asked it rhetorically, but he saw Charlie's eyes go still and look off
into space, and he knew a lecture was coming.

"I dated four women before I met June. I was in my twenties, like
you. I had a little more money than most guys my age, like you. The
difference, Dad, is I wasn't spending it like water pouring out of an
open drain!" He smiled and chuckled. Charlie's laugh was disarming. He
could tell you that you were the world's biggest fool and laugh, and you
would not be offended.

"I felt different about June and asked myself why. I thought of the
four other women. Two of them I felt very comfortable with, like I'd
known them for years. I felt at ease, I could be myself and I didn't
have to worry about how I said something, how I looked, how I moved. But
there was no real excitement. In a way, it was like dating your
sister.

"The other two women, I felt very excited when I saw them. Very
upbeat, almost a King Kong feeling, that I could accomplish anything,
that life was good and people were good. But I really wasn't comfortable
with them. I felt I had to think before I spoke, how did I look, did I
do this right, did I do that right.

"It hit me! With June, somehow those two seemingly mutually-exclusive
emotions were folded into a single emotion. I felt enormously
comfortable and at ease with her. In fact I was sure I had known her in
another life. But she also excited me and made me feel happy in a way
I'd never felt even with the other two women. I concluded I was in
love." June left him for another man soon after. "I've never met another
woman who made me feel like she did, relaxed and excited at the same
time."

He went quiet and gazed away, so Michael kept quiet too, knowing more
was coming.

"Dad, trading is like that. You have to be in love with it, both
relaxed and excited at the same time. Just relaxed and you'll miss good
trades. Just excited and you'll do even worse and make bad trades. It
has to be both in you at the same time!"

Years later Michael used Charlie's test himself. "It fit how I felt
perfectly."

Michael added later that Charlie often stressed an emotional sweet
spot you had to be in to succeed: focused but loose, avoiding risk but
not afraid of it.
What it means. Calm without excitement misses trades, and excitement without calm makes bad ones. Charlie asked for both at once.
Try this. Before you enter, rate yourself from 1 to 5 for calm and 1 to 5 for excitement. Trade only when both are at least 3.
22. The raccoon
The only time Charlie called him Michael.

There was a park three or four blocks from Charlie's Denver house,
half wooded and half open, with a walking trail. To reach it you had to
cross a very busy street. Charlie did not like to walk any further than
he needed, because his feet were in horrible shape from fieldwork. But a
few times, perhaps five between 1973 and 1979, he said, "Dad, let's go
to the park. My mind is too full and I need to let it clear up some
before we look at charts."

One day, as they walked down the busy street, a small raccoon
streaked out of the bushes and ran across the road toward the park. A
car going about ten miles over the limit hit it just as it dove for the
curb. It spun and landed at the edge of the park by some bushes.

Charlie stopped. "Michael, I hope he died instantly." It was one of
only two or three times he called Michael by his name instead of
"Dad."

They crossed the street. The raccoon was dead, its mouth wide open,
almost like a smile. Michael looked at Charlie, but Charlie looked away,
pulled a handkerchief from his pocket and wiped his eyes. "A man
weeping," Michael wrote.

They walked into the park and said nothing for several minutes. Then
Charlie spoke for a while. Michael cannot quote him exactly, but this
was the point:

"Dad, close only counts in horseshoes. In life you are either right
or wrong. Sometimes being wrong is not too bad for you: you fail a test
in school, you have a bad job interview. But sometimes being wrong can
be fatal, like it was for that little raccoon. If the driver had been
going five miles slower, the raccoon would have made it to the park, to
paradise: woods, a stream, people leave food, maybe he finds a little
girl raccoon. But not. We must do our best, but know that fate is always
in charge of our life."

Charlie rarely got emotional. It was very difficult for Michael to
see. They went back to Charlie's house, skipped the charts, and Michael
went home.
What it means. Do your best, and do not confuse your best with control. Both halves are true.
Try this. After a loss you could not have prevented, write down what you did right. Then close the platform for the day.

23. The boy who missed the
contest
Charlie looked where nobody else looked.

The Bache home office once sent every branch a promotional film. The
brokers and staff gathered to watch it on an old 16mm projector. It was
narrated by the Bache CEO, who began with his own story. He had been in
a state math contest for a scholarship. He could not afford school and
wanted it badly, so he studied extra hard. Only one other student could
beat him. On the morning of the contest, that other student was in a
traffic accident on the way. He was fine, but in hospital, and could not
come to the contest. The CEO won the scholarship. At the end of the film
he remembered this and said, "I was lucky that day. Who knows where I
would be if not for the scholarship? Good luck for me, bad luck for
somebody else."

The projector stopped and the lights came on. Charlie said: "I'd much
rather know what happened to the boy who missed the contest!"

Michael says this story is similar to the raccoon story and to the
day a car hit Charlie's Corvair while they studied charts. Charlie
thought: what would have happened if? And: "I am more interested in how
the boy who missed his chance handled life." "No one else looked from
that perspective, ever! Just Charlie."
What it means. The winner's story is told by everyone. The more useful lesson is usually in the story of the one who lost.
Try this. Write a short post-mortem on your worst trade as if you were the person who lost, not the one who learned.
24. The rocks on the table
A dream, September 2025.

Michael rarely dreams of Charlie, though Charlie sometimes talks to
him. One night he did. They were in the Bache lunchroom, at a small
table for two. On the table were five or six rocks, crystals and mineral
chunks, ranging from the size of a football to the size of a silver
dollar. Charlie arranged them in a row from largest to smallest.

"This is the way most people arrange them, but that's wrong," he
said.

He took the smallest one and put it in the middle, and put the others
around it.

"This is the correct way: the largest ones protect the smallest, and
the smallest keeps the others in proper order!"

Figure: The rocks in a row from largest to smallest, and Charlie's
way, with the smallest in the middle and the others around it.
What it means. A risk, a small stop, a tiny rule can hold a larger structure in order, if the large things are arranged to protect it.
Try this. Draw your own trading plan as a circle. Put your smallest rule in the center, and name the three things around it that protect it.
25. Why we invented sports
The World Series, 1977.

In the fall of 1977, the World Series was being played by the New
York Yankees and the Los Angeles Dodgers. Bache had a small TV in the
corner of the lunchroom so people could watch. Michael told Charlie
that, when you thought about it, baseball, football, hockey and
basketball were really silly.

"No, Dad, they serve a real purpose. We create games to play to
highlight and develop very specific skill sets. Gambling is sort of the
same: we create risks in order to take them. It is part of our
evolution, to develop our brains and bodies.

"You know how the immune system works? If we get sick it kicks in to
cure us. Each time it is called it gets stronger and stronger. We're
doing the same thing for our brains and bodies with sports and gambling.
Making them stronger and taking us a little further down the
evolutionary path.

"Sometimes things aren't what they seem at first, Dad. You have to
see them in a wider perspective. If you only look at the wall of a
building close up, you'll never see the city around it."
What it means. A game is a small, safe version of a risk you will meet later. Trading is a game with real stakes, so train for it like one.
Try this. Treat your next ten trades as practice reps with a score. Judge them by process points, not by profit.
26. Everything is relative
Paperboy versus the field.

One day Charlie and Michael talked about work and how hard it is to
really make money. Michael told Charlie that at twelve he had a paper
route: eighty-five papers on weekdays and one hundred and ten on the
Sunday edition, delivered in the middle of the night, riding uphill in
winter snow. He worked two hours a day, three on Sunday, plus ten hours

expected sympathy.

"Dad, during the season of planting, growing and harvesting, I worked

Michael adds a line from Xenophanes: sugar is sweet only by
convention.
What it means. Charlie never forgot where he started. He thought of trading as a soft job and treated its profits with gratitude.
Try this. Write down the hardest job you ever had. Read it before your next large trade.
27. Last Chance, Colorado
No moral. Just a good memory.

Charlie and Michael were returning from the dog track in Byers,
Colorado, about forty miles east of Denver, out on the prairie. It was
pitch black, with no markers or signs to say where they were. After a
few miles Charlie said, "Dad, are you sure we're headed in the right

"I'm not sure, Charlie. Nothing looks familiar of what little I can
see." They kept driving. After another ten miles or so they saw a sign:
WELCOME TO LAST CHANCE, COLORADO!

They both laughed a little. Charlie said, "Dad, I think this is your

Michael wrote: "Good memories... fifty years ago close now."
Try this. No exercise. Tell someone a funny story today.
28. Everything is a 1-2-3
Thrust, parry, thrust, canine style.

In September 2026 Michael sent a small story about two little dogs
out on a walk together, an older one and a younger one.

The older dog stopped at a tree and marked it. The younger one ran

"I guess Mr. Goodman is correct: everything is 1-2-3!"
Michael called it thrust, parry, thrust, canine style.

Figure: Thrust, parry, thrust: the two dogs marking the tree as a
1-2-3.
What it means. The pattern Charlie described is not only on charts. It is in any action, response and counter-response.
Try this. Today, spot one 1-2-3 that has nothing to do with markets.
Where I Trade From

Charlie's stories in this part of the book are about the inner game.
These are my notes on the same game, written to you over five years,
Michael. I did not plan them as a system. Reading them together, I see
that they became one.

The mind is programmed
backwards

In April 2021 I wrote that we are supposed to buy at the greatest
fear and sell at the greatest happiness, and that we so often do the
opposite. "Its a bad strategy our unconscious mind will automatically
follow . Our mind program its give us a very bad out put . But we can
reprogram it slowly ." (April 24, 2021)

The word I care about now is "slowly." There is no switch. There is
only practice.

In August 2021 I described what fear does to a person: "fear when
it's come. the real power inside man disappears. evaporation." (August
8, 2021) The skill is still inside you. Fear simply makes it
unavailable.
The cycle of one trade
In May 2024 I finally wrote down the cycle I had felt for years.

Before the trade, we are excited and sure it is a winner. During the
trade, if it does not move, we think we made a mistake and feel sad; if
it moves, we forget to raise the stop, or we fear a bad stop, and we
"Run fast or not run at all." After the trade, a win makes us rush to
find the next one for more money. A loss raises the emotional
temperature: nothing will work, and an excellent trade passes by.
"Thats emotions cycles like blood circulation." (May 25, 2024)
Figure: The emotional cycle of one trade: before, during, after.

Repetition instead of
emotion

How do you leave the cycle? Not by fighting it. In February 2022 I
wrote that habit comes from the repetition of action. In October 2024 I
said it more sharply:

"Focus on Repetition instead of emotions. Let emotions distil in the
sea of Repetition." (October 2, 2024)

Repeat the same process with consistency, with a very low standard
deviation, and the emotions settle like sediment. They do not disappear.
They stop steering.
Waiting

Charlie's sitting ducks took me a long time to understand. In May
2022 I wrote: "believe me it takes me a deep breath to understand it.
waiting is the key. keys that belong to the gates, from ignorance and
unhappiness to power!" (May 14, 2022)

Waiting is not doing nothing. It is refusing to spend one of my
thirty souls on a trade I do not want. Most of my good decisions are
trades I never opened.
Process, not one result

In May 2024 I wrote about a Goodmanism, "Don't draw big conclusions
from little data," and what it means for a trader: "people tend to take
the source of knowledge from the "Results" of their actions . , and
forget about the right decision they make ." (May 7, 2024)

A good decision can lose. A bad one can win, as my AUDCAD trade did.
If I learn only from outcomes, I learn the wrong lessons. Even in 2021 I
wrote that it is like football: the most important thing is who wins at
the end of the game.
The crowd

In October 2022 I told you about the clearest lesson I ever had about
other people. "I trade from 25 trades, i win 21 trades out of 25." Then
I traded together with others, "and when I traded with some I lose 10
trades in a row ." When I reviewed it, the reason was simple: "I simply
i did not trade for My needs, i just trade for begin Right, wrong."
(October 11, 2022)

With a crowd, I was no longer trading my plan. I was trading to be
right. And the crowd keeps you looking at the wrong things. You cannot
even blame them; they are a group. Charlie knew this. He kept other
people's opinions away from his facts, so he would not lose the power of
his judgment. I learned to do the same: avoid, and be alone with the
chart.
Greed is a road to poverty

In May 2023 I compared the "crazy mode" of greedy people with my own
way: "i trade many of trades because "low risk idea" , i can controll
the risk . even if fail." The rule that governs it is one line: Profit
Exceeds Expense. (May 27, 2023)

A year later I wrote it again, more simply: "Just take a little
eveytime from the market. Let equity curve very very smooth. Slowly
rich." And I remembered Charlie's story about greed: if I am greedy, the
system will fail. (May 25, 2024)

Greed feels like wanting more. In practice it is the fastest way to
have less. It is the y = k/x of the emotions.
Self-control in drawdowns

Drawdowns are part of every system, and my answer to them is very
plain. In November 2023 I wrote: "If not happy with that dropdown , i
just lower the risk per trade . Self-control very important in these
drop down." (November 24, 2023)

I do not argue with the drawdown. I do not try to win it back fast. I
make the next steps smaller until I am calm again.
Mistakes are controllable

In February 2025 I gave myself a definition I still use: "Mistakes =
any controllable action in wrong time." (February 3, 2025) A loss is not
a mistake. A loss is the market. A mistake is something I could have
controlled and did not: a late entry, a moved stop, a skipped rule.

My cure is a feedback loop: capture every trade, make a bathtub
analysis, make a small enhancement, and never change the core. By April
2026 I saw it as risk language: "Making mistake is a operations risk to
the system." (April 3, 2026) The market, the system and the trader must
all be aligned. A good system with a trader who cannot follow it still
loses.
Discipline is a fruit

People tell traders to be disciplined as if discipline were a muscle
you flex. In June 2025 I wrote what I believe: "Becuase the source of
discipline is depends how one have a high self esteem . A very high
evaluation about himself. The displane just a reaction or a fruit of
high self esteem." (June 1, 2025)

If I respect myself, I keep my promises to myself. My trading plan is
one of those promises.
Systematic, not perfect

In February 2025 I wrote: "What happens to a trader , looks for
perfection , insted we need to think in Systematic approach , make
little changes (enhance) every time . never change the core ." (February
17, 2025)

Perfection makes a trader rebuild everything after every loss. A
system lets him improve one small thing and keep going.
Relaxed and excited

Charlie said a trader must be relaxed and excited at the same time.
In December 2024 I copied another of his lines into a letter to you
because it said the same thing: "You have to be laser focused but at the
same time ‘loose-as-a-goose’ ." Under it I wrote about my own practice:
"I like to trade in many times around 0 ~ 5 % ROR. Laser focus. As well
calm." (December 10, 2024)

This is where I trade from. Excitement without calm becomes the crazy
mode. Calm without excitement misses the sitting duck. Fear is tense and
flat, and the real power evaporates. The place I want is the corner
where both are high.

Figure: Calm and excitement: the four states, and the one I trade
from.
Looking back

In 2021 I knew the mind was programmed backwards. By 2026 I had a
map: the cycle, the cure of repetition, the patience of waiting, the
danger of the crowd and of greed, the plain tools of smaller size and
honest labels, and the quiet ground of self-respect. None of it is
perfect. All of it is systematic. That is enough.

29. Navid
Excellent trader, wrong week.

Michael told me this story twice, saying it was important for me.
Navid was a student around 2012: an excellent understanding of Goodman,
a quick learner who saw patterns easily, a young man, very nice and
polite. After the course he started a 30-trade exercise in October.
Every week he sent his MT4 summary. For the first thirty trades he
traded only the Under, with no Line. "He does FANTASTIC." He traded only
five thousand lots.

Then he started a second 30-trade exercise at ten thousand lots.
Michael sensed he was in a hurry to start making real money. Michael
kept warning him. After about ten trades Navid said, "I'm going for
it!"

He made two terrible mistakes. First, he raised his lot size too
fast, to one hundred thousand. Raise lot size slowly. Second, he did it
at the top of his equity cycle, after a good run of profitable trades.
Always add after a down cycle in equity. "Counterintuitive, but must
do!" The pressure was too much. He made four or five bad trades, and
everything from October was gone. He wrote to say thank you for
everything and goodbye, and went back to his old job. "I cry for him
when I read it," Michael wrote.
What it means. The method held. The trader was rushed. Size is where an honest trader gets hurt.
Try this. Write a size-increase rule with a number. For example: increase only after a drawdown, and by no more than one step.

Market Adventure (2021)

In this study I follow four pairs on the daily chart until I find a
trade candidate: EURUSD, AUDUSD, GBPUSD and NZDUSD. I take 14 April 2021
as "today". There was nothing special about that day; I chose it at
random. The aim is to build a campaign that helps us grow our capital,
and to show how 1-2-3s, intersections, volume, correlation and laydowns
fit together. For this book each pair's daily structure is redrawn on
real 2022 data, sometimes from another pair; each caption names the data
shown, and the dates in the text are those of my original charts.

Part 1: EURUSD on 14 April
2021

Figure: The chart as it stands on the study day, before any marks:
bars and volume only. Real data: NZDUSD, 1-hour, 14–24 February 2022.
(The original chart was EURUSD daily, January 2020 to 14 April 2021;
this one shows the same structure.)

Reading the chart as an
equilibrium

My first objective is to look at the chart as what I call a Nash
equilibrium. It explains where buyers reach their maximum, and where
sellers reach theirs, at the best option each side has.

I look at the efforts of buyers and sellers as three steps: the
1-2-3. The 1-2-3 is the basic component that buyers and sellers must
follow. In Goodman it is an axiom. So let me show how the buyers'
efforts made a 1-2-3.

Because we are dealing with the market's past, before the current
day, I think it is best to draw a larger 1-2-3. My focus is on the end
of each maximum effort of buyers and sellers in the race.

Figure: The large 1-2-3: swing 1 runs up from the low to point 1,
then swing 2 corrects down to point 2. Real data: NZDUSD, 1-hour, 14–24
February 2022. (The original chart was EURUSD daily, January 2020 to 14
April 2021; this one shows the same structure.)
Jumbo 1

The market shows a Jumbo 1, a large swing 1. On my original EURUSD
daily chart, its BP is on 20 March 2020 and its EP on 6 January 2021.
Hope dominated the market for more than six months. It shows how strong
the buyers were in the past.

Intersections instead of
Fibonacci

Before negotiating with swing 2, I look at how intersections work in
Goodman. In Goodman we prefer an intersection to a Fibonacci number.

In brief, an intersection is where buyers and sellers struggled in
the past. Watch it like a history film: that location was the deadliest
conflict of the past. In Goodman we call it a Return Zone. Swing 2
returns to that deadliest intersection, and this phenomenon can happen
on every time frame.

A bonus: when the zone holds a sideways movement for more than a few
weeks, it is stronger. That makes it more likely that swing 2 stops at
that zone.

So I ask a question. At which price level in swing 1 did buyers
struggle with sellers for a long time, fighting there again and again?
Can you split swing 1 into its own 1-2-3?

Figure: Swing 1 split into its own 1-2-3; the box marks the struggle
inside swing 1, and EP is the low that ends it. Real data: NZDUSD,
1-hour, 14–24 February 2022. (The original chart was EURUSD daily,
January 2020 to 14 April 2021; this one shows the same structure.)

Buyers struggled with sellers for weeks in the box zone. Swing 2
stopped exactly between the EP-FPS and the EP-SS. When swing 2
intersects an old EP-SS, there is a high probability that sellers are
losing their power. Buyers take control of the trend again at 2 and walk
into swing 3.

Where can swing 3 stop? Five
tools

original chart was EURUSD daily, January 2020 to 14 April 2021; this one
shows the same structure.)

February 2022. (The original chart was EURUSD daily, January 2020 to 14

1. The Matrix Overlay at 1.

In my opinion EURUSD cannot move back up to 1, because:

1. Jumbo 1 took more than six months, and that amount of time destroyed the demand.

2. At 2, sellers moved on very small volume, as the volume shows.

3. The cycles are incomplete, because the market moves without buyers. Compare the buyers at 1 (the BP of the Jumbo) with the buyers at 2.

I also do not think the market will move below the BP of the Jumbo.
Wave 2 showed no great amount of sellers, no LARGE SELLERS. It is just
that buyers no longer want to enjoy the market. When the SPS moves down,
it will test 2 again and again, trying to break it.

So I think the market will follow this laydown: an incomplete cycle
and a sell that stops before the BP of the Jumbo (see the EURUSD panel

chart changes. A laydown is a vision of the future of the pair. It is
better to move one step at a time and wait for the market to confirm it.

Part 4: A Map for Every
Market

What about the other forex pairs? My goal is to build an overlay for
each market, as I did for these four pairs. Here is my diagram.

• Any pair that does not follow its market, or moves by itself with no clear correlation, I avoid and mark with an X.

  • Any pair that leads its market, I use as the market's flag: a red flag when down, a green flag when up.

I enter the market only when there are two confirmations. For
example: a Goldilocks in AUDUSD and a Goldilocks in EURUSD. Then I enter
a trade, shown on the map by a small bulb, which means both have a
Setup. The more Setups in one market, the more strength. It means the
market is ready to sell.

I also add a mark to show which markets are fastest to weaken. Here,
a green mark sits behind the USD pairs.

Figure: A laydown for all markets: one map per currency group (USD,
JPY, NZD, CHF), with flags for the leader and bulbs where two Setups
confirm.

My job is only to draw a laydown for each of them. It takes around
one hour a day. This system works best on a large time frame such as
daily or weekly. In this study I made the market laydown only for the
USD pairs.

From it I can know when the market is best to trade. As shown here,
the USD markets are best when they turn into a Dagger. I use the laydown
as a timing tool. For example, I know I need around several weeks before
the market prepares to move up.
The Four Pillars
So we have:

1. Time estimation: the laydown.

2. Price projection: the 3-C and the intersection.

3. Market following: correlation and the leader.

4. Setup confirmation: correlation, Nested Overlay and Overlay.

Next I will build this for each market pair, to make a general market
laydown. I think in this study I have put the main concepts together in
a very simple way.
Thank you.

The purpose was never to forecast. It was to practice reading, in

studies in order so that you can see the market change its mind, and see
me change mine with it. For this book each chart is redrawn on real 2022

The Forex Bullish
Consensus Reports (2022–2023)

In 2022 Michael and I wrote a short booklet together: Using Contrary Opinion and Bullish Consensus in the FOREX Markets — A new and unique trading edge for currency traders. It explains the method behind the FOREX Bullish Consensus Report (FBCR), which we then ran week after week. This chapter sets out that method, and then shows what the weekly reports actually recorded.
Part one: the method
What the FOREX market lacks

Compared with equities and futures, FOREX has clear advantages.
Liquidity is much better than in futures. Leverage is many times higher
than in futures, even with the CFTC's constraints on margin.

Its single biggest weakness is the lack of a central exchange. Next
to the futures markets, three types of information are missing:

• Volume. Each FOREX broker aggregates volume from its own liquidity providers. This does not reflect total volume across the FX world. Adding up several platforms does not help either, because one liquidity provider often serves many platforms, so the data stays skewed.

  • Open interest. Open interest counts the contracts outstanding. It rises when a new buyer and a new seller enter, falls when an existing buyer liquidates to an existing seller, and stays the same when a new party replaces an existing one. This needs a central exchange, which FOREX does not have.

  • Hedgers versus speculators. Futures markets publish the Commitment of Traders (CoT) report, which splits participants into large and small speculators and hedgers. Used properly, it is a valuable predictive tool. FX has nothing like it.

Michael, a futures trader since 1973, has always found open interest
worth studying as a predictive indicator. He worked for a long time on a
"synthetic open interest" for currencies, built from price, range and
other factors. In his words: "Currently close, but at this writing no
cigar!"

Some years ago his team wrote a program called Mercury Charts. It
shows a standard daily OHLC bar chart with one enhancement: the colour
of each bar carries two extra pieces of information. The upper half
shows whether volume rose or fell from the previous day. The lower half
shows whether open interest rose or fell.

In most cases, aggregating information in FOREX does not work. But
there is one wonderful exception that gives FOREX traders real
predictive information: trader opinion.

Contrary opinion and
discounting

Every seasoned trader knows the adage: "Buy on the rumor, sell on the
news." It is an example of contrary opinion and of the market process
called discounting.

Michael tells an old story from the 1970s futures markets. For decades there had been a "February Bounce" in wheat futures, tied to the winter wheat crop. By the time he arrived in 1973, so many traders knew about it, and bought in advance, that the bounce was gone. On several occasions there was a February break instead, as the early buyers took profits.
The logic is simple:

1. Enough traders anticipate an event and buy or sell before it happens.

2. When the event arrives, there is no buying power or selling pressure left to move the market much further.

3. The event may even push the market in the opposite direction.

This is discounting. As Charles B. Goodman put it: "To many traders
making too much money too quickly-Watch Out!"

The classic bar chart patterns show the same thing. So many traders
learned the Head and Shoulders pattern that the right shoulder grew
weaker and weaker from anticipated buying or selling. One small tip: in
today's world of automated trading and "expert advisors", the old bar
chart formations may again be worth a look.

"If you use the techniques and methods of the majority – you will
fail like the majority." A corollary is to use techniques and methods
that are not popular with the majority.

Contrary opinion, going against the crowd, works in much the same way
as discounting. When a large majority of traders are bullish or bearish,
at some point there is not enough buying power or selling pressure left
to push the market further. For a short time an imbalance of buyers or
sellers exists. The market then moves, sometimes sharply, in the
opposite direction to correct it.

Bullish consensus:
measuring contrary opinion

Contrary opinion is the phenomenon. Bullish consensus is the
technique that measures it, so it can be analyzed, studied and used to
predict.

The consensus belongs to a defined group of traders. It is the
percentage of traders in that pool who are bullish.

• Above 90% bullish: the market is a Sell. You go against the crowd.

  • Below 20% bullish: the market is a Buy.

Why 20 and not the mirror image of 10? Because it takes more to turn
a bull market down than to turn a bear market up. These were Hadady's
original numbers. As a tribute to his ground-breaking work, we believe
they remain valid and the most accurate half a century later.

Bullish consensus is naturally systems-neutral. It can be added to
any timing indicator or method, and it complements every trader's
toolkit.

The Triad: consensus
plus a timing tool

When Michael first traded futures at Peavey & Company (later
acquired by Geldermann, and then by the later defunct Refco), he met one
of the few successful traders there, an elderly gentleman. This trader
used a very simple system that blended a moving average, a
relative-strength-type indicator and Hadady's bullish consensus numbers.
He called it the Triad.
It can be used in two ways:

1. Consensus as a filter. The bullish consensus acts as a secondary tool that removes false signals from common indicators.

2. Consensus as the primary tool. A common indicator then helps time the proper entry.

Bullish consensus works best together with a simple timing tool.
Michael rebuilt the Triad with a rule base, and it was published weekly
in the FOREX Bullish Consensus Report.

Remember: even when bullish consensus is your primary indicator, you
still rely on a timing tool, such as a moving average, for entry. A
market, especially a bull market, can stay above 90% while prices keep
rising. Readings can stay above 90% or below 20% for a short time, and
in a bull market two or three days can mean a significant price
change.

The original booklet showed examples of bullish consensus filtering a
moving average and a relative strength indicator on currency pairs. In
those examples the consensus helped avoid false signals. Divergences
between the consensus and prices or indicators often gave excellent
entry points.
Where the opinions come from

You could scour the internet for free advice on currency trends, or
subscribe to many market gurus. Both are time consuming and expensive.
Neither gives clear opinions on specific pairs over a specific period,
so neither works well as a predictive tool.

Over his half-century in commodity futures, currencies and equities,
Michael built and nurtured a very large network of traders, professional
and amateur. The FBCR draws its figures from that network. Every Friday
it asks one question:
"Are you bullish or bearish on [Currency Pair] for the next week?" If no opinion, please skip this pair.
There are two separate pools:

• Professionals. This is the group most followed: money managers, bank and corporate traders, and individuals who trade larger amounts. They are less swayed by news reports and other outside influences. So when most of them agree, and the numbers are very high or very low, "things happen." Each Friday 45–50 professionals are polled on the eighteen most active currency pairs.

  • Amateurs. Michael's original FBC, published by FXstreet.com some years ago, reported professionals only. Amateur behaviour is more erratic, but the basic 90/20 numbers still apply and often prove insightful. Each Friday 55–60 amateurs are polled on the same eighteen pairs.
Torturing the data

There is much more in the raw bullish consensus than the 90/20 rule.
The late James L. Bickford, a mathematics and statistics genius Michael
worked with for nearly 40 years, used to say: "You can torture the data,
but can you make it talk?"

The answer is yes, if you torture it correctly. In FOREX the
consensus is not usually above 90% or below 20%. Yet the underlying
data, properly worked, gives useful predictive insight even between the
two extremes. Standing alone, the raw figures offer all but the
shortest-term traders a meaningful edge.

So the FBCR also offered several indicators built from the raw
data:

• the Triad,

  • the week-to-week change,

  • recurring patterns,

  • professional versus amateur comparison,

  • divergence with prices and common indicators,

  • and other insights from over a decade of studying professional and amateur consensus data.

One common and very useful pattern is a divergence: prices fail to
exceed a recent high, but the bullish consensus rises.

Michael's background behind
the pool

The trader pool rests on Michael's long career. He counts his first
trade, in silver, from September 1973. His research in technical
analysis goes back to his college years (1968–1972), on a Data General
Nova computer at the University of Colorado Physics Department. He has
been registered as a CTA with the CFTC and as an Investment Advisor with
the SEC, and he opened and owned a commodity futures brokerage in
Honolulu.

His automated futures trading program was, as he describes it, the first AI program in any market, averaging 48% per annum with a very high Sharpe Ratio according to Managed Account Reports. He has lectured on AI and technical analysis, wrote Getting Started in Currency Trading for John Wiley & Sons (four editions, 2005–2012), and has mentored over 200 new traders. The hundreds of contacts he made over that half-century form the professional and amateur pools of the report.

Part two: what the
weekly reports recorded

Each weekly report was a workbook. The HOME sheet gave the week's
polling summary: the percentage of professionals and of amateurs bullish
on each pair. Every pair then had its own sheet holding the full weekly
history of both readings.

The pairs covered were the eighteen in the method: AUDCAD, AUDJPY,
AUDNZD, AUDUSD, CHFJPY, EURAUD, EURCAD, EURCHF, EURGBP, EURJPY, EURUSD,
GBPCHF, GBPJPY, GBPUSD, NZDUSD, USDCAD, USDCHF and USDJPY. By 2023 the
reports also tracked crude oil (CL), gold (AU), the S&P 500 (SPX)
and Bitcoin (BTCUSD), and the last report added the 10-year Treasury
note (TY10).

The reports I kept run from the week of 1 January 2023 to the week of
8 July 2023. The history inside them starts on 4 September 2022, so the
last workbook holds 44 weekly polls per pair.

Figure: Weekly professional bullish consensus for EURUSD, GBPUSD,
USDJPY and USDCAD from September 2022 to July 2023, with the 90% Sell
zone and 20% Buy zone shaded.
What the professional readings show over those 44 weeks:

• Extremes were rare, as the method expects. Most readings sat between the two thresholds. USDCAD and AUDCAD never reached either extreme.

  • The crowd swung hard on the majors. EURUSD stood at 19% on 4 September 2022 and climbed to 91–93% through January 2023. GBPUSD sat at 17–20% from mid-September to early October 2022, and stood at 91% in the week of 8 July 2023.

  • USDJPY crossed from one extreme to the other. It read between 85% and 92% through September and October 2022. By January 2023 it had fallen to 20%, 20% and 17%. From late May 2023 it was back above 90% in most weeks, at 92% in the final report.

  • Yen crosses dominated the high readings. CHFJPY and USDJPY each recorded 11 weeks at 90% or above, EURJPY six and GBPJPY five.

  • The low readings clustered in autumn 2022 and January 2023. GBPUSD, GBPCHF, AUDUSD and NZDUSD gave readings of 20% or below in September and October 2022. USDCHF and USDJPY did so in January 2023.

In the week of 8 July 2023, the last report, the professional
readings at or above 90% were EURCAD (91), GBPJPY (90), GBPUSD (91) and
USDJPY (92).

In sixth grade, in 1962, Michael saw a picture of a ten-speed racing
bike in a magazine. "I totally fall in love, want one, want to race

American boy 1962 - baseball was kid's dream." For two summers he rode

He never stopped laughing at himself about it. "Like chess, no talent
but did OK by hard work."

The lesson: hard work can make you a state champion; only the wider arena tells you where you really stand. A trader who wins in a small pond should expect a faster rider somewhere, and keep his size modest until he meets him.

As a sophomore Michael wanted to take a graduate-level class on the
Presocratic philosophers. The professor, Dr Ed Miller, gave him a quick
quiz of four or five questions; he answered them all and was admitted.
Most of the class compared translations of the Fragments. Dr Miller came
with a box of eleven or twelve books, his "Portable Pre Socratic

what Kirk and Raven say, let's see what Wheelwright say."

During the eleven-day spring break Michael had an idea. He gathered
the translations from his own shelf, the school library and the Denver

inner circle.

The lesson: organize the material before you study it. Michael did for a philosophy class what a good trader does with his charts: put every view of the same thing side by side, and the work goes faster for everyone.

During the Bobby Fischer craze of 1972, Michael was school champion
and president of the university chess club, which "went from 20-25
members to 150 almost overnight!" He taught classes and private lessons,
and he began every class the same way:
"If you want to just learn chess and play for fun, go to the left side of the room. If you want to learn to be a really good player go to the right side of the room."

"Maybe 30 in class, 27-28 go to left, 2-3 go to right. Everyone wants
to play right away... BIG MISTAKE if want to be serious player." The few

never get very good." Looking back he admitted: "I'm sure if I had
learned the way I taught I would have been a stronger player."

The lesson: this is exactly how he later taught Goodman. Learn the board before you play; study the setups and run a pitch-penny account before you trade real size. Most students choose the left side of the room, and the market charges them for it.
