Kroll, Gould and the sitting
ducks
Why the slower trader won.

In about 1977, Michael read the letter of a trader named Bruce Gould
and was impressed. At about the same time John van Eck, who ran the big
International Investors gold fund, decided to start a commodity fund.
Such things were very new. He would give three traders $50,000 each, and
the best would manage the fund. One of Michael's brokers, a top salesman
for the firm, persuaded Van Eck to use Michael as one of the three.

Van Eck asked Michael if he knew anybody else. Michael recommended
Gould and asked him. Gould said no: "I am happy as is. I sit in a quiet
office, trade, and talk story with my elderly father who joins me every
day." He traded and learned life lessons from his father. Michael made a
friend for life. Charlie reminded him: "Just go for the high percentage
sitting ducks, Dad!"

Van Eck also chose Stanley Kroll, a very well-known trader with a big
mouth and a big reputation. In three weeks Michael made about 5% in two
trades. Kroll burned up his entire $50,000 and came back hat in hand to
ask for another try. Van Eck gave him another $50,000.

At the end of six months Kroll was up over 100%, trading in and out
like a madman. Michael had made about ten trades and was up 38%. Van
Eck, impressed by Kroll, gave him a fund with $1 million to start. Kroll
burned through it quickly, lost 50%, and the fund closed. Van Eck said
commodities were a bad deal and he would never try again. "I think the
Dutchman would understand risk, but not. Only saw reward."
What it means. A fast 100% looks better than a slow 38% until you ask what the person was risking to get it. Charlie preferred the sitting ducks.
Try this. Rank your last twenty trades by risk taken, not by profit. Notice which kind you would repeat.

They promised to monitor every trade against strict parameters. His very
first trade the next week, in the S&P 500, was a large winner, and
the parameters were forgotten at once. His verdict: "Emotions trump due
diligence, always. Human nature."

The lesson: even professionals with every model and every interview fall for one good trade. If the big firms cannot keep emotion out of their decisions, the private trader must build his rules before the excitement arrives.
The Car Owns You (2023-11-15)

Since 1962 Michael had wanted a Jaguar XKE. In the 1970s he found one
like new and told Charlie he was going to buy it. Charlie said: "Dad,
you won't own the car, the car will own you!" Michael pointed out that
Charlie had a dozen or more Corvairs. "Yes, and I own THEM. I never
worry someone steal or hit."

About a year after Charlie was gone, Michael bought a nearly new
Ferrari. He drove it only on Sundays, on the back road to visit Jim
Bickford. But he parked near Jim's apartment and worried the whole time
that someone would hit it, steal it or scratch it. One day he told Jim
he had to go and check on the car. Jim said: "I think the car owns
you!!" Michael laughed, and he could almost hear Charlie chuckle: "I
told you so, Dad!"
The lesson: anything you must watch all the time does not belong to you; you belong to it. A position too big to stop thinking about is the same Ferrari.

The Burning Cadillac
(2026-10-04)

"Nothing upset or perturbed Jim," Michael wrote. Around 1989 he
bought a client's family car, a perfectly kept 1979 Cadillac, and the
next evening he drove it to Boulder for dinner. On the way home, at
dusk, people on the street began waving. He waved back, thinking they
admired the car. The waving grew wilder; someone pointed behind him.
"There was a wall of flame behind us two blocks long!" The starter had
shorted, gas was leaking, and the car was burning. The fire department
came, then the tow truck, whose driver said: "I can't tow this car, it's
still on fire!" Back came the fire department.

Near eleven at night, badly shaken, Michael phoned Jim, who lived
four blocks away, and asked him to bring a few things from the store.
Jim, woken from sleep, only wondered how he would get to Golden with the
buses stopped. Fifteen minutes later he came walking down Arapahoe
Street with his backpack, handed over the bag, looked at the burnt-out
car and calmly asked if everyone was all right. Then he walked home.
"Never showed any shock or surprise, just sort of focused on the task at
hand and everything else was irrelevant! No superfluous conversation,
ever."
The lesson: when everything is on fire, the most valuable person is the calm one who does the next useful thing. That is the trader you want to be when a market explodes against you.

The Random Walk at
Midnight (2023-10-24)

Around 1990 Michael bought soybeans. "LOTS of soybeans. Somewhere I
still have news tape say, 'large money manager buys 500 cars of
beans'... 'money manager continues to buy beans, 300 cars.'" He went to
bed. "Middle of the night I wake up in hot sweat think, 'What if market
really is only a random walk!!!' Ahaha."

The lesson: even a trader with a method, a record and seventeen years of experience feels doubt when the position is large. The cure is not to remove the doubt but to size the trade so that you can sleep with it.

Kant and the Late Paper
(2024-11-17)

In college Michael once handed in a philosophy paper late. The rule
was strict: a late paper loses one grade. He went to the professor and
pleaded his case.

"He said, 'You know Kant's categorical imperative! No exceptions. If you can find an exception to CI by Wednesday morning when I start grading papers I will give you regular grade.' I rack my brain two days, cannot find exceptions but several interesting ideas... I go in Wednesday, admit cannot find exceptions but some interesting ideas! 'Go ahead, I'm listening!' So I talk several minutes my ideas... He says, 'You really dug deep on CI! I'll go ahead and give you regular grade.'"

The lesson: he did not win by finding the answer. He won by the honesty of saying he had not found it, and by the depth of the search. Teachers, and markets, reward serious work more than clever excuses.

The Chess Exhibition
(2025-06-20)

Around 1980, Michael, a former university chess champion, visited a
coffee shop owned by an old college friend, with chessboards on every
table. The friend asked him to give a small simultaneous exhibition, one
player against several boards. Michael agreed to six or seven.

One opponent was said to be very strong. He played the Ruy Lopez
straight out of the book for ten or twelve moves. Then, suddenly, he
took his knight and put it back on its original square. Then the other
knight. Then a bishop, then the queen, then the other bishop, "soon,
only pawns out, no pieces." Michael advanced easily and gave checkmate a
few moves later. The man jumped up, and Michael thought he was about to
be hit. Instead he said: "You are only player who has been able to beat
my strategy!" and walked away.

The lesson: a memorized opening is not a method. The man knew twelve moves of theory and nothing about why they were played, so he invented a "strategy" that undid them. Many traders do the same with a pattern copied from a book. Without understanding, they eventually pull every piece back home.

Write It or Lose It
(2023-05-15)

In college Michael carried small pocket-size spiral notebooks.
"Whenever have thought, stop and write it in the book. I soon number
subjects - think eventually 17 - like 17.1, 17.2 and put date start on
cover of each book." By graduation he had well over a hundred of them,
and the summer before he began trading he typed them all out and carried
the pages through every move for years.

Then, back from Hawaii, the family's young puppy found the box while
no one was home. "Chew half of the pages, pee on other half, haha, dog
say 'this is what I think of your philosophy!' I salvaged about 15 pages
is all."
The lesson: write your ideas down the moment they come, number them, date them, and keep a copy somewhere safer than a cardboard box. A trading journal is the same discipline. "Write it or lose it."

Jim
Bickford and Jonathan's Wave (2026-10-02, 2025-07-15)

"I met Jim in 1966 at Denver chess club. NO ONE, I mean NO ONE more
loyal friend than Jim!"

In the summer of 1984 Michael came back from Hawaii with the design
for a trading program he called Jonathan's Wave: "multiple indicators
talk to each other in language of ME... I thought brilliant at the
time." He asked Jim if he could program it. Jim was never one for
compliments, "just all facts, focus." He looked and said, "This looks
like it could actually work," which from Jim was a big compliment. "But
I can't do it in BASIC."

Michael bought a full Smalltalk package for the research. Jim learned
Smalltalk in less than a week, then said, "I don't think this will work
either." So Michael bought an early Prolog. "Jim learn it in less than a
week... write entire program bug free == two weeks!... Program run
almost six years, returns are well documented!"

There were other Jim stories. Once the two of them lost the
initialization string for an old modem; Jim started looking at 6 pm and
found it around 4 am. Around 2002 a broker experimented with "box
options": draw a box, and if price hits it, you win. "Jim play around,
discover big hole in algorithm... We go in hit, hit, hit ahahaha... then
they jiggle algorithm... Jim figure out again, hit, hit, hit... Third
time, same thing! LOL! Next time we go in, no more Box Options!!!"

Michael used to drive the side road from Denver to Boulder every
Sunday morning to meet Jim. "Brings back good memories of when Jim
Bickford and I explored a lot of ideas."

The lesson: a good idea needs a good partner. Michael had the design; Jim had the patience to learn whatever language the idea required. And loyalty, more than talent, is what Michael remembered first.
The English Horn (2025-06-12)

Around 2003 Michael answered a newspaper ad for an English horn, an
instrument he wanted to learn at home. The seller was a widow in a small
house in an old part of Denver, selling belongings to pay the bills; the
horn had belonged to her husband's brother, a professional musician. He
paid $500. At a music shop the man looked it over: a top-of-the-line
Loree, almost new. "I don't buy these but I think you could get $7k-$8k
easily."

"I tell him I'll sell the horn as is, buy something inexpensive...
and pocket several thousand dollars." Then, driving home: "IT HITS ME -
The Oboe Story with Walter!!!" It was Charlie's oboe story, told earlier
in this book, from twenty-five years before. Michael took the horn back
to the woman and connected her with a buyer. She received $7,000,
returned his $500 and was very happy. "Talk about deja vu!!!!"

The lesson: a lesson is only learned when you obey it against your own interest. Michael heard the oboe story in the 1970s; a quarter of a century later it cost him several thousand dollars, and he paid it gladly.

The Borrowed Picture
(2025-06-18)

Michael owned a web conferencing company from 1998 to 2010. Around
2005 he hired an outside team to refresh its website. "They do nice work
- home page has beautiful, relevant image!!! ... everyone compliment me
on new look." Soon a courier brought a letter: the image was
copyrighted, and a Canadian company demanded payment or it would sue. He
hired an internet lawyer, took the image down and settled. Later he
learned that removing it on notice would probably have been enough. "So,
$7k + $3k for attorney down toilet."
The lesson: check where your material comes from before you publish it, and get good advice before you pay, not after. Both are cheap compared with skipping them.

Bet on the Method
(2025-07-22)

Around 2010 a good friend of Michael's, a keen Go player, argued that
computers had beaten chess but would need decades to beat Go, because
the game is so much larger. Michael had been in touch with a researcher
in the UK combining heuristic algorithms with Monte Carlo sampling. "I
told my friend 'less than ten years' Go lose to computers." In 2016
AlphaGo beat the world champion Lee Sedol with exactly that kind of
search plus sampling.
The lesson: do not judge the future by the size of the problem; judge it by the method being applied to it. Michael read the method, not the headlines.

Watch for Blue Hondas
(2023-09-27)

Michael taught his students that seeing needs a hypothesis. He
borrowed Charlie's line about the traders in the Peavey gallery, "They
look but do not see," and added an exercise of his own: "You drive to
next city, call me. I ask, 'How many blue Hondas you see?' No idea. Tell
them, 'Watch for blue Hondas, then can know!'"
The lesson: you find on a chart what you have decided to look for. Know the setup you want before you open the screen, or a hundred setups will drive past unseen.

The Screenshot Track
Record (2025-06-17)

Some years ago a wealthy man who wanted to start an FX fund asked
Michael for advice. One day he announced that he had found a great AI
system. Michael asked for the developer's track record so he could
analyze it. "All I get is screenshot of pretty MT4 chart, lots and lots
of colors, numbers, line... I tell man doesn't make sense - MQL4 not
strong enough script to make real AI." The man invested anyway and lost
nearly all of it in two days.
The lesson: a screenshot is not a track record. Ask for the statement, the trade list and the drawdown; if all you get is pretty colors, you already have your answer.

The Bargain Chess Books
(2024-11-04)

Michael once ordered three very large boxes of chess books from a
dealer in the Czech Republic, mostly foreign-language editions. The
books cost about $200 and the postage almost as much, "but still good
deal." Then customs called: they wanted $1,100 to release the boxes. He
found a customs agent who negotiated it down to $300, but her own fee
was another $300. "Think I get great bargain on books, cost me
$1000!!!"
The lesson: count every cost before you call it a bargain. Commissions, spreads and swaps do to a "cheap" trade what customs did to the cheap books.

In college a friend from the music department begged Michael to
switch his major to music theory and composition; he said Michael had
perfect pitch and a gift for melody. Michael stayed with philosophy, and
with the drum. Fifty-five years later, in June 2023, he bought an alto
saxophone. "First time spend money on myself in long time!!" And true to
his own method: "Maybe I take a few private lessons to get good start,
like chess, ahaa!"
The lesson: it is never too late to begin, but it is always too late to unlearn a bad start. At seventy-three Michael still took his own advice: get a teacher first, play later.

The Glass Ball at
Heidelberg (2021-10-16)

Not every Archer story is about Archer. Some are stories he collected
and passed on because of what they teach. This one, he said, "actually
happened at the University of Heidelberg, sometime in the early
1960s."

A physics professor leaned on a large decorative glass ball outside
the physics building and burned his arm. Strangely, the shady side was
hot and the sunny side was cool. He spent hours at his blackboard and at
last produced a page of equations proving why the shady side should be
the hot one. The next day he proudly showed his graduate student. They
walked outside together, just in time to see two workmen in asbestos
gloves turning the ball 180 degrees. "At this time of day the way the
sun shine makes one-half of the ball extremely hot; people have burnt
themselves. So we always rotate the ball."

The lesson: before you explain the chart, check what actually happened on it. A beautiful theory can prove anything, even the opposite of the truth. Charlie said the same thing in his own way: look at the market first.

When I read these stories together, I hear the same voice Michael
heard from Charlie in that car on the mountain pass: a teacher who
prefers an example to a lecture. He gave me the stories; I am giving
them to my students, as he hoped I would.

Rung 10 · The
System: How Does It All Move Together?

Nine rungs took the trader apart. Being asked who stands behind the
chart. Knowing asked how truth is learned. Seeing asked what a market
is. Deciding asked whether this is a Setup. Acting asked how to manage
the trade. Measuring asked how much to risk. Doing Right, Feeling and
Learning asked how we treat others, where we trade from, and who carries
the method on.

This last rung puts the pieces back together. A trader is not a list
of skills. He is a system: every part pushes on every other part, and
the pushes come back. In August 2026 I wrote to Michael that I was
"thinking on system dynamic with A Philosophical Look at System
Dynamics." This chapter is what that thinking became.
The parts that move

A system is a set of parts with arrows between them. In my trading
the parts are the rungs. What I see (Seeing) feeds what I decide
(Deciding). What I decide becomes an order (Acting). The order becomes a
number in my journal (Measuring). The number touches my feelings
(Feeling). My feelings either wait for the next good setup or chase the
market. Then the review (Learning) changes how I will see the next
chart. The loop closes.

I saw this loop early, before I had a name for it. On 2021-05-10 I
wrote after one of Michael's lessons:
"Qualify the trades, Proactive, FeedBack Loop. Three simple secrets. to investigate before investing and after."
On 2022-12-09, writing about chess, I tried to say it again:
"I think its means the loop between visualize and tactics as a learning process. In every win or lose. This loop function must work."
"Trading success is based on the compound factor. Loops."

A loop can work for you or against you. System dynamics gives the two
kinds names: reinforcing and balancing.
The reinforcing loop

A reinforcing loop feeds itself. In the plate below every arrow on
the left carries a plus sign: more of one thing gives more of the next.
A run of wins brings confidence. Confidence turns to overconfidence.
Overconfidence makes the lot bigger and the rules looser. A bigger lot
gives bigger wins for a while, and bigger wins bring more
confidence.

Nothing inside this loop says stop. That is its danger. It grows
until something outside it breaks it, and in trading that something is
one large loss.

Navid's story in Rung 9 is this loop exactly. He did FANTASTIC on the
first thirty trades with a small lot and only the Under. Then he doubled
the lot for the second thirty; Michael sensed he was in a hurry to make
real money. After about ten trades he said, "I'm going for it!" The loop
had no brake. When Michael and I discussed the story on 2023-05-18, I
wrote that traders who lose their edge "enter into the psychological
cycle. Between extremely optimistic to extremely pessimistic." The same
loop, at the scale of a whole market, made my real-estate example in
that letter: land nobody wanted in the 1970s, and everyone still buying
in 2023 at the extreme of optimism.

Figure: The trader as a dynamic system. Left: the reinforcing loop
(R), every link positive. Right: the balancing loop (B), one negative
link that turns it back. Below: the tipping point where one loop gives
way to the other.
The balancing loop

A balancing loop corrects itself. It has one link that points the
other way, a minus sign, so the loop pulls the system back toward a goal
instead of running away.

My balancing loop is built from the rules of Rung 6. Losing trades
bring drawdown. Drawdown makes me cut the lot, because the lot is never
free: I decide my maximum drawdown first and divide it into thirty
trades. On 2025-03-05 I put it this way:
"Keep in mind we are trading the money not the market... you do not have many souls in the market, have only 30 souls!"

A smaller lot means I survive and get back to breakeven, which was
Charlie's first goal for every trader. Survival gives me time to learn:
I label every trade, I watch the Golden Ratio every ten trades, I do the
bathtub review. Learning lowers the next drawdown. That is the minus
sign that closes the loop.
On 2023-11-24 I wrote the rule in one line:
"If not happy with that dropdown , i just lower the risk per trade . Self-control very important in these drop down."
And on 2022-02-11 I wrote what happens when the loop is missing:
"the first alarm after 30 trades one losing ... when the door it's closed by now beliefs after 30 trades of losing. the other door will open by the feedback process."

The balancing loop does not stop losses. Nothing does. On 2025-01-04
I wrote, "So its kind of balance rather than trying to eliminate risk
from the equation." The loop only keeps a loss from becoming a
catastrophe.
The tipping point

Which loop runs the account? Most days the balancing loop. But
systems have points where a small push changes everything. Catastrophe
theory studies these jumps. Michael and his old partner Jim had worked
with it, and from 2024 it kept coming back in our letters.
On 2024-12-13 I wrote:
"Catastrophe ... Is a great model to describe the market . I think all other Thoerys just a description. Looks great only in books."

On 2025-05-23 I tried to picture it as two layers, a heavy stone
resting on an egg, and then I connected it to a Goodmanism:

"A stable state is exactly part of the nature of the system , while the catastrophe is outside of the system , destroying the system ... I think Charlie when he says , a small profit is a loss . to prevent a catastrophe."

The clearest version came on 2025-11-06, in a letter about the
smoothie and tracking:

"3c is a point where market conditions are between hope/fear . like a saddle point, just a little from the curve everything will change. followed by a propagation being out of equilibrium point . newborn trend ."

A saddle point is a place that looks still from one direction and
falls away from another. The 3C is that place in the market: buyers and
sellers in equilibrium, but "will not stay forever." The trader has the
same point inside him. After a run of wins he sits on the saddle between
confidence and greed. One step one way and the balancing loop holds. One
step the other way and the reinforcing loop takes over. The rules of
Rung 6 exist to be obeyed at exactly that moment, when they feel least
necessary.
Robustness

A system that works only in good times is not a system. On 2025-02-17
I wrote to Michael from my years as a programmer:

"I think the most important feature in any system is Robustness . When I programming this factor is most important , how my codes stand very well against the errors / Bugs ! ... The system simply is an automatic rule or protocol , that organizes the effort that put in the input to minimum (Simple and fast as possible) at same time increase from the productively (output)."

In the same letter: "What happens to a trader , looks for perfection
, insted we need to think in Systematic approach , make little changes
(enhance) every time . never change the core ."

Robustness is what the balancing loop buys. On 2025-04-20 I wrote
that freedom "is a result of embrace the risk . With the vision of long
run , robustness under difficult time. As well the better times." The
core stays the same, the 1-2-3, the thirty souls, the review. The small
things improve. The system bends and does not break.
The ladder is a circle

When I put the ten rungs on paper as a loop, the last one led back to
the first. Learning changes the trader, and the changed trader is a new
Being who sees the next chart with new eyes. On 2024-05-06 I wrote, "I
did a feedback loop ." and found it better to add to a winning trade in
re-propagation than to look for a new one. That small change came out of
the loop and went back into it.

Figure: The ladder is a circle. The ten rungs read clockwise; the
System feeds back into Being.

Charlie said everything is a 1-2-3. A trader is one too. A beginning,
a tipping point, an end, and the end is the beginning of the next.
Truth: The Goodmanisms

Michael wrote to me on 2022-09-05: "I can't think of a single
Goodmanism that isn't still true!" Here they are, every saying of
Charlie's that reached me in Michael's letters, exactly as he wrote
them, with the date of the letter. Where Michael told the same saying
more than once, I give the first date. Some came as Charlie's own words;
some Michael gave in his own words, and I mark those as reported.

Where I Stand Today

This book climbed a ladder, from being to knowing, seeing, deciding,
acting, measuring, doing right, feeling and learning. Before my last
letter to Michael, I want to say plainly how I trade now, in 2026. Not
how I wish I traded. How I do it.

A small family of charts. I do not watch the whole market. I keep a short list and let it change slowly: EURCAD, GBPAUD, EURAUD, AUDCAD, NZDCAD, gold, silver, sometimes the Nasdaq or Bitcoin. On 2026-06-06 I wrote: "today i added two charts to my watchlist . I picked one . neglect another ." That is the whole job of a watchlist. It is for saying no.

From the most general to the most specific. I start Outward, on the chart where the Propagation is, and move inward only if something there interests me. On 2026-07-11 I shorted EURAUD because "i see it more than 3 propgation in daily chart. Oh its time to short". The daily told me the story was old. The smaller charts told me when.

Two speeds. For quick trades I use FireStarter, on 15-minute charts inside the 4-hour picture. On 2026-06-10 I wrote: "I trade Firestarter in the morning here." On 2026-08-31 I gave Michael three reasons I value it: many trades a month, "high frequency less emotional", and a high win rate with good risk/reward. For the larger trades I still wait for the full setup, a Molokai or a PTS, with an Outward overlay. On 2026-09-08 I passed on EURCAD because I was "waiting for a nest , the bar it's risky. Bad money management", and on a Bitcoin 66 because it had "nice setup but no overlay".

Size is decided before the chart. I still decide my maximum drawdown first and divide it across thirty trades. Every trade spends one soul. In FireStarter the size never changes, in losses or in profits. In my other trading, the Golden Ratios every ten trades tell me whether to keep the size or lower it.

The high-percentage duck. On 2026-07-11 I wrote: "The key for long-term success is to find high percentage duck trade." And the aim inside each trade is still breakeven first. When the stop is at breakeven, I can let the market take its time.

Volume as a witness. I read volume beside price, but only volume that persists. My own indicator, Continuity + Consensus Extreme, lets volume build only while the same side keeps winning, bar after bar, and marks the record peak just before the streak breaks. I described it to Michael on 2026-09-04: "No ratios, no smoothing, no cumulative-forever sums — just raw volume, gated by whether the same side kept winning bar after bar." I also try other views of the same truth. On 2026-09-26 I wrote that I had programmed a Pugh chart on TradingView: "less noise".

Discipline built into the tools. I do not trust my willpower on a bad day. In May 2026 I programmed a trading journal with an automatic alert "if less than golden ratio , or BIG size lot". In September I finished the Poka-Yoke expert, with its twelve layers. The tools hold the rules so that my mind can stay on the chart.

Being proactive. Charlie's question is still my first question: "What do I see now and what do I want to see next!" On 2026-04-28 I wrote back: "Proactive actually affects my life positively." Before a session I mark the charts. During it, I wait for what I said I wanted to see.

What I still study. On 2026-08-13 I wrote: "Sometimes I make several notes: probability, combinations and the chart!. Even if it fails, it gives a hint." I still study Market Environments, the relation between volatility and volume, the logic of abduction, and the Codex. Every course I build teaches me again. "I learn from these courses!! a lot !!!!!" I wrote on 2026-08-22.

On 2026-07-11 I told Michael: "Actually i enjoy goodman. Now become
my second nature." That is where I stand. Fifty years in, the method is
no longer something I apply. It is the way I look. Everything is a
1-2-3.
A Last Letter to Michael
Dear Michael,

The first letter you wrote me began with "Hello - Thank You!" and a
note that the CODEX was a little out of date. That was September 2020. I
answered that every single word of the Goodmanisms must be memorized by
any serious trader. I did not know then that I would spend six years
learning what those words meant, one chart and one letter at a time.

You never explained everything. You did what Charlie did with you:
you showed me a chart, asked a question, and waited. When I sent you
something wrong, you told me. When I sent you something right, you said
Charlie would be pleased. On 2023-03-18 you wrote, "Charlie say,
'Mohamed is Magic Man.'" I laughed, and I kept that line close on the
bad weeks.
On 2025-06-22 you wrote the sentence I read more than any other:
"Everything Goodman soon yours - Friend, Brother, Son Mohamed!"

In the same letter you said that after the article on Abduction and
the Playbook, I would "take over for Charlie and Me." I do not think
anyone takes over for Charlie. But I understood what you were giving me.
Not the books. The responsibility.

On 2025-12-20, when I sent you the Power diagrams, you wrote that you
were "almost in tears. ... What a miracle Charlie and I found you!!!!"
Michael, the miracle was the other way. A man on the other side of the
world wrote to a man in Colorado about a theory almost nobody remembers,
and the man in Colorado answered every letter for six years.
On 2026-09-28 you wrote:
"if it wasn't for you all the stories of charlie would surely be lost!...i don't know if they will ever inspire anyone else - but at least they are preserved!"

This book is my answer. The stories are not mine. They were yours
first, and Charlie's before that. I only kept them in order. You carried
them for fifty years in your head, the bus station, the old woman's
money, the boxcars that did not buck, the lake and the bathtub. I put
them on the ladder so that whoever climbs it after us can hear Charlie's
voice the way you still hear it.

You taught me that the goal is breakeven, that a Setup is set up to
go, that we always leave something for the Line. This book is my Line. I
took the Under over six years of letters. This part I leave running, for
whoever comes next.
Thank you, Master.
Your friend, brother and son,
Mohamed
